Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ: TSLA ) has officially unveiled the awaited Roadster high-performance vehicle , showing off the car's hovering capabilities powered by thrusters from Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ).

In a post on the social media platform X following the Roadster debut event , Musk shared a clip of the vehicle launching itself over a row of Tesla's Cybercab, Cybertruck, the Semi, the Model 3 and the Model Y.
The clip showcased the Roadster's thrusters making the car do a 'barrel roll' mid-air like an aircraft. "Turns out the future does have flying cars," Musk said in the post.
Turns out the future does have flying cars pic.twitter.com/6fexPp6SXI

Influencer and Tesla investor Sawyer Merritt also shared a clip from the Roadster event, which showcased the car climbing up a 90-degree road before it was upside down at the top and flew off the ramp, doing a barrel roll mid-flight, with the thrusters helping to stabilize the car's landing.
OMG the Tesla Roadster just flew in the air! pic.twitter.com/vdIabzyyPx
— Sawyer Merritt (@SawyerMerritt) October 16, 2026

The Roadster features an angular design, which is not as aggressively futuristic as the Cybertruck. The reveal car features an aerospace-inspired 'Ano White' finish, gold-tinted glass and a white interior with a touchscreen infotainment system in the center.

The Roadster, according to Tesla's official website, is available in three trim levels: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. The Performance trim is the base trim with the multi-mode suction system and active aero. It does not feature cold-gas thrusters.
Tesla's U.S. reservation page requires a $50,000 reservation payment for the Performance version, consisting of $5,000 upfront and another $45,000 within 10 days.

On the other hand, Tesla says that the Thrust trim, which will be a limited release , will feature seating for two and its multi-mode suction system paired with cold-gas thrusters that result in an under-1-second 0-60 mph time.

The Rocket trim is currently not approved for public-road use and will feature seating for one and have cold-gas thrusters in the periphery of the vehicle to support "forward" and "upward acceleration" as well as "lateral rotational movement." Tesla says that the trim will also feature the multi-mode suction system and is invite-only.

The multi-mode suction system, according to the automaker, is a "downforce generator" that pulls air out from beneath the vehicle, providing enough "suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary."

CEO Musk, during the launch event, said that the Roadster will enter production in 2028. Tesla also said that the car will feature a range of more than 300 miles and a redesigned steer-by-wire system with a steering yoke.
Tesla also said that the thrusters work with electric actuators and complete "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second" to help stabilize the vehicle in flight.
Price Action: TSLA shares were up 2.93% to $373.06 during overnight trading on Thursday.

passages: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”
Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years.
Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car.
Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.
Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair.
The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026.
Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again.
It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”
Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price.
The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.
The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

extraction.body: Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.” Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion. “This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.” Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car. All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour. Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.” Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels. Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket. Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster. “If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said. “This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’” Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event. In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet. “Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions. Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024. As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again. “Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay. These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman. “They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again.
It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”
Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price.
The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.
The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

sources.title: Tesla reveals pre-production flying Roadster with air thrusters - Autocar India
passages: Tesla has revealed a pre-production electric sports car, called the Roadster, which will enter production in 2028.
It will be available in a standard Performance trim, and Thrust and Rocket packages (or 'augments' in Tesla-speak).
It gets an underbody suction fan for additional grip, and optional air thrusters that help the Roadster perform airborne manoeuvres.
Tesla claims a 0-100kph time of under a second for the new Roadster, although final production powertrain specifications, including battery capacity, motor output and range, are yet to be revealed.
The Rocket version drops the passenger seat to make room for the additional hardware required for its flight system, setting it apart from the two-seat Performance and Thrust versions.
The redesigned pre-production model adopts a more angular, wedge-shaped silhouette like the Tesla Cybertruck, with aircraft-inspired styling from the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-35 fighter jet.
Interestingly, the 2026 Roadster concept has seen a thorough exterior and interior redesign from the 2017 concept, now sporting two seats but missing out on a removable roof.
The thrusters use pressurised cold air expelled through nozzles to generate thrust, allowing the Roadster to briefly lift off the ground and control its movement in the air.
The system is distinct from a conventional rocket engine, as it relies on stored pressurised air rather than burning propellant.
The front gets concealed headlights, while the rear features a full-width LED tail-light and a prominent active rear wing.
Flush-mounted surfaces and slim-spoke wheels contribute to the cleaner design, with the wing adjusting to balance downforce and aerodynamic drag.
Tesla has also introduced an ‘Ano White’ paint finish, alongside gold-tinted glass and titanium accents.
The yoke is designed to work with a steer-by-wire system, while braking and throttle inputs are also electronically controlled.
The interior is finished in white, with grey microsuede detailing and more heavily bolstered seats.

extraction.body: Tesla has revealed a pre-production electric sports car, called the Roadster, which will enter production in 2028. It will be available in a standard Performance trim, and Thrust and Rocket packages (or 'augments' in Tesla-speak). Bookings for the Performance trim and Thrust package are underway in India at Rs 5 lakh, while the Rocket augment is an invite-only programme. It gets an underbody suction fan for additional grip, and optional air thrusters that help the Roadster perform airborne manoeuvres. Interestingly, the 2026 Roadster concept has seen a thorough exterior and interior redesign from the 2017 concept, now sporting two seats but missing out on a removable roof. The upcoming electric sports car will mark the second run for the Roadster nameplate after it was discontinued in 2012. The thrusters use pressurised cold air expelled through nozzles to generate thrust, allowing the Roadster to briefly lift off the ground and control its movement in the air. The system is distinct from a conventional rocket engine, as it relies on stored pressurised air rather than burning propellant. The Performance trim features an underbody suction fan that can generate 2G of grip. As mentioned earlier, it serves as the base for the other two configurations. The Thrust package adds four rear-mounted thrusters, and the Rocket package adds 10 more thrusters, which enable airborne manoeuvres. Tesla claims a 0-100kph time of under a second for the new Roadster, although final production powertrain specifications, including battery capacity, motor output and range, are yet to be revealed. The new design marks a significant departure from the original concept from 2017, which featured a rounded nose, flowing bodywork and a removable glass roof. The redesigned pre-production model adopts a more angular, wedge-shaped silhouette like the Tesla Cybertruck, with aircraft-inspired styling from the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-35 fighter jet. The front gets concealed headlights, while the rear features a full-width LED tail-light and a prominent active rear wing. Flush-mounted surfaces and slim-spoke wheels contribute to the cleaner design, with the wing adjusting to balance downforce and aerodynamic drag. Tesla has also introduced an ‘Ano White’ paint finish, alongside gold-tinted glass and titanium accents. The 2017 Roadster concept featured a curved central touchscreen, a conventional two-plus-two seating layout and a removable glass roof. The redesigned model adopts a more focused, two-seat cabin, with a yoke-style steering unit with physical controls and a central touchscreen. The yoke is designed to work with a steer-by-wire system, while braking and throttle inputs are also electronically controlled. Tesla has opted for a fixed seating position, with the cabin using lightweight materials such as carbon fibre, magnesium and titanium to help keep weight in check. The interior is finished in white, with grey microsuede detailing and more heavily bolstered seats. The Rocket version drops the passenger seat to make room for the additional hardware required for its flight system, setting it apart from the two-seat Performance and Thrust versions. Tesla says the Rocket is “not approved for public road use”, but the road legality of the standard Performance with the suction fan and the Thrust augment, which features additional air thrusters in the rear, is uncertain in India.

Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ: TSLA ) has officially unveiled the awaited Roadster high-performance vehicle , showing off the car's hovering capabilities powered by thrusters from Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ).
CEO Musk, during the launch event, said that the Roadster will enter production in 2028.

In a post on the social media platform X following the Roadster debut event , Musk shared a clip of the vehicle launching itself over a row of Tesla's Cybercab, Cybertruck, the Semi, the Model 3 and the Model Y.

The multi-mode suction system, according to the automaker, is a "downforce generator" that pulls air out from beneath the vehicle, providing enough "suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary."

OMG the Tesla Roadster just flew in the air! pic.twitter.com/vdIabzyyPx
Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”
Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years.
Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car.
Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.
Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair.
The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026.
Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again.

Tesla says that the trim will also feature the multi-mode suction system and is invite-only. — Sawyer Merritt (@SawyerMerritt) October 16, 2026

The Roadster features an angular design, which is not as aggressively futuristic as the Cybertruck. The reveal car features an aerospace-inspired 'Ano White' finish, gold-tinted glass and a white interior with a touchscreen infotainment system in the center.

The Roadster, according to Tesla's official website, is available in three trim levels: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. The Performance trim is the base trim with the multi-mode suction system and active aero. It does not feature cold-gas thrusters.
Tesla's U.S. reservation page requires a $50,000 reservation payment for the Performance version, consisting of $5,000 upfront and another $45,000 within 10 days.

On the other hand, Tesla says that the Thrust trim, which will be a limited release , will feature seating for two and its multi-mode suction system paired with cold-gas thrusters that result in an under-1-second 0-60 mph time.

The Rocket trim is currently not approved for public-road use and will feature seating for one and have cold-gas thrusters in the periphery of the vehicle to support "forward" and "upward acceleration" as well as "lateral rotational movement." Tesla says that the trim will also feature the multi-mode suction system and is invite-only.

The multi-mode suction system, according to the automaker, is a "downforce generator" that pulls air out from beneath the vehicle, providing enough "suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary."

CEO Musk, during the launch event, said that the Roadster will enter production in 2028. Tesla also said that the car will feature a range of more than 300 miles and a redesigned steer-by-wire system with a steering yoke.
Tesla also said that the thrusters work with electric actuators and complete "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second" to help stabilize the vehicle in flight.

extraction.body: Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.” Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion. “This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.” Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car. All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour. Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.” Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels. Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket. Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster. “If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said. “This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’” Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event. In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet. “Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions. Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024. As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again. “Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay. These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman. “They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. Sunday Guardian Live By: Amreen Ahmad Last Updated: October 16, 2026 14:15:24 IST Tesla Roadster Launch Date: The Tesla Roadster makes a comeback in the limelight, but this time the electric supercar aims higher than regular driving. The latest design of the Roadster flew short distances in the air through a technology that Tesla and SpaceX jointly developed. The car was driven upside down along a custom-made ramp, did an in-air rotation and landed successfully in a controlled fly test conducted in Texas. Although the name ‘flying car’ seems to be a little misleading here, this is what the demo showed us as short flights, but nothing more. Tesla’s next generation of Roadster concept was first presented to the public in November 2017, with the deliveries scheduled for 2020. However, due to several delays, Tesla’s Roadster did not appear in showrooms until October 15, 2026, when it was presented. It is important to note that this is still a planned production date rather than a date of deliveries to customers. The final purchase price of the redesigned Roadster has not been firmly confirmed. Reported reservation amounts provide an indication of its premium positioning. These figures represent reported reservation payments, not necessarily the complete vehicle prices. Tesla’s reservation terms explain that final purchase prices may change as configurations are confirmed. The Indian consumer might have to wait past the projected production start date to access the Roadster in India. Up till now, there is no official launch date set by Tesla for India or the showroom price. Additional costs from import taxes, logistics, duties, and homologation processes will further drive up the Indian price. Until Tesla officially announces their availability in India, any price estimate floating on the internet cannot be confirmed as the final price. Performance is one of the key elements behind the attraction of the Roadster. As part of the launch event, Tesla presented acceleration performance that was estimated to get the car from 0 to 60 mph in just 0.81 second as equal to 96.6 km/h. This is an outstanding result, yet it needs to be independently tested in the case of the production car. The previous concept version of the Roadster boasted a distance of about 620 miles or 998 kilometres with a top speed above 250 mph. The re-designed Roadster is a combination of a sleek sports car profile, aerodynamically designed body work and thrust technology. It is a two-seater with proportions focused more on speed than usability. The Roadster’s test run involved an upside-down run on a specially constructed ramp using a suction system. Whether these systems will appear unchanged in customer vehicles remains uncertain. Tesla has not given its final specification on the interior of the new Roadster. It is fair to expect the cockpit of the vehicle to be designed for performance and have digital control of the vehicle and a minimalist approach; however, one should take into consideration that these are just assumptions about the equipment of the car and not something confirmed. However, there is no definitive list of the colours for the redesigned Tesla Roadster since this is still not officially disclosed. The white-coloured version exhibited during the reveal event does not provide a clue on how many colour choices would be offered to customers. The Roadster’s most unusual feature is its cold-gas thruster system, developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Unlike conventional cars, which rely on their tyres to maintain contact with the road, the system uses compressed gas to help the vehicle perform brief aerial manoeuvres. During the Texas demonstration, the Roadster lifted off, performed a rotation and returned to the ground. The company also showcased the vehicle jumping over a row of Tesla models. sources.title: Tesla reveals pre-production flying Roadster with air thrusters - Autocar India
passages: Tesla has revealed a pre-production electric sports car, called the Roadster, which will enter production in 2028.
It will be available in a standard Performance trim, and Thrust and Rocket packages (or 'augments' in Tesla-speak).
It gets an underbody suction fan for additional grip, and optional air thrusters that help the Roadster perform airborne manoeuvres.
Tesla claims a 0-100kph time of under a second for the new Roadster, although final production powertrain specifications, including battery capacity, motor output and range, are yet to be revealed.
The Rocket version drops the passenger seat to make room for the additional hardware required for its flight system, setting it apart from the two-seat Performance and Thrust versions.
The redesigned pre-production model adopts a more angular, wedge-shaped silhouette like the Tesla Cybertruck, with aircraft-inspired styling from the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-35 fighter jet.
Interestingly, the 2026 Roadster concept has seen a thorough exterior and interior redesign from the 2017 concept, now sporting two seats but missing out on a removable roof.
The thrusters use pressurised cold air expelled through nozzles to generate thrust, allowing the Roadster to briefly lift off the ground and control its movement in the air.
The system is distinct from a conventional rocket engine, as it relies on stored pressurised air rather than burning propellant.
The front gets concealed headlights, while the rear features a full-width LED tail-light and a prominent active rear wing.
Flush-mounted surfaces and slim-spoke wheels contribute to the cleaner design, with the wing adjusting to balance downforce and aerodynamic drag.
Tesla has also introduced an ‘Ano White’ paint finish, alongside gold-tinted glass and titanium accents.
The yoke is designed to work with a steer-by-wire system, while braking and throttle inputs are also electronically controlled.
The interior is finished in white, with grey microsuede detailing and more heavily bolstered seats.

extraction.body: Tesla has revealed a pre-production electric sports car, called the Roadster, which will enter production in 2028. It will be available in a standard Performance trim, and Thrust and Rocket packages (or 'augments' in Tesla-speak). Bookings for the Performance trim and Thrust package are underway in India at Rs 5 lakh, while the Rocket augment is an invite-only programme. It gets an underbody suction fan for additional grip, and optional air thrusters that help the Roadster perform airborne manoeuvres. Interestingly, the 2026 Roadster concept has seen a thorough exterior and interior redesign from the 2017 concept, now sporting two seats but missing out on a removable roof. The upcoming electric sports car will mark the second run for the Roadster nameplate after it was discontinued in 2012. The thrusters use pressurised cold air expelled through nozzles to generate thrust, allowing the Roadster to briefly lift off the ground and control its movement in the air. The system is distinct from a conventional rocket engine, as it relies on stored pressurised air rather than burning propellant. The Performance trim features an underbody suction fan that can generate 2G of grip. As mentioned earlier, it serves as the base for the other two configurations. The Thrust package adds four rear-mounted thrusters, and the Rocket package adds 10 more thrusters, which enable airborne manoeuvres. Tesla claims a 0-100kph time of under a second for the new Roadster, although final production powertrain specifications, including battery capacity, motor output and range, are yet to be revealed. The new design marks a significant departure from the original concept from 2017, which featured a rounded nose, flowing bodywork and a removable glass roof. The redesigned pre-production model adopts a more angular, wedge-shaped silhouette like the Tesla Cybertruck, with aircraft-inspired styling from the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-35 fighter jet. The front gets concealed headlights, while the rear features a full-width LED tail-light and a prominent active rear wing. Flush-mounted surfaces and slim-spoke wheels contribute to the cleaner design, with the wing adjusting to balance downforce and aerodynamic drag. Tesla has also introduced an ‘Ano White’ paint finish, alongside gold-tinted glass and titanium accents. The 2017 Roadster concept featured a curved central touchscreen, a conventional two-plus-two seating layout and a removable glass roof. The redesigned model adopts a more focused, two-seat cabin, with a yoke-style steering unit with physical controls and a central touchscreen. The yoke is designed to work with a steer-by-wire system, while braking and throttle inputs are also electronically controlled. Tesla has opted for a fixed seating position, with the cabin using lightweight materials such as carbon fibre, magnesium and titanium to help keep weight in check. The interior is finished in white, with grey microsuede detailing and more heavily bolstered seats. The Rocket version drops the passenger seat to make room for the additional hardware required for its flight system, setting it apart from the two-seat Performance and Thrust versions. Tesla says the Rocket is “not approved for public road use”, but the road legality of the standard Performance with the suction fan and the Thrust augment, which features additional air thrusters in the rear, is uncertain in India.

extraction.body: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children. A notification from Snapchat, one of the ten platforms affected, had lit up her screen, warning she'd be booted off when the law kicked in this week – if she couldn't prove she was over 16. Though she had let Isobel use TikTok and Snapchat with tight supervision – preferring that to the teenager using it covertly – she had been hoping the ban, as promised, would help parents like her protect their children from the dangers of the online world. That hope has now wavered, as a series of experts – and kids themselves – sound the alarm on the viability and safety of the landmark policy, which is being closely watched around the globe and eyed with trepidation by some of its most influential companies. There's concern about the reliability of the technology enforcing the ban, along with fears it could isolate vulnerable children and push others into darker, less-regulated corners of the web. The question nervously being asked in the halls of Canberra, in households across the nation, and in tech boardrooms around the world: is this actually going to work? You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms. Their protestations to the contrary fall on unsympathetic ears. "We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC. The pair were among the parents and public figures who lent their voices to a headline-grabbing national campaign calling for a new minimum age for social media. Some experts, including Australia's online safety tsar, warned banning children from social media was not the solution, but their concerns were swept away by a tide of parental passion and political pressure. In November 2024, the prime minister announced the legislation, promising parents and children wouldn't be penalised. It'd be up to the platforms to take "reasonable steps" to ensure account-holders were at least 16 years old, or face fines of up to $49.5m (US$33m, £25m) for the most serious breaches. "This one is for the mums and dads... They, like me, are worried sick about the safety of our kids online," Anthony Albanese said. The policy – limited versions of which have been attempted with little success by other jurisdictions around the world – would help free children from addictive algorithms exposing them to harmful content like violence, pornography and misinformation, proponents said. It would also reduce cyber-bullying and online child exploitation. It would force kids outside, help them sleep better, improve their physical and mental health, it was suggested. Noticeably absent from Albanese's announcement was a plan on exactly how the government was going to do this – it gave itself a year to work that out. A government-funded, industry-run trial looked at the main methods of age assurance and earlier this year reported all were technically possible – but none were foolproof and all carried risks. Verification using IDs was the most accurate approach, but that requires users to hand over sensitive and important documents when polling shows most Australians don't trust social media firms. Age inference, which draws conclusions based on users' online activity, and facial assessment technology both lacked the precision to be reliably applied to teenagers. Its findings weren't without controversy. Two former advisory board members levelled accusations of bias and "privacy-washing". And though the trial considered ways teenagers might bypass barriers, it was not tasked with testing them. Tips have flooded social media: everything from signing up with a parent's email and moving to platforms not explicitly named on the government's hit list, to using VPNs, which can disguise a user's location. There was a temporary surge in VPN use in the UK after it introduced tougher age checks for pornography earlier this year, and experts are expecting the same here. Polling conducted for the government in May indicated a third of parents intended to help their kids circumvent the ban, and an experiment by the University of Melbourne showed that a $22 Halloween mask was enough to defeat facial assessment technology in some cases. "If I do end up getting banned, I'll just find another app to use." That's up for discussion, Mel clarifies. But she and a host of others fear the platforms and the regulator are set for a relentless game of "whack-a-mole" – identifying and shutting down loophole after loophole, and listing emerging platforms only for kids to flock to another. The social media firms also have a motive to subtly undermine the policy, lest other countries follow suit, analysts say, and the vague "reasonable steps" outlined by the government leave the door ajar. "They're going to try to drive a truck through [it]," says Stephen Scheeler, who led Facebook in Australia and New Zealand between 2013 and 2017. The key question is not can children get around it, Mr Allen says; that answer is yes. But will enough of them be bothered to? "To be a successful policy, it doesn't have to get to a point where 100% of children aren't on social media," he says. "It only really has to get about 80% of them and the rest will follow." Some exasperated parents just want to be able to say it is illegal. They don't want their kids to feel entitled – or pressured – to access social media. "We've always said, whether the law was enforceable or not, our main aim in all of this was to establish a new social norm," Mr Elachi says. "You're not stopping behaviour, you're just moving that behaviour to other platforms," says Tim Levy, head of online safety company Qoria and one of the trial advisers who quit. "Telling the concerned Australian parents that it's all good now is a very dangerous message." The science on social media and health is complex and still evolving too. Alongside the studies linking it to poor outcomes is also evidence it can be a lifeline for some children, particularly for those from LGBTQ+, neurodivergent or rural communities. "We've heard very little officially about what is being done to address the unmet needs of these more vulnerable children who for positive reasons have sought help or a sense of belonging and connection online," former children's commissioner Anne Hollonds tells the BBC. Before her agency was officially charged with implementing this policy, eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman-Grant made similar arguments. "We do not fence the ocean or keep children entirely out of the water, but we do create protected swimming environments that provide safeguards and teach important lessons from a young age," she said in June last year. To that, Minister Wells counters: "We can police the sharks" – a biting reference to social media firms. Many of the critics are right about the challenges ahead, she told the BBC. But this is just a starting point – a digital duty of care, a legal obligation that firms prevent foreseeable harm to their users, is next on her list. The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.

extraction.body: Age gates can be staggeringly counterproductive, pushing kids to darker corners of the web. Closing loopholes will only make things worse. Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked. Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences. Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place. For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want. Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands. Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business. Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are. Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization's work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census . Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

passages: Azerbaijan has joined a growing list of countries imposing social media restrictions on minors, passing a law that bars under-16s from platforms at a time when governments worldwide are questioning whether the digital industry can regulate itself.Australia became the first country to implement a nationwide social media ban for children under 16.France has tightened its laws on the age of digital consent, the UK passed the Online Safety Bill, and the EU has been increasing pressure on technology companies.Now Baku has decided to move in the same direction.Social media addiction, self-esteem problems and cyberbullying are producing documented psychological consequences among teenagers.

They organise social experience, and they shape habits before beliefs, and attention before judgment."Nazarova described recent legislation as an attempt by states to rebuild protective barriers around childhood that digital feeds had dismantled."From this perspective, the proposed age limit in Azerbaijan reflects a transformation in the way states understand their role," she said.The practical test of Azerbaijan's law, experts agree, will come after its adoption: whether the restrictions can be enforced in practice, and whether they are accompanied by the education and support structures needed to change behaviour rather than simply push it underground.

"Schools should focus on replacing screen time with meaningful digital activities, such as programming, robotics, and media literacy clubs," Dadashova explained."While a social media ban can offer positive effects, the real solution lies in cultivating healthy digital behaviour and real-world communication skills."What do digital platforms actually do?Laman Nazarova, a geopolitical analyst at the Caspian Analytical Centre, argued that the legislative push reflected a broader reassessment of what digital platforms actually do."Platforms have become one of the main environments where children acquire language, values, and social norms," Nazarova told Euronews.These functions previously belonged to families and schools, she added.

Unlike bullying, online harassment follows children into their homes and is harder to escape.Narmina Ismayilzada, a child and adolescent psychologist with 16 years of experience, told Euronews teenagers exposed to digital bullying frequently develop "a very strong sense of shame, decreased self-confidence, and anxiety," leading to social isolation and school avoidance.She supports state-level age restrictions but warns that a ban alone will not solve the underlying problems."Prohibiting something at this age can create reverse psychology," Ismayilzada said."Children show more interest in what is prohibited and may try to use these things in hidden ways," she pointed out."If parents forbid something without explaining the reasoning behind it, children simply hide their actions.

A healthy approach requires supervision paired with mutual trust and open dialogue."She said algorithmic feeds exploit adolescents' heightened sensitivity to physical appearance and social acceptance, damaging attention spans and academic motivation."Concentration problems and divided attention are among our most serious issues today.

It makes them more aggressive and impulsive," Ismayilzada said."When children compare themselves to idealised images on social networks, it naturally leads to self-confidence problems, body-image dissatisfaction, and, in worst cases, depressive symptoms."The solution, she said, begins at home.

It makes them more aggressive and impulsive," Ismayilzada said."When children compare themselves to idealised images on social networks, it naturally leads to self-confidence problems, body-image dissatisfaction, and, in worst cases, depressive symptoms."The solution, she said, begins at home.

If a proper emotional connection is established, then every word the parent says will be accepted normally by the adolescent," Ismayilzada said.How to teach children to use the internet safelyThe debate among politicians and psychologists looks different from the perspective of teachers.

VPNs and fake birth dates are widely used by children, and the gap between legislation and technical enforcement remains significant.Kamala Dadashova, an informatics and digital skills teacher at School No.

161, said the ban addressed real problems she observed every day — peer comparison, "like" dependency, cyberbullying and disrupted sleep — but questioned whether restriction alone was the right frame."The aim should not be to distance children from the internet, but to prepare them to use it safely," Dadashova told Euronews.
"In the 21st century, escaping the digital environment is impossible; the priority is making it safer.""Furthermore, it is wrong to place the entire burden solely on the child or the parents.
Platforms themselves have an obligation to create safe environments for minors," Dadashova said.She said schools needed to go beyond restricting access.

"Schools should focus on replacing screen time with meaningful digital activities, such as programming, robotics, and media literacy clubs," Dadashova explained."While a social media ban can offer positive effects, the real solution lies in cultivating healthy digital behaviour and real-world communication skills."What do digital platforms actually do?Laman Nazarova, a geopolitical analyst at the Caspian Analytical Centre, argued that the legislative push reflected a broader reassessment of what digital platforms actually do."Platforms have become one of the main environments where children acquire language, values, and social norms," Nazarova told Euronews.These functions previously belonged to families and schools, she added.
"Governments have begun to recognise that digital platforms do not merely transmit information.

They organise social experience, and they shape habits before beliefs, and attention before judgment."Nazarova described recent legislation as an attempt by states to rebuild protective barriers around childhood that digital feeds had dismantled."From this perspective, the proposed age limit in Azerbaijan reflects a transformation in the way states understand their role," she said.The practical test of Azerbaijan's law, experts agree, will come after its adoption: whether the restrictions can be enforced in practice, and whether they are accompanied by the education and support structures needed to change behaviour rather than simply push it underground.

coreStoryFacts.text: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children.
You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms.
Their protestations to the contrary fall on unsympathetic ears.
"To be a successful policy, it doesn't have to get to a point where 100% of children aren't on social media," he says.

The social media firms also have a motive to subtly undermine the policy, lest other countries follow suit, analysts say, and the vague "reasonable steps" outlined by the government leave the door ajar.
"They're going to try to drive a truck through [it]," says Stephen Scheeler, who led Facebook in Australia and New Zealand between 2013 and 2017.
They don't want their kids to feel entitled – or pressured – to access social media.
The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.
"We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC.
Many of the critics are right about the challenges ahead, she told the BBC.
Indonesia is set to become the second country to outright ban children under 16 from using major social media platforms.
Australia imposed similar restrictions last year, and laws banning social media for kids are advancing across Europe.

In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.
When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services.
The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations.

In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents.

When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence.
It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities .

extraction.body: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children. A notification from Snapchat, one of the ten platforms affected, had lit up her screen, warning she'd be booted off when the law kicked in this week – if she couldn't prove she was over 16. Though she had let Isobel use TikTok and Snapchat with tight supervision – preferring that to the teenager using it covertly – she had been hoping the ban, as promised, would help parents like her protect their children from the dangers of the online world. That hope has now wavered, as a series of experts – and kids themselves – sound the alarm on the viability and safety of the landmark policy, which is being closely watched around the globe and eyed with trepidation by some of its most influential companies. There's concern about the reliability of the technology enforcing the ban, along with fears it could isolate vulnerable children and push others into darker, less-regulated corners of the web. The question nervously being asked in the halls of Canberra, in households across the nation, and in tech boardrooms around the world: is this actually going to work? You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms. "We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC. The policy – limited versions of which have been attempted with little success by other jurisdictions around the world – would help free children from addictive algorithms exposing them to harmful content like violence, pornography and misinformation, proponents said. Noticeably absent from Albanese's announcement was a plan on exactly how the government was going to do this – it gave itself a year to work that out. Polling conducted for the government in May indicated a third of parents intended to help their kids circumvent the ban, and an experiment by the University of Melbourne showed that a $22 Halloween mask was enough to defeat facial assessment technology in some cases. "They're going to try to drive a truck through [it]," says Stephen Scheeler, who led Facebook in Australia and New Zealand between 2013 and 2017. Some exasperated parents just want to be able to say it is illegal. They don't want their kids to feel entitled – or pressured – to access social media. To that, Minister Wells counters: "We can police the sharks" – a biting reference to social media firms. Many of the critics are right about the challenges ahead, she told the BBC. But this is just a starting point – a digital duty of care, a legal obligation that firms prevent foreseeable harm to their users, is next on her list. extraction.body: Age gates can be staggeringly counterproductive, pushing kids to darker corners of the web. Closing loopholes will only make things worse. Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked. Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences. Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place. For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want. Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands. Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business. Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are. Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization's work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census . Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

passages: Azerbaijan has joined a growing list of countries imposing social media restrictions on minors, passing a law that bars under-16s from platforms at a time when governments worldwide are questioning whether the digital industry can regulate itself.Australia became the first country to implement a nationwide social media ban for children under 16.France has tightened its laws on the age of digital consent, the UK passed the Online Safety Bill, and the EU has been increasing pressure on technology companies.Now Baku has decided to move in the same direction.Social media addiction, self-esteem problems and cyberbullying are producing documented psychological consequences among teenagers.

They organise social experience, and they shape habits before beliefs, and attention before judgment."Nazarova described recent legislation as an attempt by states to rebuild protective barriers around childhood that digital feeds had dismantled."From this perspective, the proposed age limit in Azerbaijan reflects a transformation in the way states understand their role," she said.The practical test of Azerbaijan's law, experts agree, will come after its adoption: whether the restrictions can be enforced in practice, and whether they are accompanied by the education and support structures needed to change behaviour rather than simply push it underground.

"Schools should focus on replacing screen time with meaningful digital activities, such as programming, robotics, and media literacy clubs," Dadashova explained."While a social media ban can offer positive effects, the real solution lies in cultivating healthy digital behaviour and real-world communication skills."What do digital platforms actually do?Laman Nazarova, a geopolitical analyst at the Caspian Analytical Centre, argued that the legislative push reflected a broader reassessment of what digital platforms actually do."Platforms have become one of the main environments where children acquire language, values, and social norms," Nazarova told Euronews.These functions previously belonged to families and schools, she added.

Unlike bullying, online harassment follows children into their homes and is harder to escape.Narmina Ismayilzada, a child and adolescent psychologist with 16 years of experience, told Euronews teenagers exposed to digital bullying frequently develop "a very strong sense of shame, decreased self-confidence, and anxiety," leading to social isolation and school avoidance.She supports state-level age restrictions but warns that a ban alone will not solve the underlying problems."Prohibiting something at this age can create reverse psychology," Ismayilzada said."Children show more interest in what is prohibited and may try to use these things in hidden ways," she pointed out."If parents forbid something without explaining the reasoning behind it, children simply hide their actions.

A healthy approach requires supervision paired with mutual trust and open dialogue."She said algorithmic feeds exploit adolescents' heightened sensitivity to physical appearance and social acceptance, damaging attention spans and academic motivation."Concentration problems and divided attention are among our most serious issues today.

It makes them more aggressive and impulsive," Ismayilzada said."When children compare themselves to idealised images on social networks, it naturally leads to self-confidence problems, body-image dissatisfaction, and, in worst cases, depressive symptoms."The solution, she said, begins at home.
