extraction.body: Apple and Meta have worked together to run Metas new Muse Spark Open AI model entirely on Mac Studio hardware, with no cloud servers involved. It is an unusual partnership, given how often the two companies have clashed over privacy and advertising. Here, though, both have something to gain.Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model that Meta announced on October 15. The model is huge, as it has 816 billion parameters, with 42 billion active at any time, and its compressed weights alone take up about 493GB.You will need more than one Mac StudioA single Mac cannot hold a model this big. Apple says you need either two M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 512GB of unified memory each, or four with 256GB each. The four-machine setup works today, while the 512GB configuration ships only in late October.Apples open-source MLX framework splits the model across the connected Macs, which talk to each other over Thunderbolt 5. In Apples own tests, four Mac Studios generated more than 36 tokens per second. In demos, the model fixed bugs in an open-source iOS app and cut vertical clips from footage in DaVinci Resolve, all on local hardware.The catch is the price. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio starts at Rs 6,29,900 in India, so four base units alone cost over Rs 25 lakh before any memory upgrades. This is clearly meant for developers, research labs and companies that do not want sensitive code leaving the office.What is the Windows equivalent?On the PC side, the closest match is Nvidias DGX Station for Windows, which Nvidia built with Microsoft and announced at Computex 2026. It runs on the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra chip with up to 748GB of memory, enough to fit a model like Muse Spark Open in a single box instead of four. Meta says Muse Spark Open also supports Nvidia, AMD and Intel hardware, but it has not shown the model running on a Windows workstation yet.For regular PC buyers, a model this size is out of reach on any platform. Laptops and mini PCs with AMDs Ryzen AI Max chips and 128GB of memory can run smaller open models. That includes Metas own 30-billion-parameter Muse Glimmer, which was released in August and runs on a single GPU.Muse Spark Open is available on Hugging Face, and developers without the hardware can use it through hosted API providers.

extraction.body: India’s information-technology stocks are poised to beat their global semiconductor rivals by the most in two decades this week, with analysts saying the sector is set to keep outperforming as the artificial-intelligence rally unwinds. An index of India’s biggest software exporters surged over 10% week, while a MSCI gauge of global chip stocks tumbled 7.4%, putting the former on course for the biggest weekly outperformance since 2004. AI shares have tumbled in recent days as slowing revenue growth, concerns about infrastructure financing, and renewed fears of rate hikes have fueled concerns that the companies are overvalued. “If the correction in semiconductors gains momentum, as it has this week, foreign investors will start looking at Indian IT stocks,” said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia strategist at Societe Generale SA in Bengaluru. “We could probably see the end of de-rating in these companies, which itself should bring stability.” There have also been some positive signs for IT shares. HCL Technologies Ltd. raised its full-year sales growth guidance this week, while Ireland-based Accenture Plc said it expects to increase revenue growth and profit margins through 2029. India’s largest IT firms were swept up in a global selloff in software stocks earlier this year, as some investors feared that AI could disrupt their business models. Slowing revenue growth amid geopolitical concerns and rising client demand for lower prices also sapped investor sentiment. On Friday, Nifty IT Index gained as much as 3% in early trading, extending an advance to the fourth day. The gauge has climbed over 22% from its July low, but it’s still down about 17% this year, putting it on track for its worst annual performance since 2022. “Although valuations appear reasonable now, on a relative and absolute basis, the sector lacks near-term catalysts,” Morgan Stanley analysts led by Gaurav Rateria wrote in a note this week. The latest survey of chief information officers globally showed stable growth in 2027, and together with Accenture’s earnings, that points to steady-to-decelerating revenue growth for Indian IT firms, the Morgan Stanley analysts said. Still, software stocks are now the cheapest they have been since the pandemic year. Stocks in the Nifty IT Index trade at less than 17 times their one-year forward earnings, nearly two standard deviations below the five-year average. The sector’s bellwether, Infosys Ltd., is due to release its second-quarter earnings and commentary on Oct. 23, with the Bengaluru-based firm expected to report revenue growth of just 1.8%. Looking ahead, at least some in the market see a longer rebound. “An analysis of major innovations in the past indicates that while early stages of transition did witness a slowdown, it was immediately followed by a longer period of growth,” said Sumanta Khan, fund manager for equity at Edelweiss Asset Management Ltd. An index of India’s biggest software exporters surged over 10% week, while a MSCI gauge of global chip stocks tumbled 7.4%, putting the former on course for the biggest weekly outperformance since 2004. AI shares have tumbled in recent days as slowing revenue growth, concerns about infrastructure financing, and renewed fears of rate hikes have fueled concerns that the companies are overvalued.

“If the correction in semiconductors gains momentum, as it has this week, foreign investors will start looking at Indian IT stocks,” said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia strategist at Societe Generale SA in Bengaluru. “We could probably see the end of de-rating in these companies, which itself should bring stability.”

There have also been some positive signs for IT shares. HCL Technologies Ltd. raised its full-year sales growth guidance this week, while Ireland-based Accenture Plc said it expects to increase revenue growth and profit margins through 2029.

India’s largest IT firms were swept up in a global selloff in software stocks earlier this year, as some investors feared that AI could disrupt their business models. Slowing revenue growth amid geopolitical concerns and rising client demand for lower prices also sapped investor sentiment.

On Friday, Nifty IT Index gained as much as 3% in early trading, extending an advance to the fourth day. The gauge has climbed over 22% from its July low, but it’s still down about 17% this year, putting it on track for its worst annual performance since 2022.
“Although valuations appear reasonable now, on a relative and absolute basis, the sector lacks near-term catalysts,” Morgan Stanley analysts led by Gaurav Rateria wrote in a note this week.

The latest survey of chief information officers globally showed stable growth in 2027, and together with Accenture’s earnings, that points to steady-to-decelerating revenue growth for Indian IT firms, the Morgan Stanley analysts said.

Still, software stocks are now the cheapest they have been since the pandemic year. Stocks in the Nifty IT Index trade at less than 17 times their one-year forward earnings, nearly two standard deviations below the five-year average.
The sector’s bellwether, Infosys Ltd., is due to release its second-quarter earnings and commentary on Oct. 23, with the Bengaluru-based firm expected to report revenue growth of just 1.8%.
Looking ahead, at least some in the market see a longer rebound.

“An analysis of major innovations in the past indicates that while early stages of transition did witness a slowdown, it was immediately followed by a longer period of growth,” said Sumanta Khan, fund manager for equity at Edelweiss Asset Management Ltd.

“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”

extraction.body: Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences. The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform , which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build. These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.” The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era. Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this. “Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.” When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles. To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang. “Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.” That network today has 47 million registered users , though it’s seen a decline in engagement , as some users who tested it out later returned to X. Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said. “There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.” Get 50% off a second pass Cover more ground at TechCrunch’s ultimate founder bootcamp of the year by bringing your co-founder or partner. passages: Bluesky is expanding its AI-powered Attie platform to let users create websites, games, polls, quizzes, and other interactive experiences using simple text prompts.

extraction.body: Bluesky is expanding its AI-powered Attie platform to let users create websites, games, polls, quizzes, and other interactive experiences using simple text prompts. Announced at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on October 15, the update moves Attie beyond its original focus on personalised social feeds, giving users a way to build small digital experiences and share them with online communities without traditional coding skills. The expansion reflects a broader shift in AI-powered software development, where people can describe what they want to create and let AI handle much of the technical work. But Bluesky is positioning Attie differently from conventional AI coding tools: its goal is to make creating experiences for groups and communities as accessible as building something for yourself. When Attie launched in March 2026, it focused on helping users create custom feeds by describing the content they wanted to see. The new capabilities expand that concept into lightweight applications that can be generated from prompts and shared through individual website links. Examples include quizzes, interactive polls, simple games, dashboards, and a music-making drum machine. Bluesky has also showcased Flappy Butterfly, a game inspired by the familiar Flappy Bird format, alongside other experimental projects. Each creation receives its own link on the attie.site domain, with attribution identifying its creator. Users can describe an idea in everyday language rather than manually writing code. Attie then generates an experience that can be refined and shared with others. The platform also connects creations to the user’s identity within the AT Protocol ecosystem, which supports Bluesky and other decentralised social applications. Attie remains an experimental creation tool rather than a replacement for professional software development platforms. The early examples are generally lightweight experiences, but they demonstrate how AI can lower the barrier to creating interactive digital content. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider described the concept as “social vibe coding”, an approach that shifts AI-assisted creation from a mostly individual activity towards making things for groups of people. Much of the current enthusiasm around AI coding centres on individuals building websites, prototypes, and applications with assistance from AI models. However, creating something useful is only part of the challenge. Developers and creators must also find people willing to use it. Bluesky believes its existing social network could help address that problem. Users can create experiences for their friends, interest groups, and wider communities, then share them through a platform where those audiences already interact. The company’s chief operating officer, Rose Wang, has highlighted distribution as one of the major obstacles facing AI-powered creation tools. Attie’s connection to Bluesky provides a potential advantage by linking the building process to an existing social network rather than leaving every creator to find an audience independently. For example, a community could build a quiz around a shared interest, create a poll to settle a disagreement, or develop a small interactive game for its members. Instead of every interaction taking place through posts and replies, users could participate in experiences designed specifically for their group. Attie’s connection to the AT Protocol, commonly known as ATProto, is another important part of the strategy. The protocol underpins Bluesky and a wider collection of decentralised social applications, creating an ecosystem in which services can connect through shared infrastructure. By building Attie around this ecosystem, Bluesky can tie user-created experiences to identities and communities beyond a standalone AI application. The approach also supports the company’s broader interest in encouraging developers to build products and services on top of its technology. Attie also gives users flexibility in their AI workflows, with the option to bring their own AI model or use open-weight alternatives. This could appeal to creators who want more control over the tools they use, although the usefulness of the resulting experiences will depend on their quality and how well they work for other users. Bluesky has also said that support for private data is being tested in alpha, with a wider rollout planned by the end of 2026. That development could expand what developers can build across the ecosystem, although the precise implications for Attie-created experiences remain to be seen. The expansion comes as Bluesky looks for ways to strengthen activity beyond its main social networking app. The network had approximately 47 million registered users at the time of the announcement, although reporting has pointed to softer engagement after an earlier period of growth. Attie offers a potential way to give users more reasons to participate. Instead of visiting Bluesky only to read posts, share opinions, or follow conversations, communities could create and interact with small digital experiences connected to their interests. The strategy also gives Bluesky an opportunity to attract users interested in AI-assisted creation, even if they are not primarily looking for another social network. Creators could use Attie to experiment with ideas, share projects, and connect those experiences with communities already active across the AT Protocol ecosystem. There are limitations, however. Generating a simple game or poll is different from building a reliable application that can support complex features, substantial traffic, or sensitive user data. The initial examples demonstrate accessibility and experimentation, but sustained adoption will depend on whether users find enough practical value to return regularly. Attie also needs to prove that its connection to Bluesky creates meaningful distribution rather than simply giving creators another place to publish links. Ultimately, the expansion shows how Bluesky is exploring AI as more than a tool for recommending content or personalising feeds. By allowing users to create small interactive experiences for their communities, the company is testing whether social platforms can become places where people not only communicate but also build things together. The opportunity is to make creation more accessible while giving those creations an audience. Whether Attie becomes a lasting part of the decentralised social web will depend on how successfully Bluesky turns that idea into useful experiences that communities want to keep sharing. coreStoryFacts.text: The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform , which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds.
With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app.
At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.

“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”
Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.
When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity.
Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.

These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.
Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers.
Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.
Bluesky expanded its experimental artificial intelligence application Attie so users can create sites, games, quizzes, and other interactive experiences.

TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 hosted the announcement, and Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider described the approach as “social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.” Bluesky tied Attie creations to AT Protocol (ATProto), and the tool positioned those projects as experiences for groups rather than only for organizing what one person sees.
Bluesky expands Attie for creating websites and games with AI — TechCrunch
The Verge described Attie as letting people make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that can be shared with others as their own websites.
Bluesky COO Rose Wang said the resulting sites and games can tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, while Bluesky also linked Attie builders to their ATProto identity.
Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more

Bluesky framed Attie’s expansion as a shift from AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds toward everyday users creating experiences that previously required software development skills.
Bluesky said the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data was a major request from developers, and Schneider said private data was “now in alpha testing.”
Bluesky’s AI tool now lets you make games and apps to share on social

Announced at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on October 15, the update moves Attie beyond its original focus on personalised social feeds, giving users a way to build small digital experiences and share them with online communities without traditional coding skills. The expansion reflects a broader shift in AI-powered software development, where people can describe what they want to create and let AI handle much of the technical work. But Bluesky is positioning Attie differently from conventional AI coding tools: its goal is to make creating experiences for groups and communities as accessible as building something for yourself. When Attie launched in March 2026, it focused on helping users create custom feeds by describing the content they wanted to see. The new capabilities expand that concept into lightweight applications that can be generated from prompts and shared through individual website links. Examples include quizzes, interactive polls, simple games, dashboards, and a music-making drum machine. Bluesky has also showcased Flappy Butterfly, a game inspired by the familiar Flappy Bird format, alongside other experimental projects. Each creation receives its own link on the attie.site domain, with attribution identifying its creator. Users can describe an idea in everyday language rather than manually writing code. Attie then generates an experience that can be refined and shared with others. The platform also connects creations to the user’s identity within the AT Protocol ecosystem, which supports Bluesky and other decentralised social applications. Attie remains an experimental creation tool rather than a replacement for professional software development platforms. The early examples are generally lightweight experiences, but they demonstrate how AI can lower the barrier to creating interactive digital content. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider described the concept as “social vibe coding”, an approach that shifts AI-assisted creation from a mostly individual activity towards making things for groups of people. Much of the current enthusiasm around AI coding centres on individuals building websites, prototypes, and applications with assistance from AI models. However, creating something useful is only part of the challenge. Developers and creators must also find people willing to use it. Bluesky believes its existing social network could help address that problem. Users can create experiences for their friends, interest groups, and wider communities, then share them through a platform where those audiences already interact. The company’s chief operating officer, Rose Wang, has highlighted distribution as one of the major obstacles facing AI-powered creation tools. Attie’s connection to Bluesky provides a potential advantage by linking the building process to an existing social network rather than leaving every creator to find an audience independently. For example, a community could build a quiz around a shared interest, create a poll to settle a disagreement, or develop a small interactive game for its members. Instead of every interaction taking place through posts and replies, users could participate in experiences designed specifically for their group. Attie’s connection to the AT Protocol, commonly known as ATProto, is another important part of the strategy. The protocol underpins Bluesky and a wider collection of decentralised social applications, creating an ecosystem in which services can connect through shared infrastructure. By building Attie around this ecosystem, Bluesky can tie user-created experiences to identities and communities beyond a standalone AI application. The approach also supports the company’s broader interest in encouraging developers to build products and services on top of its technology. Attie also gives users flexibility in their AI workflows, with the option to bring their own AI model or use open-weight alternatives. This could appeal to creators who want more control over the tools they use, although the usefulness of the resulting experiences will depend on their quality and how well they work for other users. Bluesky has also said that support for private data is being tested in alpha, with a wider rollout planned by the end of 2026. That development could expand what developers can build across the ecosystem, although the precise implications for Attie-created experiences remain to be seen. The expansion comes as Bluesky looks for ways to strengthen activity beyond its main social networking app. The network had approximately 47 million registered users at the time of the announcement, although reporting has pointed to softer engagement after an earlier period of growth. Attie offers a potential way to give users more reasons to participate. Instead of visiting Bluesky only to read posts, share opinions, or follow conversations, communities could create and interact with small digital experiences connected to their interests. The strategy also gives Bluesky an opportunity to attract users interested in AI-assisted creation, even if they are not primarily looking for another social network. Creators could use Attie to experiment with ideas, share projects, and connect those experiences with communities already active across the AT Protocol ecosystem. There are limitations, however. Generating a simple game or poll is different from building a reliable application that can support complex features, substantial traffic, or sensitive user data. The initial examples demonstrate accessibility and experimentation, but sustained adoption will depend on whether users find enough practical value to return regularly. Attie also needs to prove that its connection to Bluesky creates meaningful distribution rather than simply giving creators another place to publish links. Ultimately, the expansion shows how Bluesky is exploring AI as more than a tool for recommending content or personalising feeds. By allowing users to create small interactive experiences for their communities, the company is testing whether social platforms can become places where people not only communicate but also build things together. The opportunity is to make creation more accessible while giving those creations an audience. Whether Attie becomes a lasting part of the decentralised social web will depend on how successfully Bluesky turns that idea into useful experiences that communities want to keep sharing. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider described the concept as “social vibe coding”, an approach that shifts AI-assisted creation from a mostly individual activity towards making things for groups of people.

Much of the current enthusiasm around AI coding centres on individuals building websites, prototypes, and applications with assistance from AI models. However, creating something useful is only part of the challenge. Developers and creators must also find people willing to use it.

Bluesky believes its existing social network could help address that problem. Users can create experiences for their friends, interest groups, and wider communities, then share them through a platform where those audiences already interact.

The company’s chief operating officer, Rose Wang, has highlighted distribution as one of the major obstacles facing AI-powered creation tools. Attie’s connection to Bluesky provides a potential advantage by linking the building process to an existing social network rather than leaving every creator to find an audience independently.

For example, a community could build a quiz around a shared interest, create a poll to settle a disagreement, or develop a small interactive game for its members. Instead of every interaction taking place through posts and replies, users could participate in experiences designed specifically for their group.

Attie’s connection to the AT Protocol, commonly known as ATProto, is another important part of the strategy. The protocol underpins Bluesky and a wider collection of decentralised social applications, creating an ecosystem in which services can connect through shared infrastructure.

By building Attie around this ecosystem, Bluesky can tie user-created experiences to identities and communities beyond a standalone AI application. The approach also supports the company’s broader interest in encouraging developers to build products and services on top of its technology.

Attie also gives users flexibility in their AI workflows, with the option to bring their own AI model or use open-weight alternatives. This could appeal to creators who want more control over the tools they use, although the usefulness of the resulting experiences will depend on their quality and how well they work for other users.

Bluesky has also said that support for private data is being tested in alpha, with a wider rollout planned by the end of 2026. That development could expand what developers can build across the ecosystem, although the precise implications for Attie-created experiences remain to be seen.

The expansion comes as Bluesky looks for ways to strengthen activity beyond its main social networking app. The network had approximately 47 million registered users at the time of the announcement, although reporting has pointed to softer engagement after an earlier period of growth.

Attie offers a potential way to give users more reasons to participate. Instead of visiting Bluesky only to read posts, share opinions, or follow conversations, communities could create and interact with small digital experiences connected to their interests.

The strategy also gives Bluesky an opportunity to attract users interested in AI-assisted creation, even if they are not primarily looking for another social network. Creators could use Attie to experiment with ideas, share projects, and connect those experiences with communities already active across the AT Protocol ecosystem.

There are limitations, however. Generating a simple game or poll is different from building a reliable application that can support complex features, substantial traffic, or sensitive user data. The initial examples demonstrate accessibility and experimentation, but sustained adoption will depend on whether users find enough practical value to return regularly.
Attie also needs to prove that its connection to Bluesky creates meaningful distribution rather than simply giving creators another place to publish links.

Ultimately, the expansion shows how Bluesky is exploring AI as more than a tool for recommending content or personalising feeds. By allowing users to create small interactive experiences for their communities, the company is testing whether social platforms can become places where people not only communicate but also build things together.

The opportunity is to make creation more accessible while giving those creations an audience. Whether Attie becomes a lasting part of the decentralised social web will depend on how successfully Bluesky turns that idea into useful experiences that communities want to keep sharing.

extraction.body: An OpenAI research model stuck without funds on an Ethereum test network went looking for someone else’s wallet, found one through recovery phrases that were already public, and spent from it to finish a coding assignment, the company disclosed Thursday. The incident occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25, according to its incident report . The model needed no hacking skills to get in. A recovery phrase, also called a seed phrase, is a list of words that generates a wallet’s secret keys; whoever has those words can recreate the accounts and spend from them without ever touching the owner’s device. The assignment let the model deploy contracts, programs that run on a blockchain, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the fees. After its attempts to get free test tokens failed, it wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers and found one with enough money. “But using public known key/funds ethically?” the model asked itself in its recorded reasoning, before deciding that a public phrase and test tokens made it acceptable. The spending happened on Sepolia, a separate network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications before launching them. Its tokens only pay for testing and aren't linked to the ether traded on Ethereum’s main network. The deployment went through, and the wallet paid the fees. When the model reported back, it said the work was done and left out where the money came from. OpenAI said it has since added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring. Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person signing off on each step. OpenAI’s model ran out of money mid-task, found a wallet that wasn’t its own and spent from it without asking. Had it been on Ethereum’s main network, that would have been real ether taken from someone else’s account. sources.title: Bluesky’s Attie Launches Site Builder for Small Social Apps and Games - Unite.AI
passages: Bluesky’s Attie, the AI building tool the company introduced earlier in 2026, announced a site builder on October 15, 2026, giving users a way to create small social pages such as games, quizzes, AMAs, guestbooks, and surveys, each published at its own shareable address.
On the Attie homepage , the product offers a direct flow: a user describes a small social app, and Attie builds it with them.
The page lists three properties of the sites it produces.
No code is needed, since the user describes the idea in plain words.
The sites are social from day one, with friends able to sign in with Bluesky to vote, RSVP, or sign.
And every site gets its own link that can be shared anywhere.

The official Attie account announced the feature in a thread on Bluesky , saying that “starting today, Attie users can build small social pages like an AMA, a guestbook, or a survey your friends will argue about for a week.” The account said the team had made a few starter sites to get people going and invited users to make a better one and share it, pointing them to attie.ai.
The site builder also arrives during a documented leadership transition at Bluesky.

Graber stepped back as CEO on March 9, 2026, to become the company’s Chief Innovation Officer, and Bluesky named Toni Schneider permanent CEO on July 10, 2026, after he had held the role on an interim basis since March.
Attie’s original function was building custom Bluesky feeds from natural-language descriptions, and the account’s posting history documents a series of additions from there.
On August 7, 2026, the account published Things Going Right, a feed of science wins, community successes, and quiet progress that never trends.

On August 26, 2026, it highlighted a Bird of the Day feed built for Bluesky’s daily birding game, with the day’s theme at the top, the best entries underneath, and bots and tag-scraper accounts filtered out.
The first starter site in the thread is Flappy Butterfly, a game in which players dodge bad takes, collect likes, and try to avoid getting ratioed, with a leaderboard for top scores.

The second is Poster Alignment Chart, a 3×3 poster-persona quiz that runs a user through ten posting scenarios; after the user signs in with an Atmosphere account, the site reads their last 100 posts and plots both who they think they are and who their posts say they are on one chart.
It lives at gleaming-giddy-bonnet.attie.site.
The third, Ask the Attie Team, is an AMA site that takes questions anonymously and posts selected answers back to Bluesky, at drumming-limber-atlas.attie.site.
Aiden Cross is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , covering AI product strategy, execution, and the practical challenges of turning experimental models into scalable, market-ready products.
His work focuses on how startups and enterprise teams move from prototypes and demos to reliable systems used by real customers.
Advertiser Disclosure : Unite.AI is committed to rigorous editorial standards to provide our readers with accurate information and news.
We may receive compensation when you click on links to products we reviewed.

extraction.body: MADISON, Ill. (April 17, 2026) – Rawlings Sports Business Management Program students at Maryville University enjoyed an on-campus pit stop earlier this week courtesy of NTT INDYCAR SERIES driver David Malukas and World Wide Technology Raceway Owner Curtis Francois. The 24-year-old Team Penske driver was in the St. Louis-area market to promote the June 6-7 Bommarito Automotive Group 500 presented by Axalta and Valvoline at World Wide Technology Raceway, with Maryville serving as a valuable community-focused visit less than 20 miles from downtown St. Louis. Malukas and Francois shared complementary perspectives on the motorsports industry, speaking to approximately 30 students in the program that ranged from first-year to fourth-year students. Malukas offered an inside look at the sport from the driver’s seat, detailing his path to the NTT INDYCAR SERIES and Team Penske, the critical role of partners and sponsors in a driver’s career, and the importance of social media in building a personal brand and connecting with fans. “It was pretty surreal for me to speak to the students in the sports business management program at Maryville University because I’m not much older than most of them that were in the room. Seeing so many students interested in the business of motorsports was a great thing,” said David Malukas, driver of the No. 12 Verizon Chevrolet. “They were very engaged with both me and Curtis Francois. Motorsports – and sports in general – is an ever-evolving landscape so these types of programs are vital for the future health of the sport.” Francois provided the promoter’s perspective, outlining his journey from aspiring race car driver to track owner. His discussion included how he revitalized World Wide Technology Raceway from a dormant facility into a thriving economic engine for the region, now uniquely positioned as one of the only U.S. venues to host NASCAR, INDYCAR and NHRA events. Like Malukas, Francois also emphasized the importance of partnerships and their role in successfully executing national-scale events. “Opportunities like this, especially when we can partner with institutions like Maryville University, allow us to inspire and engage students in meaningful ways,” said Francois. “Having David Malukas join us makes it even more special, giving the students a chance to connect firsthand with someone who represents the passion and possibilities within our sport. It’s a partnership we truly value and one that continues to strengthen the community around us.” Following the discussion, students engaged in an interactive Q&A session, with questions ranging from career values and industry entry points to how major events are curated with fans in mind. Many of the students also will gain additional hands-on experience as volunteers during the upcoming INDYCAR race weekend, further connecting classroom learning with real-world application. “Monday’s event with WWTR was really inspiring—hearing how Curtis Francois used his racing background to bring a shut-down track back to life and build it into a fan-first experience was incredible. His success in creating consistent, high-quality events and attracting major races shows what strong vision and execution can do,” said Camryn Skaggs, a second-year student in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. It was also really interesting to hear from David Malukas as a current driver—learning how he’s built his personal brand through authenticity gave a great perspective on what it takes to succeed in the industry today.” “We have not previously had a professional athlete speak to the program,” said Josh Parrish, Program Coordinator, Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. David’s perspective provided a more holistic view of the business of auto racing and what it takes to build a personal brand. He discussed several disciplines we cover in the program, including sponsorship, sales and event operations. These areas extend beyond racing and apply to the broader sport business industry landscape.” “We sincerely value our partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway and the opportunity it provides for our students to gain hands-on industry experience by working events at the track,” said Jason Williams, a Professor & Associate Dean, John E. Simon School of Business and Director, Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. “Having David Malukas and Curtis Francois speak to our students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program was immensely beneficial. We continually seek opportunities to connect classroom learning with real-time industry experiences, and this engagement provided a unique perspective by highlighting the same race through both a driver’s and a track owner’s lens. Their insights reinforced the competitive nature of the racing industry and emphasized the importance of preparation, relationships, and adaptability.” World Wide Technology Raceway (WWTR) is the home of NASCAR, INDYCAR and NHRA racing in St. Louis’ Metro East region. Located just five minutes from downtown St. Louis and covering 700 acres, WWTR is the largest outdoor entertainment facility in the area. WWTR’s facilities include a 1.25-mile superspeedway; 1/4-mile drag strip; 2.0-mile road course; the Gateway Kartplex state-of-the-art karting facility; and the adjacent Gateway National Golf Links. WWTR and Owner & CEO Curtis Francois have been recognized with several awards, including: 2023 St. Louis Sports Hall of Fame induction; 2023 Innovation in Philanthropy Award by the St. Louis Business Journal; 2022 Explore St. Louis Hospitality Hero Recognition; 2022 Best in Show and Best Event & Festival from the Illinois Governor’s Conference on Tourism; 2021 Comcast Community Champion of the Year; 2021 Jack Buck Award; 2020 NASCAR Drive for Diversity Track Award; 2018 Innovator Award from the St. Louis Convention & Visitors Commission; 2017 Outstanding Facility of the Year Award from the Race Track Business Conference; and the 2017 Spirit of St. Louis Award from the St. Louis Attractions Association. Our mission: We are committed to making a difference in our community, while providing first-class entertainment and memories that last a lifetime. passages: MADISON, Ill. (April 17, 2026) – Rawlings Sports Business Management Program students at Maryville University enjoyed an on-campus pit stop earlier this week courtesy of NTT INDYCAR SERIES driver David Malukas and World Wide Technology Raceway Owner Curtis Francois.

The 24-year-old Team Penske driver was in the St. Louis-area market to promote the June 6-7 Bommarito Automotive Group 500 presented by Axalta and Valvoline at World Wide Technology Raceway, with Maryville serving as a valuable community-focused visit less than 20 miles from downtown St. Louis.
Malukas and Francois shared complementary perspectives on the motorsports industry, speaking to approximately 30 students in the program that ranged from first-year to fourth-year students.

Malukas offered an inside look at the sport from the driver’s seat, detailing his path to the NTT INDYCAR SERIES and Team Penske, the critical role of partners and sponsors in a driver’s career, and the importance of social media in building a personal brand and connecting with fans.

“It was pretty surreal for me to speak to the students in the sports business management program at Maryville University because I’m not much older than most of them that were in the room. Seeing so many students interested in the business of motorsports was a great thing,” said David Malukas, driver of the No. 12 Verizon Chevrolet. “They were very engaged with both me and Curtis Francois. Motorsports – and sports in general – is an ever-evolving landscape so these types of programs are vital for the future health of the sport.”

Francois provided the promoter’s perspective, outlining his journey from aspiring race car driver to track owner. His discussion included how he revitalized World Wide Technology Raceway from a dormant facility into a thriving economic engine for the region, now uniquely positioned as one of the only U.S. venues to host NASCAR, INDYCAR and NHRA events. Like Malukas, Francois also emphasized the importance of partnerships and their role in successfully executing national-scale events.

“Opportunities like this, especially when we can partner with institutions like Maryville University, allow us to inspire and engage students in meaningful ways,” said Francois. “Having David Malukas join us makes it even more special, giving the students a chance to connect firsthand with someone who represents the passion and possibilities within our sport. It’s a partnership we truly value and one that continues to strengthen the community around us.”

Following the discussion, students engaged in an interactive Q&A session, with questions ranging from career values and industry entry points to how major events are curated with fans in mind. Many of the students also will gain additional hands-on experience as volunteers during the upcoming INDYCAR race weekend, further connecting classroom learning with real-world application.

“Monday’s event with WWTR was really inspiring—hearing how Curtis Francois used his racing background to bring a shut-down track back to life and build it into a fan-first experience was incredible. His success in creating consistent, high-quality events and attracting major races shows what strong vision and execution can do,” said Camryn Skaggs, a second-year student in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. It was also really interesting to hear from David Malukas as a current driver—learning how he’s built his personal brand through authenticity gave a great perspective on what it takes to succeed in the industry today.”

“We have not previously had a professional athlete speak to the program,” said Josh Parrish, Program Coordinator, Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. David’s perspective provided a more holistic view of the business of auto racing and what it takes to build a personal brand. He discussed several disciplines we cover in the program, including sponsorship, sales and event operations. These areas extend beyond racing and apply to the broader sport business industry landscape.”

“We sincerely value our partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway and the opportunity it provides for our students to gain hands-on industry experience by working events at the track,” said Jason Williams, a Professor & Associate Dean, John E. Simon School of Business and Director, Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. “Having David Malukas and Curtis Francois speak to our students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program was immensely beneficial. We continually seek opportunities to connect classroom learning with real-time industry experiences, and this engagement provided a unique perspective by highlighting the same race through both a driver’s and a track owner’s lens. Their insights reinforced the competitive nature of the racing industry and emphasized the importance of preparation, relationships, and adaptability.”

World Wide Technology Raceway (WWTR) is the home of NASCAR, INDYCAR and NHRA racing in St. Louis’ Metro East region. Located just five minutes from downtown St. Louis and covering 700 acres, WWTR is the largest outdoor entertainment facility in the area. WWTR’s facilities include a 1.25-mile superspeedway; 1/4-mile drag strip; 2.0-mile road course; the Gateway Kartplex state-of-the-art karting facility; and the adjacent Gateway National Golf Links. WWTR and Owner & CEO Curtis Francois have been recognized with several awards, including: 2023 St. Louis Sports Hall of Fame induction; 2023 Innovation in Philanthropy Award by the St. Louis Business Journal; 2022 Explore St. Louis Hospitality Hero Recognition; 2022 Best in Show and Best Event & Festival from the Illinois Governor’s Conference on Tourism; 2021 Comcast Community Champion of the Year; 2021 Jack Buck Award; 2020 NASCAR Drive for Diversity Track Award; 2018 Innovator Award from the St. Louis Convention & Visitors Commission; 2017 Outstanding Facility of the Year Award from the Race Track Business Conference; and the 2017 Spirit of St. Louis Award from the St. Louis Attractions Association. Our mission: We are committed to making a difference in our community, while providing first-class entertainment and memories that last a lifetime.

extraction.body: The last few weeks have been exciting for students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program at Maryville University. Nearly 100 first-year students assisted in set-up and operations for both the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series and Enjoy Illinois 300 NASCAR Cup Series Chase races held at the World Wide Technology Raceway in Madison, Il. By design, Rawlings Sport Business Management students don’t just study the business of sport — they live it, and as raceway crew, they logged about 600 hours on-site during two set-up days, plus another 300 hours during event days. For many, this was their first opportunity to work in the industry. Their impact on the success of the motor sport events did not go unnoticed. “Rawlings Sport Business Management students are excellent, and we appreciate having them assist us with these national events,” said Declan O’Neil, vice president of partnership marketing at World Wide Technology Raceway. Through such important experiential learning opportunities, students develop a wide range of industry skills. They also see how knowledge gained in the classroom plays out in the real world, said Daniel Schmidt, 10′, MBA ’16, instructor in the program. “Their work at World Wide Technology Raceway involves corporate sponsorship, activation, event management and operations as well as ticketing and customer communication,” he said. “They also get exposed to motor sports — a part of the sports industry they’ve probably never considered before.” Students appreciate the opportunity to practice skills, expand their resumes, build professional networks and discover first-hand what it takes to host a successful major event. First-year student Karli Dean learned that being adaptable and paying attention to details is important. Student, Parker Medina, agreed. “The little details really go a long way when setting up these events,” Medina said. “Putting so much time and effort on the small things really shows how much the hosts care about their events as well as how much it means to the consumers and sponsors.” Charlie Phillips, discovered the ticketing department involves much more than just selling tickets. “Ticketing covers a lot more to make sure fans are happy and have a great experience — so they’ll come back again and again,” said Phillips, a Rawlings Sport Business Management student. Andra Alexander helped lead her team of fellow students as they hung scrim along fences on the racetrack as well as near fan engagement areas. “This really made me realize how much work gets put into any kind of event and is going to make me appreciate my experiences even more, whether I’m behind the scenes or in the stands,” Alexander said. Erick Gates, who will enter the job market when he graduates in spring, understands the value of such opportunities. “Diversifying my resume with experiential experiences has been key,” he said. extraction.body: MADISON, Ill. (April 17, 2026) – Rawlings Sports Business Management Program students at Maryville University enjoyed an on-campus pit stop earlier this week courtesy of NTT INDYCAR SERIES driver David Malukas and World Wide Technology Raceway Owner Curtis Francois. The 24-year-old Team Penske driver was in the St. Louis-area market to promote the June 6-7 Bommarito Automotive Group 500 presented by Axalta and Valvoline at World Wide Technology Raceway, with Maryville serving as a valuable community-focused visit less than 20 miles from downtown St. Louis. Malukas and Francois shared complementary perspectives on the motorsports industry, speaking to approximately 30 students in the program that ranged from first-year to fourth-year students. Malukas offered an inside look at the sport from the driver’s seat, detailing his path to the NTT INDYCAR SERIES and Team Penske, the critical role of partners and sponsors in a driver’s career, and the importance of social media in building a personal brand and connecting with fans. “It was pretty surreal for me to speak to the students in the sports business management program at Maryville University because I’m not much older than most of them that were in the room. Seeing so many students interested in the business of motorsports was a great thing,” said David Malukas, driver of the No. 12 Verizon Chevrolet. “They were very engaged with both me and Curtis Francois. Motorsports – and sports in general – is an ever-evolving landscape so these types of programs are vital for the future health of the sport.” Francois provided the promoter’s perspective, outlining his journey from aspiring race car driver to track owner. His discussion included how he revitalized World Wide Technology Raceway from a dormant facility into a thriving economic engine for the region, now uniquely positioned as one of the only U.S. venues to host NASCAR, INDYCAR and NHRA events. Like Malukas, Francois also emphasized the importance of partnerships and their role in successfully executing national-scale events. “Opportunities like this, especially when we can partner with institutions like Maryville University, allow us to inspire and engage students in meaningful ways,” said Francois. “Having David Malukas join us makes it even more special, giving the students a chance to connect firsthand with someone who represents the passion and possibilities within our sport. It’s a partnership we truly value and one that continues to strengthen the community around us.” Following the discussion, students engaged in an interactive Q&A session, with questions ranging from career values and industry entry points to how major events are curated with fans in mind. Many of the students also will gain additional hands-on experience as volunteers during the upcoming INDYCAR race weekend, further connecting classroom learning with real-world application. “Monday’s event with WWTR was really inspiring—hearing how Curtis Francois used his racing background to bring a shut-down track back to life and build it into a fan-first experience was incredible. His success in creating consistent, high-quality events and attracting major races shows what strong vision and execution can do,” said Camryn Skaggs, a second-year student in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. It was also really interesting to hear from David Malukas as a current driver—learning how he’s built his personal brand through authenticity gave a great perspective on what it takes to succeed in the industry today.” “We have not previously had a professional athlete speak to the program,” said Josh Parrish, Program Coordinator, Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. David’s perspective provided a more holistic view of the business of auto racing and what it takes to build a personal brand. He discussed several disciplines we cover in the program, including sponsorship, sales and event operations. These areas extend beyond racing and apply to the broader sport business industry landscape.” “We sincerely value our partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway and the opportunity it provides for our students to gain hands-on industry experience by working events at the track,” said Jason Williams, a Professor & Associate Dean, John E. Simon School of Business and Director, Rawlings Sport Business Management Program. “Having David Malukas and Curtis Francois speak to our students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program was immensely beneficial. We continually seek opportunities to connect classroom learning with real-time industry experiences, and this engagement provided a unique perspective by highlighting the same race through both a driver’s and a track owner’s lens. Their insights reinforced the competitive nature of the racing industry and emphasized the importance of preparation, relationships, and adaptability.” World Wide Technology Raceway (WWTR) is the home of NASCAR, INDYCAR and NHRA racing in St. Louis’ Metro East region. Located just five minutes from downtown St. Louis and covering 700 acres, WWTR is the largest outdoor entertainment facility in the area. WWTR’s facilities include a 1.25-mile superspeedway; 1/4-mile drag strip; 2.0-mile road course; the Gateway Kartplex state-of-the-art karting facility; and the adjacent Gateway National Golf Links. WWTR and Owner & CEO Curtis Francois have been recognized with several awards, including: 2023 St. Louis Sports Hall of Fame induction; 2023 Innovation in Philanthropy Award by the St. Louis Business Journal; 2022 Explore St. Louis Hospitality Hero Recognition; 2022 Best in Show and Best Event & Festival from the Illinois Governor’s Conference on Tourism; 2021 Comcast Community Champion of the Year; 2021 Jack Buck Award; 2020 NASCAR Drive for Diversity Track Award; 2018 Innovator Award from the St. Louis Convention & Visitors Commission; 2017 Outstanding Facility of the Year Award from the Race Track Business Conference; and the 2017 Spirit of St. Louis Award from the St. Louis Attractions Association. Our mission: We are committed to making a difference in our community, while providing first-class entertainment and memories that last a lifetime. extraction.body: The last few weeks have been exciting for students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program at Maryville University. Nearly 100 first-year students assisted in set-up and operations for both the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series and Enjoy Illinois 300 NASCAR Cup Series Chase races held at the World Wide Technology Raceway in Madison, Il. By design, Rawlings Sport Business Management students don’t just study the business of sport — they live it, and as raceway crew, they logged about 600 hours on-site during two set-up days, plus another 300 hours during event days. For many, this was their first opportunity to work in the industry. Their impact on the success of the motor sport events did not go unnoticed. “Rawlings Sport Business Management students are excellent, and we appreciate having them assist us with these national events,” said Declan O’Neil, vice president of partnership marketing at World Wide Technology Raceway. Through such important experiential learning opportunities, students develop a wide range of industry skills. They also see how knowledge gained in the classroom plays out in the real world, said Daniel Schmidt, 10′, MBA ’16, instructor in the program. “Their work at World Wide Technology Raceway involves corporate sponsorship, activation, event management and operations as well as ticketing and customer communication,” he said. “They also get exposed to motor sports — a part of the sports industry they’ve probably never considered before.” Students appreciate the opportunity to practice skills, expand their resumes, build professional networks and discover first-hand what it takes to host a successful major event. First-year student Karli Dean learned that being adaptable and paying attention to details is important. Student, Parker Medina, agreed. “The little details really go a long way when setting up these events,” Medina said. “Putting so much time and effort on the small things really shows how much the hosts care about their events as well as how much it means to the consumers and sponsors.” Charlie Phillips, discovered the ticketing department involves much more than just selling tickets. “Ticketing covers a lot more to make sure fans are happy and have a great experience — so they’ll come back again and again,” said Phillips, a Rawlings Sport Business Management student. Andra Alexander helped lead her team of fellow students as they hung scrim along fences on the racetrack as well as near fan engagement areas. “This really made me realize how much work gets put into any kind of event and is going to make me appreciate my experiences even more, whether I’m behind the scenes or in the stands,” Alexander said. Erick Gates, who will enter the job market when he graduates in spring, understands the value of such opportunities. “Diversifying my resume with experiential experiences has been key,” he said. passages: Collins Aerospace Airport Solutions has reached a deal to become part of SITA .
The planned merger adds popular passenger processing, baggage handling and airport operations technologies to SITA’s large and growing portfolio of biometrics.
acquisitions | airport biometrics | biometrics | Collins Aerospace | digital travel | SITA
SITA CEO David Lavorel says in the announcement that air transport industry growth demands coordination across each part of the traveller journey to prevent or quickly fix disruptions.
Collins Aerospace is a subsidiary of RTX Corporation, formerly known as Raytheon Technologies.
Collins has deployed biometric solutions at airports around the world, including Tokyo, Las Vegas and the Philippines , and is planning to deploy biometric gates in Fiji .

“Ask an airport what it wants from a technology provider, and the answer is a trusted partner,” says Nathalie Altwegg, SVP of airports at SITA. “That means understanding its environment, working closely with its teams, and being there when support is needed.
This acquisition will strengthen our ability to do that for more customers across the industry.”
SITA is one of several major aviation industry players who have joined forces to lobby European policy-makers about responsible biometrics use in the travel industry.
The company also acquired Materna IPS in 2024.
The acquisition follows SITA adding AI operational decision-making platform Big Blue Analytics in June.
At the time SITA for Aircraft CEO Yann Cabaret described that acquisition as a first step toward the creation of a larger vision for an Intelligent Operations Control Center.

extraction.body: SITA has reached an agreement to acquire Collins Aerospace’s airport technology unit. SITA said the deal to buy Collins Aerospace Airport Solutions is expected to close in the first half of 2027. The acquisition price was not disclosed. Both companies offer technology—particularly self-service solutions—to facilitate more efficient passenger movement through airports. Collins Aerospace, a subsidiary of RTX, describes its airport technology business on its website as offering “integrated and intelligent solutions for passenger processing and facilitation, airport operations and baggage management.” It adds that its self-service technology enables the streamlined movement of high volumes of passengers through airports. SITA CEO David Lavorel said the acquisition “extends” the company’s capabilities. Collins Aerospace provides “mission-critical systems that keep airport operations running,” SITA added. “Our industry increasingly needs technology, innovation and people working together to connect each part of the journey, so disruptions are prevented, or fixed fast when they happen,” Lavorel said. Aaron Karp is a Senior Editor at Air Transport World.

extraction.body: SITA has reached an agreement to acquire Collins Aerospace’s airport technology unit. SITA said the deal to buy Collins Aerospace Airport Solutions is expected to close in the first half of 2027. The acquisition price was not disclosed. Both companies offer technology—particularly self-service solutions—to facilitate more efficient passenger movement through airports. Collins Aerospace, a subsidiary of RTX, describes its airport technology business on its website as offering “integrated and intelligent solutions for passenger processing and facilitation, airport operations and baggage management.” It adds that its self-service technology enables the streamlined movement of high volumes of passengers through airports. SITA CEO David Lavorel said the acquisition “extends” the company’s capabilities. Collins Aerospace provides “mission-critical systems that keep airport operations running,” SITA added. “Our industry increasingly needs technology, innovation and people working together to connect each part of the journey, so disruptions are prevented, or fixed fast when they happen,” Lavorel said. Aaron Karp is a Senior Editor at Air Transport World.

extraction.body: Capital B, a France-listed corporate Bitcoin treasury firm, reported a steep accounting loss for the first half of 2026, citing a large Bitcoin impairment charge. The company said its net loss totaled €69.5 million (about $78 million), largely driven by a non-cash write-down tied to the value of its Bitcoin holdings as of June 30. Despite the reported loss, Capital B also disclosed that it continued adding to its Bitcoin position while raising new capital. In parallel with the fundraising, the firm’s strategy remains focused on accumulating Bitcoin through additional equity and financing capacity—an approach that is increasingly tested by how accounting rules translate crypto market moves into earnings. In its first-half 2026 report, Capital B attributed the bulk of its net loss to an impairment charge tied to Bitcoin price movements. The company said the calculation reflected Bitcoin prices as of June 30 and, importantly, that the impairment did not have a direct cash impact. This distinction matters for readers because corporate treasury firms often present a split between accounting earnings and underlying cash economics. When a company measures crypto holdings under impairment or fair-value accounting approaches, declines in market prices can rapidly translate into losses on the income statement—without necessarily affecting liquidity. According to the filing, Capital B’s consolidated revenue rose 3.5% year-over-year to $6.5 million, but profitability remained negative: adjusted EBITDA came in at -$1.2 million. EBITDA is a widely used metric that excludes interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, and its negativity suggests that operational and/or structured costs were not fully offset by revenue in the period. The report, published Thursday, also underscores how sensitive treasury strategies can be to the timing of accounting measurement dates. For investors, the key question becomes whether future impairments will reverse in subsequent reporting periods when Bitcoin prices rise again—or whether the company’s financial performance will continue to be dominated by non-cash accounting volatility. While the impairment pushed reported results lower, Capital B stated that it continued its Bitcoin accumulation effort during the first half of the year. The company said it raised capital totaling $30 million in the period and increased its holdings by 11%—from 2,823 BTC at the start of the year to 3,139 BTC by June 30. Capital B later disclosed a further expansion of its treasury: total holdings reached 3,538 Bitcoin by Sept. 30. Compared with the beginning of 2026, that represents roughly a 25% increase in holdings. The company’s growing treasury places it among the most prominent corporate Bitcoin balance sheets. Bitcointreasuries data shows Capital B holds about $290 million worth of Bitcoin and ranks as the world’s 25th-largest corporate Bitcoin treasury, and Europe’s second-largest by holdings—behind Germany-based Bitcoin Group. For traders and long-term investors alike, the juxtaposition is important: even when accounting metrics deteriorate, Capital B appears willing to keep buying. That implies management believes additional exposure to Bitcoin aligns with its mandate, provided it can access funding and manage accounting volatility through future reporting cycles. Capital B’s fundraising and corporate structuring actions appear designed to broaden its investor base and sustain accumulation. In July, the company approved a 10-for-1 reverse stock split intended to broaden its institutional investor reach. Earlier, in June, shareholders approved up to $120 billion in financing capacity, including both equity and credit instruments, to support the Bitcoin accumulation strategy. These actions align with how treasury firms typically scale: securing capital flexibility can reduce reliance on a single funding window, especially when market conditions may affect both equity issuance appetite and perceived risk. However, investors should also recognize the potential for dilution or financing costs to influence shareholder value—even if the treasury’s Bitcoin exposure increases. The company’s stock performance reflects this tension. Yahoo Finance data shows the share price rose 0.5% in early Friday trading, but was down 25% year-to-date at the time of reporting. For investors, that divergence between continued accumulation and weak share performance suggests that markets may be weighing reported losses, accounting impairment optics, and broader equity pricing rather than solely tracking Bitcoin holdings growth. Capital B’s first-half results highlight a recurring challenge for corporate Bitcoin treasuries: accounting losses can emerge quickly from Bitcoin volatility even when the strategy remains intact. The impairment mechanism used in the company’s reporting—based on Bitcoin prices at specific dates—means reported earnings could remain uneven across quarters, depending on market moves around measurement cutoffs. Going forward, investors should watch for how impairment charges evolve in the next reporting periods, whether capital raises and the approved financing capacity are fully utilized, and whether corporate actions like the reverse split translate into improved liquidity or investor demand. For anyone evaluating treasury models, the next quarter’s figures may be as telling for sentiment and funding access as they are for the Bitcoin balance sheet itself. extraction.body: French bitcoin (BTC) treasury firm Capital B reported a wider net loss for the first half of this year, mainly driven by an additional bitcoin impairment charge, as the company continued to expand its crypto reserves. The firm posted a net loss of €69.5 million ($78.1 million) for the first six months of this year, compared to a €1.9 million ($2.1 million) net loss in the same period last year, according to its half-year results released Thursday. The report attributed roughly €67.5 million ($75.9 million) of the loss to an additional bitcoin impairment charge based on bitcoin's price as of June 30, which the company said had no cash impact. Meanwhile, its revenue rose 3.5% year-on-year to €5.8 million ($6.5 million), compared with €5.6 million for the first half of 2025. Stacked market caps of bitcoin treasury companies. Bitcoin holdings grow The bitcoin treasury company continued to focus on accumulating the world's largest cryptocurrency. 30, its strategic bitcoin reserve grew to 3,538 BTC, up 25.3% from 2,823 BTC in January. The company reported a total acquisition cost of €310.6 million ($349.4 million), averaging €87,805 ($98,768) per bitcoin. Capital B also reported a BTC yield of 2.2% for the first nine months of this year, a metric that measures the percentage change in bitcoin holdings per fully diluted share. To support its bitcoin treasury strategy, the company announced capital raises totaling €27.5 million ($30.9 million) during the first half of this year, followed by another €31.7 million ($35.6 million) between July 1 and Oct. Formerly known as The Blockchain Group, Capital B rebranded in July 2025 to focus on its bitcoin treasury strategy. In September, the company acquired 376 BTC for €25.3 million ($28.4 million), marking its largest bitcoin purchase of the year. The bitcoin acquisition was funded through recent capital raises, including investments from Blockstream CEO Adam Back.

extraction.body: Capital B, a France-listed corporate Bitcoin treasury firm, reported a steep accounting loss for the first half of 2026, citing a large Bitcoin impairment charge. The company said its net loss totaled €69.5 million (about $78 million), largely driven by a non-cash write-down tied to the value of its Bitcoin holdings as of June 30. Despite the reported loss, Capital B also disclosed that it continued adding to its Bitcoin position while raising new capital. In parallel with the fundraising, the firm’s strategy remains focused on accumulating Bitcoin through additional equity and financing capacity—an approach that is increasingly tested by how accounting rules translate crypto market moves into earnings. In its first-half 2026 report, Capital B attributed the bulk of its net loss to an impairment charge tied to Bitcoin price movements. The company said the calculation reflected Bitcoin prices as of June 30 and, importantly, that the impairment did not have a direct cash impact. This distinction matters for readers because corporate treasury firms often present a split between accounting earnings and underlying cash economics. When a company measures crypto holdings under impairment or fair-value accounting approaches, declines in market prices can rapidly translate into losses on the income statement—without necessarily affecting liquidity. According to the filing, Capital B’s consolidated revenue rose 3.5% year-over-year to $6.5 million, but profitability remained negative: adjusted EBITDA came in at -$1.2 million. EBITDA is a widely used metric that excludes interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, and its negativity suggests that operational and/or structured costs were not fully offset by revenue in the period. The report, published Thursday, also underscores how sensitive treasury strategies can be to the timing of accounting measurement dates. For investors, the key question becomes whether future impairments will reverse in subsequent reporting periods when Bitcoin prices rise again—or whether the company’s financial performance will continue to be dominated by non-cash accounting volatility. While the impairment pushed reported results lower, Capital B stated that it continued its Bitcoin accumulation effort during the first half of the year. The company said it raised capital totaling $30 million in the period and increased its holdings by 11%—from 2,823 BTC at the start of the year to 3,139 BTC by June 30. Capital B later disclosed a further expansion of its treasury: total holdings reached 3,538 Bitcoin by Sept. 30. Compared with the beginning of 2026, that represents roughly a 25% increase in holdings. The company’s growing treasury places it among the most prominent corporate Bitcoin balance sheets. Bitcointreasuries data shows Capital B holds about $290 million worth of Bitcoin and ranks as the world’s 25th-largest corporate Bitcoin treasury, and Europe’s second-largest by holdings—behind Germany-based Bitcoin Group. For traders and long-term investors alike, the juxtaposition is important: even when accounting metrics deteriorate, Capital B appears willing to keep buying. That implies management believes additional exposure to Bitcoin aligns with its mandate, provided it can access funding and manage accounting volatility through future reporting cycles. Capital B’s fundraising and corporate structuring actions appear designed to broaden its investor base and sustain accumulation. In July, the company approved a 10-for-1 reverse stock split intended to broaden its institutional investor reach. Earlier, in June, shareholders approved up to $120 billion in financing capacity, including both equity and credit instruments, to support the Bitcoin accumulation strategy. These actions align with how treasury firms typically scale: securing capital flexibility can reduce reliance on a single funding window, especially when market conditions may affect both equity issuance appetite and perceived risk. However, investors should also recognize the potential for dilution or financing costs to influence shareholder value—even if the treasury’s Bitcoin exposure increases. The company’s stock performance reflects this tension. Yahoo Finance data shows the share price rose 0.5% in early Friday trading, but was down 25% year-to-date at the time of reporting. For investors, that divergence between continued accumulation and weak share performance suggests that markets may be weighing reported losses, accounting impairment optics, and broader equity pricing rather than solely tracking Bitcoin holdings growth. Capital B’s first-half results highlight a recurring challenge for corporate Bitcoin treasuries: accounting losses can emerge quickly from Bitcoin volatility even when the strategy remains intact. The impairment mechanism used in the company’s reporting—based on Bitcoin prices at specific dates—means reported earnings could remain uneven across quarters, depending on market moves around measurement cutoffs. Going forward, investors should watch for how impairment charges evolve in the next reporting periods, whether capital raises and the approved financing capacity are fully utilized, and whether corporate actions like the reverse split translate into improved liquidity or investor demand. For anyone evaluating treasury models, the next quarter’s figures may be as telling for sentiment and funding access as they are for the Bitcoin balance sheet itself. For example, on July 25, the Senate voted 91-7 to amend the National Defense Authorization Act to (1) prohibit businesses based in China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea from purchasing US farmland and (2) require CFIUS review of specific types of land purchases by investors from any other foreign country. [12] While some of these proposals address the issue of federal preemption, many are silent on the subject. [13] STATE LEGISLATIVE SOLUTIONS Some state governments have promulgated laws and regulations governing the purchase of real estate by foreign investors.
