[21] In 2013, the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ruled that Florida’s “Cuba Amendment,” which prevented companies that did business in Cuba from bidding on public contracts worth at least $1 million, was unconstitutional, as it conflicted with federal sanctions on Cuba. [22] Although the state statutes did not (1) expressly contradict or (2) implicitly preempt the federal sanctions, they did attempt to regulate an interest in the federal domain which weakened the president’s ability to unilaterally conduct foreign relations.
On the other hand, since 1789, national security and foreign affairs have been the primary responsibility of the US federal government.

CFIUS maintains a list of ports and military installations for this purpose, and Appendix A to Part 802 to Title 31 of the Code of Federal Regulations identifies 211 currently sensitive US military installations across the United States.

extraction.body: Jurisdictional limits on the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) regarding the review of certain real estate transactions have led Congress to introduce proposals expanding its jurisdiction and certain states to adopt more restrictive laws and regulations on real estate acquisition by certain foreign persons. Some of these state laws may be subject to challenges on constitutional and other grounds, and Florida SB 264 may be the first such test case. Historically, national security issues only occasionally arose in real estate transactions based on the proximity of the real estate to military bases and strategic ports and the rights of the foreign investor in the real estate. The Foreign Investment Risk Review and Modernization Act of 2018 (FIRRMA) and the implementing regulations clarified and expanded the rules determining when a real estate transaction constituted a “covered real estate transaction” separate and apart from the acquisition of control over a US business, [1] although filing remained (and remains) voluntary. [2] In December 2022, CFIUS determined that it did not have jurisdiction to review Chinese company Fufeng Group Limited’s (Fufeng) proposed $700 million corn milling project in North Dakota. [3] The news came after CFIUS completed a three-month review and investigation of Fufeng’s purchase from a private citizen of a 370-acre greenfield site in Grand Forks, North Dakota, to build a wet corn mill. Criticized for this decision, CFIUS has recently proposed additions to the list of covered real estate. The Fufeng decision reinvigorated Congressional efforts to expand CFIUS’s jurisdiction to cover agricultural and other lands. Congress members have proposed changes to CFIUS as part of amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) as well as through independent legislation. Some of the proposals would expressly preempt conflicting state action while others are silent on the subject. Various states have filled the gap created by the jurisdictional limitations of CFIUS and passed legislation restricting the ability of certain foreign persons to acquire real estate in their state. Some of these states cite national security as the statutory basis, creating potential challenges on the basis of federal preemption. For example, Florida SB 264, which prohibits the purchase of real property by persons in or from the People’s Republic of China, was passed in May 2023 and has been challenged on the grounds of federal preemption, as well as violations of equal protection and the Fair Housing Act. CURRENT CFIUS REGIME The US Department of the Treasury, which chairs CFIUS, has the authority to review foreign investment in US businesses as well as certain real estate transactions. When CFIUS reviews such transactions, they can block the transaction from occurring or enforce mitigation measures that are negotiated as part of a national security agreement. However, Congress limited CFIUS’ authority to only review purchases of real estate in air or maritime ports or in a prescribed proximity to military installations (defined as within 100 miles of the base). CFIUS maintains a list of ports and military installations for this purpose, and Appendix A to Part 802 to Title 31 of the Code of Federal Regulations identifies 211 currently sensitive US military installations across the United States. Disclosure of the transaction to CFIUS remains voluntary, although CFIUS can conduct a national security review at any time for covered transactions that were not submitted for clearance by CFIUS—the so-called non-notified outreach. This statutory and regulatory confinement of CFIUS’ jurisdiction has resulted in very few reviews of real estate as noted in CFIUS annual reports. [4] Therefore, CFIUS continues to expand its jurisdiction to review real estate transactions that may impact US national security. PROPOSED CHANGES TO CFIUS REAL ESTATE REGULATIONS On May 5, 2023, the Treasury Department published a proposed rule in the Federal Register to expand the list of sensitive military installations subject to review under CFIUS' authority, applicable to certain real estate transactions involving foreign investors or acquirers. [5] The proposed rule would add eight new military installations to Appendix A, including seven US Air Force bases principally involved in the ongoing development of the B-21 Raider stealth bomber aircraft, as well as the Iowa National Guard Joint Force Headquarters, all of which would be added to Part 2 and thus be subject to the expanded 100-mile geographic range. Importantly, the proposed rule, if adopted, would not change the filing requirements associated with real estate transactions, which would remain voluntary under CFIUS' real estate regulations (Part 802). The eight additions to Appendix A include: Air Force Plant 42, Palmdale, California Dyess Air Force Base, Abilene, Texas Ellsworth Air Force Base, Box Elder, South Dakota Grand Forks Air Force Base, Grand Forks, North Dakota Iowa National Guard Joint Force Headquarters, Des Moines, Iowa Lackland Air Force Base, San Antonio, Texas Laughlin Air Force Base, Del Rio, Texas Luke Air Force Base, Glendale, Arizona However, these additions may be heralding additional changes to CFIUS’ authority to review real estate transactions. CONGRESSIONAL PROPOSALS TO EXPAND CFIUS JURISDICTION Fueled by the Fufeng decision by CFIUS determining that it did not have jurisdiction, the current area of greatest bipartisan concern is foreign ownership of farmland. For example, on July 25, the Senate voted 91-7 to amend the National Defense Authorization Act to (1) prohibit businesses based in China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea from purchasing US farmland and (2) require CFIUS review of specific types of land purchases by investors from any other foreign country. [12] While some of these proposals address the issue of federal preemption, many are silent on the subject. [13] STATE LEGISLATIVE SOLUTIONS Some state governments have promulgated laws and regulations governing the purchase of real estate by foreign investors. Since January 2023, more than half of the states have proposed at least one bill relating to foreign investment in real estate with the most recent states being Michigan and Wisconsin. [14] These range from an absolute prohibition on certain acquisitions, to narrowed permissions for specific purposes, while others merely require reporting to the state. Lawmakers in other states are watching these activities and considering whether to pass similar measures. [15] Because state interests, types of land, and public needs vary greatly between the states, there is no one-size-fits-all solution; [16] each can tailor its statute or proposal to address its respective concerns. Like the federal government, many states are currently considering some regulation focused on foreign ownership of farmland. [17] A state survey can be found at the National Agricultural Law Center. [18] Challenges to state legislation restricting acquisitions by certain foreign persons are likely to face challenges on this ground, as well as other constitutional and federal statutory grounds, including equal protection and the Federal Housing Act. FEDERAL PREEMPTION Under the US Constitution, federal laws will generally preempt state law where federal and state law conflict or the federal government has or may occupy the field. [19] The analysis of whether a state law is preempted by federal law can be quite complex. There are two types of implied preemption—field and conflict: Conflict preemption is when compliance with conflicting federal and state regulations is either impossible or the state law presents an obstacle to compliance with the federal law. Field preemption is when a state attempts to regulate an interest in the federal domain. [20] Because foreign affairs and national security traditionally fall under the purview of the federal government, states have only been permitted to pass statutes relating to national security when the federal government had not previously acted in that area, such as in the following instances: The US Supreme Court ruled in Crosby v. National Foreign Trade Council that a conflict inherently existed when both the federal and state government imposed various sanctions on Burma. [21] In 2013, the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ruled that Florida’s “Cuba Amendment,” which prevented companies that did business in Cuba from bidding on public contracts worth at least $1 million, was unconstitutional, as it conflicted with federal sanctions on Cuba. [22] Although the state statutes did not (1) expressly contradict or (2) implicitly preempt the federal sanctions, they did attempt to regulate an interest in the federal domain which weakened the president’s ability to unilaterally conduct foreign relations. However, unlike sanctions, trade, and embargoes, which have historically been recognized as the responsibility of the federal government, federal preemption in the context of the regulation of private ownership of land is less clear. Removing (or curtailing) a state’s ability to regulate local ownership of land within its borders undermines one of the fundamental roles of local government. Historical precedent also demonstrates that the federal government can (and should) instruct states on what types of rules and regulations are appropriate in the context of civil rights and the prevention of racial discrimination. Even eminent domain—a right for the government to take and convert property to public use—is exercised by both the federal and state governments. On the other hand, since 1789, national security and foreign affairs have been the primary responsibility of the US federal government. The failure of individual states to cooperate and manage their own foreign affairs was a primary motivation for the creation of the original Constitutional Convention. Whether it be the signing of treaties, declarations of war, commanding of the armed forces, regulating international and interstate trade, conducting diplomacy, or managing other aspects of national security, the federal government is the primary, and usually sole, authority. [23] As an interagency committee made up of US government agency members, CFIUS occupies a unique role to identify, assess, and mitigate any risks to US national security related to the acquisition of real estate.

extraction.body: "I think CFIUS is probably one of the least-known acronyms in D.C. nomenclature. We're doing our best to try to get it out there more," Chris Pilkerton said. Terry Gerton The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, or CFIUS, just updated its website. Normally an updated website is not big news, but there are newsy bits here. And so I want to go through some of them with you. In my experience, CFIUS is sort of shrouded in mystery, but the focus of the website is on more transparency. Why does it seem like that is so important right now? Chris Pilkerton You’re right. Oftentimes, updates to a website for the federal government are not something that are newsworthy. But we really think this is, in large part because while national security will always be the North Star and the mission of CFIUS, the secretary and the president are very focused on ensuring that we are engaging with the public and ensuring that they understand the process as much as possible. So you’ve talked about this idea of CFIUS being shrouded in secrecy. The reality is we’re trying to demystify CFIUS. Now, there are components of it that will certainly remain in that so-called black box because of the work that we do with the intelligence community to ensure that we are securing our national security concerns. But this is big news for us because the website itself, and I would say probably the biggest thing, is when companies are coming to look to do transactions in the United States, to make investments — as opposed to immediately going out and getting counsel and conducting a large, timely filing that could certainly be, you know, very expensive — we want to be able to identify issues and connect them with a case officer. So there is a pre-filing consultation link that allows them to put some information about the transaction, anonymized if need be. And once again, as you know, CFIUS is confidential, all the information associated with it. So this information coming to the website would be confidential. What that does is it immediately gets them to a case officer who can review that information and then set up a follow-up call with the idea being, let’s talk through the transaction before it happens. And that’s incredibly important in the work that we do, because if someone has a transaction where there would be CFIUS jurisdiction and they end up closing the transaction, sometimes it’s hard to reopen that transaction if CFIUS needs to come in and present some mitigation options from a national security perspective. Join WTOP Nov. 17 for the Critical Infrastructure and Digital Trust webinar where experts will examine how government and industry can work together to modernize the grid and ensure the nation’s most critical operations have dependable power. Register today! Terry Gerton How have your case officers seen the quality of the information that they received change since you opened this portal? Chris Pilkerton So it’s relatively new, but we’ve gotten a lot of outreach. And obviously we work with a lot of different counsel and people. You know, for good reason we’ll work with counsel to put that information in because if it’s more comprehensive, obviously we can give more feedback. But I will tell you that we’re seeing entrepreneurs who aren’t represented, present some information and share that with us. And there’s a couple of really important things about that. One, this idea of talking more about CFIUS from a customer service perspective serves the American people well because folks who, for no nefarious reason, may not inform us of their transactions; now we know about the transactions and they know about potential concerns. So that’s a big part of it. But I will also say that because we’re seeing historic levels of investment — as you might imagine, we’re see massive investment in the technology space. So, one of the programs that we’ve developed, and this is discussed on the website, is something called the Investment Security Technology Initiative. And the program is essentially working not just with all the subject matter experts throughout the U.S. government, but working with universities, working with corporate R&D, to see where pre-commercialized tech is going. And we’re not looking at anything proprietary there, we’re looking at any particular cases. What we want to know is, from a CFIUS perspective, can we be looking around corners to identify a risk that may be coming for all kinds of new things? So whether it’s quantum, whether it supercomputing, whether its hypersonics or biotech, are there ideas and concepts that are being discussed in the academic or in the R&D world? Well, we can be a part of those conversations to ensure that those companies, once they come through CFIUS, have the ability to grow, prosper and create jobs. Terry Gerton Chris Pilkerton is the assistant secretary for investment security at the U.S. Treasury Department. One of the other features of the new website is the risk matrix. How does that help the public in general understand the risks that you all are looking at, and how are you measuring and assessing them? Chris Pilkerton So it goes back to the point that you made earlier that when people have engaged with CFIUS in the past, they haven’t necessarily known what is CFIUS looking at, right? We know that CFIUS supports national security, but what does that actually mean? So going back to the concept of customer service, what we wanted to do is help put the public in the mind of a CFIUS case officer. So the risks that are on there, this is the first time this has ever happened, identify some of the more common risks that we see in program. But it’s not just the risks themselves; it’s also the applicable mitigation that we might want to work with the stakeholders on to be able to mitigate those risks. So things around, you know, privacy data and things that obviously potentially could compromise the American people or present some kind of national security issue — we want to be able to work with those parties in advance. And so it really is about kind of beginning that dialog. Because it’s not just about, like I said before, this historic investment in the United States, but it’s what those investments actually do for the economic development and the larger economy. I travel the country where we have companies that have come through the CFIUS process. And when I meet with them, inevitably, at the table are also the local economic development officials. Because there’s a number of programs and vendors that have been identified that are domestic companies that are able to support those CFIUS companies that come through. So we’re working closely with the Department of War and the Small Business Administration because we want to help identify those vendors so that these CFIUS companies really have the option to utilize a very large swath of incredibly talented domestic vendors. Terry Gerton So I’m a foreign vendor, I’ve put my early information in, I’ve gotten in touch with my case officer, I know what risks you’re looking at, but now I have no idea what happened to my application, right? It’s gone into the bureaucratic black box. The new website offers a little more clarity there as well. Tell us how you’re helping people kind of know where they are in the process. Chris Pilkerton So obviously you have the touch points with the case officer. There’s a variety of different stages in the CFIUS process, but from a statutory perspective, at its longest, there’s a 90-day statutory framework. And what we’ve also done for the first time is create something called Operation Shot Clock. So as you know, CFIUS is made up of nine different agencies. So you’ve got a lot of folks that have different inputs, different ideas, different concerns around national security. And part of my job is to coordinate all of that to ensure that we present a sort of timely and predictable process for the folks that are applying. So Operation Shot Clock basically says we have to pick particular days within that 90-day calendar, so to speak, that if we don’t have the information that we need from agencies, it immediately escalates. So it goes from the staff level to the director level to my level and ultimately up to the secretary as well. And the reason that’s important, and all of the secretaries who make up the committee have committed to this, the reason it’s important is to try to give that level of certainty and predictability. Because we certainly appreciate that a lot of people submit forms to the federal government and just get on their knees and hope and pray they’re going to hear back. We don’t want to be part of that process. Terry Gerton A lot of companies only interact with CFIUS periodically, maybe even only once. As you’re putting more of this information out there on the web and folks are having a chance to consider it in advance, what makes a successful CFIUS application? What should companies be thinking about if they’re going down this road? Chris Pilkerton So it’s a great point that you make. Because we do see what I’ll call, you know, one-off companies coming through, but we also do see companies that are coming back time and time again. And as part of that, we’re creating something called the Known Investor Program. When you think about a CFIUS transaction, you’ve got the parties that are making the transaction and then you’ve gotten the actual details of the transaction itself. And in that 90-day period, we have to focus on both of those. What this program will allow us to do is sort of do essentially a super-due diligence on companies that may be coming through the process more than once, so that we can focus our concerns around the risk, around the transaction itself. But as far as the applications go, as I mentioned in the pre-filing consultation, you can put as much or as little information as you want. We have a standard that we don’t start an application until we have all the information. So I think the advice that I would give is to be as comprehensive as you can — once again, CFIUS has confidentiality associated with this, that’s in statute — but also give sort of what your larger framework is going to be. Why are you doing this? Because it’s helpful to understand that. So for example, you may have someone that’s interested in coming in and making an investment in some kind of artificial intelligence company, but then they also may be interested down the road in getting involved in some sort of energy platform. So it’s important for us to kind of understand comprehensive approach that this company may want, and to the point that we were just talking about, if they’re going to come through again and again, it helps us better understand who that company is, what they’re about and who’s sort of across all the different stakeholders. Terry Gerton And as we said earlier, the website is fairly new, but are you seeing the impact in the way you expected as you watched the early filings come in? Chris Pilkerton We absolutely are. I think CFIUS is probably one of the least-known acronyms in all of D.C. nomenclature. And we’re doing our best to try to get it out there more — that’s part of this conversation. But I have talked to a number of folks that engage in our process, the legal bar around CFIUS is relatively small, and I’ve had conversations with a number the lawyers, but also the companies, saying this is just incredibly helpful. Being able to understand what you need is something that will allow us, when we’re putting our package together and sharing information with you, we just didn’t know exactly what you needed before. Now we’re hoping to make sure that people better understand it. Copyright © 2026 Federal News Network. All rights reserved. But this is big news for us because the website itself, and I would say probably the biggest thing, is when companies are coming to look to do transactions in the United States, to make investments — as opposed to immediately going out and getting counsel and conducting a large, timely filing that could certainly be, you know, very expensive — we want to be able to identify issues and connect them with a case officer. So there is a pre-filing consultation link that allows them to put some information about the transaction, anonymized if need be. And once again, as you know, CFIUS is confidential, all the information associated with it. So this information coming to the website would be confidential. What that does is it immediately gets them to a case officer who can review that information and then set up a follow-up call with the idea being, let’s talk through the transaction before it happens. And that’s incredibly important in the work that we do, because if someone has a transaction where there would be CFIUS jurisdiction and they end up closing the transaction, sometimes it’s hard to reopen that transaction if CFIUS needs to come in and present some mitigation options from a national security perspective.

Terry Gerton How have your case officers seen the quality of the information that they received change since you opened this portal?

Chris Pilkerton So it’s relatively new, but we’ve gotten a lot of outreach. And obviously we work with a lot of different counsel and people. You know, for good reason we’ll work with counsel to put that information in because if it’s more comprehensive, obviously we can give more feedback. But I will tell you that we’re seeing entrepreneurs who aren’t represented, present some information and share that with us. And there’s a couple of really important things about that. One, this idea of talking more about CFIUS from a customer service perspective serves the American people well because folks who, for no nefarious reason, may not inform us of their transactions; now we know about the transactions and they know about potential concerns. So that’s a big part of it. But I will also say that because we’re seeing historic levels of investment — as you might imagine, we’re see massive investment in the technology space. So, one of the programs that we’ve developed, and this is discussed on the website, is something called the Investment Security Technology Initiative. And the program is essentially working not just with all the subject matter experts throughout the U.S. government, but working with universities, working with corporate R&D, to see where pre-commercialized tech is going. And we’re not looking at anything proprietary there, we’re looking at any particular cases. What we want to know is, from a CFIUS perspective, can we be looking around corners to identify a risk that may be coming for all kinds of new things? So whether it’s quantum, whether it supercomputing, whether its hypersonics or biotech, are there ideas and concepts that are being discussed in the academic or in the R&D world? Well, we can be a part of those conversations to ensure that those companies, once they come through CFIUS, have the ability to grow, prosper and create jobs.

Terry Gerton Chris Pilkerton is the assistant secretary for investment security at the U.S. Treasury Department. One of the other features of the new website is the risk matrix. How does that help the public in general understand the risks that you all are looking at, and how are you measuring and assessing them?

Chris Pilkerton So it goes back to the point that you made earlier that when people have engaged with CFIUS in the past, they haven’t necessarily known what is CFIUS looking at, right? We know that CFIUS supports national security, but what does that actually mean? So going back to the concept of customer service, what we wanted to do is help put the public in the mind of a CFIUS case officer. So the risks that are on there, this is the first time this has ever happened, identify some of the more common risks that we see in program. But it’s not just the risks themselves; it’s also the applicable mitigation that we might want to work with the stakeholders on to be able to mitigate those risks. So things around, you know, privacy data and things that obviously potentially could compromise the American people or present some kind of national security issue — we want to be able to work with those parties in advance. And so it really is about kind of beginning that dialog. Because it’s not just about, like I said before, this historic investment in the United States, but it’s what those investments actually do for the economic development and the larger economy. I travel the country where we have companies that have come through the CFIUS process. And when I meet with them, inevitably, at the table are also the local economic development officials. Because there’s a number of programs and vendors that have been identified that are domestic companies that are able to support those CFIUS companies that come through. So we’re working closely with the Department of War and the Small Business Administration because we want to help identify those vendors so that these CFIUS companies really have the option to utilize a very large swath of incredibly talented domestic vendors.

Terry Gerton So I’m a foreign vendor, I’ve put my early information in, I’ve gotten in touch with my case officer, I know what risks you’re looking at, but now I have no idea what happened to my application, right? It’s gone into the bureaucratic black box. The new website offers a little more clarity there as well. Tell us how you’re helping people kind of know where they are in the process.

Chris Pilkerton So obviously you have the touch points with the case officer. There’s a variety of different stages in the CFIUS process, but from a statutory perspective, at its longest, there’s a 90-day statutory framework. And what we’ve also done for the first time is create something called Operation Shot Clock. So as you know, CFIUS is made up of nine different agencies. So you’ve got a lot of folks that have different inputs, different ideas, different concerns around national security. And part of my job is to coordinate all of that to ensure that we present a sort of timely and predictable process for the folks that are applying. So Operation Shot Clock basically says we have to pick particular days within that 90-day calendar, so to speak, that if we don’t have the information that we need from agencies, it immediately escalates. So it goes from the staff level to the director level to my level and ultimately up to the secretary as well. And the reason that’s important, and all of the secretaries who make up the committee have committed to this, the reason it’s important is to try to give that level of certainty and predictability. Because we certainly appreciate that a lot of people submit forms to the federal government and just get on their knees and hope and pray they’re going to hear back. We don’t want to be part of that process.

Terry Gerton A lot of companies only interact with CFIUS periodically, maybe even only once. As you’re putting more of this information out there on the web and folks are having a chance to consider it in advance, what makes a successful CFIUS application? What should companies be thinking about if they’re going down this road?

Chris Pilkerton So it’s a great point that you make. Because we do see what I’ll call, you know, one-off companies coming through, but we also do see companies that are coming back time and time again. And as part of that, we’re creating something called the Known Investor Program. When you think about a CFIUS transaction, you’ve got the parties that are making the transaction and then you’ve gotten the actual details of the transaction itself. And in that 90-day period, we have to focus on both of those. What this program will allow us to do is sort of do essentially a super-due diligence on companies that may be coming through the process more than once, so that we can focus our concerns around the risk, around the transaction itself. But as far as the applications go, as I mentioned in the pre-filing consultation, you can put as much or as little information as you want. We have a standard that we don’t start an application until we have all the information. So I think the advice that I would give is to be as comprehensive as you can — once again, CFIUS has confidentiality associated with this, that’s in statute — but also give sort of what your larger framework is going to be. Why are you doing this? Because it’s helpful to understand that. So for example, you may have someone that’s interested in coming in and making an investment in some kind of artificial intelligence company, but then they also may be interested down the road in getting involved in some sort of energy platform. So it’s important for us to kind of understand comprehensive approach that this company may want, and to the point that we were just talking about, if they’re going to come through again and again, it helps us better understand who that company is, what they’re about and who’s sort of across all the different stakeholders.
Terry Gerton And as we said earlier, the website is fairly new, but are you seeing the impact in the way you expected as you watched the early filings come in?

Chris Pilkerton We absolutely are. I think CFIUS is probably one of the least-known acronyms in all of D.C. nomenclature. And we’re doing our best to try to get it out there more — that’s part of this conversation. But I have talked to a number of folks that engage in our process, the legal bar around CFIUS is relatively small, and I’ve had conversations with a number the lawyers, but also the companies, saying this is just incredibly helpful. Being able to understand what you need is something that will allow us, when we’re putting our package together and sharing information with you, we just didn’t know exactly what you needed before. Now we’re hoping to make sure that people better understand it.

coreStoryFacts.text: This statutory and regulatory confinement of CFIUS’ jurisdiction has resulted in very few reviews of real estate as noted in CFIUS annual reports. [4] Therefore, CFIUS continues to expand its jurisdiction to review real estate transactions that may impact US national security.

For example, on July 25, the Senate voted 91-7 to amend the National Defense Authorization Act to (1) prohibit businesses based in China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea from purchasing US farmland and (2) require CFIUS review of specific types of land purchases by investors from any other foreign country. [12] While some of these proposals address the issue of federal preemption, many are silent on the subject. [13] STATE LEGISLATIVE SOLUTIONS Some state governments have promulgated laws and regulations governing the purchase of real estate by foreign investors.

National Foreign Trade Council that a conflict inherently existed when both the federal and state government imposed various sanctions on Burma. [21] In 2013, the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ruled that Florida’s “Cuba Amendment,” which prevented companies that did business in Cuba from bidding on public contracts worth at least $1 million, was unconstitutional, as it conflicted with federal sanctions on Cuba. [22] Although the state statutes did not (1) expressly contradict or (2) implicitly preempt the federal sanctions, they did attempt to regulate an interest in the federal domain which weakened the president’s ability to unilaterally conduct foreign relations.
On the other hand, since 1789, national security and foreign affairs have been the primary responsibility of the US federal government.

Since January 2023, more than half of the states have proposed at least one bill relating to foreign investment in real estate with the most recent states being Michigan and Wisconsin. [14] These range from an absolute prohibition on certain acquisitions, to narrowed permissions for specific purposes, while others merely require reporting to the state.

Like the federal government, many states are currently considering some regulation focused on foreign ownership of farmland. [17] A state survey can be found at the National Agricultural Law Center. [18] Challenges to state legislation restricting acquisitions by certain foreign persons are likely to face challenges on this ground, as well as other constitutional and federal statutory grounds, including equal protection and the Federal Housing Act.
When CFIUS reviews such transactions, they can block the transaction from occurring or enforce mitigation measures that are negotiated as part of a national security agreement.

CFIUS maintains a list of ports and military installations for this purpose, and Appendix A to Part 802 to Title 31 of the Code of Federal Regulations identifies 211 currently sensitive US military installations across the United States.

And that’s incredibly important in the work that we do, because if someone has a transaction where there would be CFIUS jurisdiction and they end up closing the transaction, sometimes it’s hard to reopen that transaction if CFIUS needs to come in and present some mitigation options from a national security perspective.

extraction.body: Jurisdictional limits on the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) regarding the review of certain real estate transactions have led Congress to introduce proposals expanding its jurisdiction and certain states to adopt more restrictive laws and regulations on real estate acquisition by certain foreign persons. Some of these state laws may be subject to challenges on constitutional and other grounds, and Florida SB 264 may be the first such test case. Historically, national security issues only occasionally arose in real estate transactions based on the proximity of the real estate to military bases and strategic ports and the rights of the foreign investor in the real estate. The Foreign Investment Risk Review and Modernization Act of 2018 (FIRRMA) and the implementing regulations clarified and expanded the rules determining when a real estate transaction constituted a “covered real estate transaction” separate and apart from the acquisition of control over a US business, [1] although filing remained (and remains) voluntary. [2] In December 2022, CFIUS determined that it did not have jurisdiction to review Chinese company Fufeng Group Limited’s (Fufeng) proposed $700 million corn milling project in North Dakota. [3] The news came after CFIUS completed a three-month review and investigation of Fufeng’s purchase from a private citizen of a 370-acre greenfield site in Grand Forks, North Dakota, to build a wet corn mill. Criticized for this decision, CFIUS has recently proposed additions to the list of covered real estate. The Fufeng decision reinvigorated Congressional efforts to expand CFIUS’s jurisdiction to cover agricultural and other lands. Congress members have proposed changes to CFIUS as part of amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) as well as through independent legislation. Some of the proposals would expressly preempt conflicting state action while others are silent on the subject. Various states have filled the gap created by the jurisdictional limitations of CFIUS and passed legislation restricting the ability of certain foreign persons to acquire real estate in their state. Some of these states cite national security as the statutory basis, creating potential challenges on the basis of federal preemption. For example, Florida SB 264, which prohibits the purchase of real property by persons in or from the People’s Republic of China, was passed in May 2023 and has been challenged on the grounds of federal preemption, as well as violations of equal protection and the Fair Housing Act. CURRENT CFIUS REGIME The US Department of the Treasury, which chairs CFIUS, has the authority to review foreign investment in US businesses as well as certain real estate transactions. When CFIUS reviews such transactions, they can block the transaction from occurring or enforce mitigation measures that are negotiated as part of a national security agreement. However, Congress limited CFIUS’ authority to only review purchases of real estate in air or maritime ports or in a prescribed proximity to military installations (defined as within 100 miles of the base). CFIUS maintains a list of ports and military installations for this purpose, and Appendix A to Part 802 to Title 31 of the Code of Federal Regulations identifies 211 currently sensitive US military installations across the United States. Disclosure of the transaction to CFIUS remains voluntary, although CFIUS can conduct a national security review at any time for covered transactions that were not submitted for clearance by CFIUS—the so-called non-notified outreach. This statutory and regulatory confinement of CFIUS’ jurisdiction has resulted in very few reviews of real estate as noted in CFIUS annual reports. [4] Therefore, CFIUS continues to expand its jurisdiction to review real estate transactions that may impact US national security. PROPOSED CHANGES TO CFIUS REAL ESTATE REGULATIONS On May 5, 2023, the Treasury Department published a proposed rule in the Federal Register to expand the list of sensitive military installations subject to review under CFIUS' authority, applicable to certain real estate transactions involving foreign investors or acquirers. [5] The proposed rule would add eight new military installations to Appendix A, including seven US Air Force bases principally involved in the ongoing development of the B-21 Raider stealth bomber aircraft, as well as the Iowa National Guard Joint Force Headquarters, all of which would be added to Part 2 and thus be subject to the expanded 100-mile geographic range. Importantly, the proposed rule, if adopted, would not change the filing requirements associated with real estate transactions, which would remain voluntary under CFIUS' real estate regulations (Part 802). The eight additions to Appendix A include: Air Force Plant 42, Palmdale, California Dyess Air Force Base, Abilene, Texas Ellsworth Air Force Base, Box Elder, South Dakota Grand Forks Air Force Base, Grand Forks, North Dakota Iowa National Guard Joint Force Headquarters, Des Moines, Iowa Lackland Air Force Base, San Antonio, Texas Laughlin Air Force Base, Del Rio, Texas Luke Air Force Base, Glendale, Arizona However, these additions may be heralding additional changes to CFIUS’ authority to review real estate transactions. For example, on July 25, the Senate voted 91-7 to amend the National Defense Authorization Act to (1) prohibit businesses based in China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea from purchasing US farmland and (2) require CFIUS review of specific types of land purchases by investors from any other foreign country. [12] While some of these proposals address the issue of federal preemption, many are silent on the subject. [13] STATE LEGISLATIVE SOLUTIONS Some state governments have promulgated laws and regulations governing the purchase of real estate by foreign investors. Since January 2023, more than half of the states have proposed at least one bill relating to foreign investment in real estate with the most recent states being Michigan and Wisconsin. [14] These range from an absolute prohibition on certain acquisitions, to narrowed permissions for specific purposes, while others merely require reporting to the state. Lawmakers in other states are watching these activities and considering whether to pass similar measures. [15] Because state interests, types of land, and public needs vary greatly between the states, there is no one-size-fits-all solution; [16] each can tailor its statute or proposal to address its respective concerns. Like the federal government, many states are currently considering some regulation focused on foreign ownership of farmland. [17] A state survey can be found at the National Agricultural Law Center. [18] Challenges to state legislation restricting acquisitions by certain foreign persons are likely to face challenges on this ground, as well as other constitutional and federal statutory grounds, including equal protection and the Federal Housing Act. FEDERAL PREEMPTION Under the US Constitution, federal laws will generally preempt state law where federal and state law conflict or the federal government has or may occupy the field. [19] The analysis of whether a state law is preempted by federal law can be quite complex. There are two types of implied preemption—field and conflict: Conflict preemption is when compliance with conflicting federal and state regulations is either impossible or the state law presents an obstacle to compliance with the federal law. Field preemption is when a state attempts to regulate an interest in the federal domain. [20] Because foreign affairs and national security traditionally fall under the purview of the federal government, states have only been permitted to pass statutes relating to national security when the federal government had not previously acted in that area, such as in the following instances: The US Supreme Court ruled in Crosby v. National Foreign Trade Council that a conflict inherently existed when both the federal and state government imposed various sanctions on Burma. [21] In 2013, the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ruled that Florida’s “Cuba Amendment,” which prevented companies that did business in Cuba from bidding on public contracts worth at least $1 million, was unconstitutional, as it conflicted with federal sanctions on Cuba. [22] Although the state statutes did not (1) expressly contradict or (2) implicitly preempt the federal sanctions, they did attempt to regulate an interest in the federal domain which weakened the president’s ability to unilaterally conduct foreign relations. However, unlike sanctions, trade, and embargoes, which have historically been recognized as the responsibility of the federal government, federal preemption in the context of the regulation of private ownership of land is less clear. Removing (or curtailing) a state’s ability to regulate local ownership of land within its borders undermines one of the fundamental roles of local government. Historical precedent also demonstrates that the federal government can (and should) instruct states on what types of rules and regulations are appropriate in the context of civil rights and the prevention of racial discrimination. Even eminent domain—a right for the government to take and convert property to public use—is exercised by both the federal and state governments. On the other hand, since 1789, national security and foreign affairs have been the primary responsibility of the US federal government. The failure of individual states to cooperate and manage their own foreign affairs was a primary motivation for the creation of the original Constitutional Convention. Whether it be the signing of treaties, declarations of war, commanding of the armed forces, regulating international and interstate trade, conducting diplomacy, or managing other aspects of national security, the federal government is the primary, and usually sole, authority. [23] As an interagency committee made up of US government agency members, CFIUS occupies a unique role to identify, assess, and mitigate any risks to US national security related to the acquisition of real estate.

Some of these state laws may be subject to challenges on constitutional and other grounds, and Florida SB 264 may be the first such test case.

Historically, national security issues only occasionally arose in real estate transactions based on the proximity of the real estate to military bases and strategic ports and the rights of the foreign investor in the real estate.

The Foreign Investment Risk Review and Modernization Act of 2018 (FIRRMA) and the implementing regulations clarified and expanded the rules determining when a real estate transaction constituted a “covered real estate transaction” separate and apart from the acquisition of control over a US business, [1] although filing remained (and remains) voluntary. [2] In December 2022, CFIUS determined that it did not have jurisdiction to review Chinese company Fufeng Group Limited’s (Fufeng) proposed $700 million corn milling project in North Dakota. [3] The news came after CFIUS completed a three-month review and investigation of Fufeng’s purchase from a private citizen of a 370-acre greenfield site in Grand Forks, North Dakota, to build a wet corn mill.
Criticized for this decision, CFIUS has recently proposed additions to the list of covered real estate.
The Fufeng decision reinvigorated Congressional efforts to expand CFIUS’s jurisdiction to cover agricultural and other lands.

Some of the proposals would expressly preempt conflicting state action while others are silent on the subject.

extraction.body: "I think CFIUS is probably one of the least-known acronyms in D.C. nomenclature. We're doing our best to try to get it out there more," Chris Pilkerton said. Terry Gerton The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, or CFIUS, just updated its website. Normally an updated website is not big news, but there are newsy bits here. And so I want to go through some of them with you. In my experience, CFIUS is sort of shrouded in mystery, but the focus of the website is on more transparency. Why does it seem like that is so important right now? Chris Pilkerton You’re right. Oftentimes, updates to a website for the federal government are not something that are newsworthy. But we really think this is, in large part because while national security will always be the North Star and the mission of CFIUS, the secretary and the president are very focused on ensuring that we are engaging with the public and ensuring that they understand the process as much as possible. So you’ve talked about this idea of CFIUS being shrouded in secrecy. The reality is we’re trying to demystify CFIUS. Now, there are components of it that will certainly remain in that so-called black box because of the work that we do with the intelligence community to ensure that we are securing our national security concerns. But this is big news for us because the website itself, and I would say probably the biggest thing, is when companies are coming to look to do transactions in the United States, to make investments — as opposed to immediately going out and getting counsel and conducting a large, timely filing that could certainly be, you know, very expensive — we want to be able to identify issues and connect them with a case officer. So there is a pre-filing consultation link that allows them to put some information about the transaction, anonymized if need be. And once again, as you know, CFIUS is confidential, all the information associated with it. So this information coming to the website would be confidential. What that does is it immediately gets them to a case officer who can review that information and then set up a follow-up call with the idea being, let’s talk through the transaction before it happens. And that’s incredibly important in the work that we do, because if someone has a transaction where there would be CFIUS jurisdiction and they end up closing the transaction, sometimes it’s hard to reopen that transaction if CFIUS needs to come in and present some mitigation options from a national security perspective. Register today! Terry Gerton How have your case officers seen the quality of the information that they received change since you opened this portal? Chris Pilkerton So it’s relatively new, but we’ve gotten a lot of outreach. And obviously we work with a lot of different counsel and people. You know, for good reason we’ll work with counsel to put that information in because if it’s more comprehensive, obviously we can give more feedback. But I will tell you that we’re seeing entrepreneurs who aren’t represented, present some information and share that with us. And there’s a couple of really important things about that. One, this idea of talking more about CFIUS from a customer service perspective serves the American people well because folks who, for no nefarious reason, may not inform us of their transactions; now we know about the transactions and they know about potential concerns. So that’s a big part of it. But I will also say that because we’re seeing historic levels of investment — as you might imagine, we’re see massive investment in the technology space. So, one of the programs that we’ve developed, and this is discussed on the website, is something called the Investment Security Technology Initiative. And the program is essentially working not just with all the subject matter experts throughout the U.S. government, but working with universities, working with corporate R&D, to see where pre-commercialized tech is going. And we’re not looking at anything proprietary there, we’re looking at any particular cases. What we want to know is, from a CFIUS perspective, can we be looking around corners to identify a risk that may be coming for all kinds of new things? So whether it’s quantum, whether it supercomputing, whether its hypersonics or biotech, are there ideas and concepts that are being discussed in the academic or in the R&D world? Well, we can be a part of those conversations to ensure that those companies, once they come through CFIUS, have the ability to grow, prosper and create jobs. Terry Gerton Chris Pilkerton is the assistant secretary for investment security at the U.S. Treasury Department. One of the other features of the new website is the risk matrix. How does that help the public in general understand the risks that you all are looking at, and how are you measuring and assessing them? Chris Pilkerton So it goes back to the point that you made earlier that when people have engaged with CFIUS in the past, they haven’t necessarily known what is CFIUS looking at, right? We know that CFIUS supports national security, but what does that actually mean? So going back to the concept of customer service, what we wanted to do is help put the public in the mind of a CFIUS case officer. So the risks that are on there, this is the first time this has ever happened, identify some of the more common risks that we see in program. But it’s not just the risks themselves; it’s also the applicable mitigation that we might want to work with the stakeholders on to be able to mitigate those risks. So things around, you know, privacy data and things that obviously potentially could compromise the American people or present some kind of national security issue — we want to be able to work with those parties in advance. And so it really is about kind of beginning that dialog. Because it’s not just about, like I said before, this historic investment in the United States, but it’s what those investments actually do for the economic development and the larger economy. I travel the country where we have companies that have come through the CFIUS process. And when I meet with them, inevitably, at the table are also the local economic development officials. Because there’s a number of programs and vendors that have been identified that are domestic companies that are able to support those CFIUS companies that come through. So we’re working closely with the Department of War and the Small Business Administration because we want to help identify those vendors so that these CFIUS companies really have the option to utilize a very large swath of incredibly talented domestic vendors. Terry Gerton So I’m a foreign vendor, I’ve put my early information in, I’ve gotten in touch with my case officer, I know what risks you’re looking at, but now I have no idea what happened to my application, right? It’s gone into the bureaucratic black box. The new website offers a little more clarity there as well. Tell us how you’re helping people kind of know where they are in the process. Chris Pilkerton So obviously you have the touch points with the case officer. There’s a variety of different stages in the CFIUS process, but from a statutory perspective, at its longest, there’s a 90-day statutory framework. And what we’ve also done for the first time is create something called Operation Shot Clock. So as you know, CFIUS is made up of nine different agencies. So you’ve got a lot of folks that have different inputs, different ideas, different concerns around national security. And part of my job is to coordinate all of that to ensure that we present a sort of timely and predictable process for the folks that are applying. So Operation Shot Clock basically says we have to pick particular days within that 90-day calendar, so to speak, that if we don’t have the information that we need from agencies, it immediately escalates. So it goes from the staff level to the director level to my level and ultimately up to the secretary as well. And the reason that’s important, and all of the secretaries who make up the committee have committed to this, the reason it’s important is to try to give that level of certainty and predictability. Because we certainly appreciate that a lot of people submit forms to the federal government and just get on their knees and hope and pray they’re going to hear back. We don’t want to be part of that process. Terry Gerton A lot of companies only interact with CFIUS periodically, maybe even only once. As you’re putting more of this information out there on the web and folks are having a chance to consider it in advance, what makes a successful CFIUS application? What should companies be thinking about if they’re going down this road? Chris Pilkerton So it’s a great point that you make. Because we do see what I’ll call, you know, one-off companies coming through, but we also do see companies that are coming back time and time again. And as part of that, we’re creating something called the Known Investor Program. When you think about a CFIUS transaction, you’ve got the parties that are making the transaction and then you’ve gotten the actual details of the transaction itself. And in that 90-day period, we have to focus on both of those. What this program will allow us to do is sort of do essentially a super-due diligence on companies that may be coming through the process more than once, so that we can focus our concerns around the risk, around the transaction itself. But as far as the applications go, as I mentioned in the pre-filing consultation, you can put as much or as little information as you want. We have a standard that we don’t start an application until we have all the information. So I think the advice that I would give is to be as comprehensive as you can — once again, CFIUS has confidentiality associated with this, that’s in statute — but also give sort of what your larger framework is going to be. Why are you doing this? Because it’s helpful to understand that. So for example, you may have someone that’s interested in coming in and making an investment in some kind of artificial intelligence company, but then they also may be interested down the road in getting involved in some sort of energy platform. So it’s important for us to kind of understand comprehensive approach that this company may want, and to the point that we were just talking about, if they’re going to come through again and again, it helps us better understand who that company is, what they’re about and who’s sort of across all the different stakeholders. Terry Gerton And as we said earlier, the website is fairly new, but are you seeing the impact in the way you expected as you watched the early filings come in? Chris Pilkerton We absolutely are. I think CFIUS is probably one of the least-known acronyms in all of D.C. nomenclature. And we’re doing our best to try to get it out there more — that’s part of this conversation. But I have talked to a number of folks that engage in our process, the legal bar around CFIUS is relatively small, and I’ve had conversations with a number the lawyers, but also the companies, saying this is just incredibly helpful. Being able to understand what you need is something that will allow us, when we’re putting our package together and sharing information with you, we just didn’t know exactly what you needed before. Now we’re hoping to make sure that people better understand it. Copyright © 2026 Federal News Network. All rights reserved. You know, for good reason we’ll work with counsel to put that information in because if it’s more comprehensive, obviously we can give more feedback. But I will tell you that we’re seeing entrepreneurs who aren’t represented, present some information and share that with us. And there’s a couple of really important things about that. One, this idea of talking more about CFIUS from a customer service perspective serves the American people well because folks who, for no nefarious reason, may not inform us of their transactions; now we know about the transactions and they know about potential concerns. So that’s a big part of it. But I will also say that because we’re seeing historic levels of investment — as you might imagine, we’re see massive investment in the technology space. So, one of the programs that we’ve developed, and this is discussed on the website, is something called the Investment Security Technology Initiative. And the program is essentially working not just with all the subject matter experts throughout the U.S. government, but working with universities, working with corporate R&D, to see where pre-commercialized tech is going. And we’re not looking at anything proprietary there, we’re looking at any particular cases. What we want to know is, from a CFIUS perspective, can we be looking around corners to identify a risk that may be coming for all kinds of new things? So whether it’s quantum, whether it supercomputing, whether its hypersonics or biotech, are there ideas and concepts that are being discussed in the academic or in the R&D world? Well, we can be a part of those conversations to ensure that those companies, once they come through CFIUS, have the ability to grow, prosper and create jobs.

Terry Gerton Chris Pilkerton is the assistant secretary for investment security at the U.S. Treasury Department. One of the other features of the new website is the risk matrix. How does that help the public in general understand the risks that you all are looking at, and how are you measuring and assessing them?

Chris Pilkerton So it goes back to the point that you made earlier that when people have engaged with CFIUS in the past, they haven’t necessarily known what is CFIUS looking at, right? We know that CFIUS supports national security, but what does that actually mean? So going back to the concept of customer service, what we wanted to do is help put the public in the mind of a CFIUS case officer. So the risks that are on there, this is the first time this has ever happened, identify some of the more common risks that we see in program. But it’s not just the risks themselves; it’s also the applicable mitigation that we might want to work with the stakeholders on to be able to mitigate those risks. So things around, you know, privacy data and things that obviously potentially could compromise the American people or present some kind of national security issue — we want to be able to work with those parties in advance. And so it really is about kind of beginning that dialog. Because it’s not just about, like I said before, this historic investment in the United States, but it’s what those investments actually do for the economic development and the larger economy. I travel the country where we have companies that have come through the CFIUS process. And when I meet with them, inevitably, at the table are also the local economic development officials. Because there’s a number of programs and vendors that have been identified that are domestic companies that are able to support those CFIUS companies that come through. So we’re working closely with the Department of War and the Small Business Administration because we want to help identify those vendors so that these CFIUS companies really have the option to utilize a very large swath of incredibly talented domestic vendors.

Terry Gerton So I’m a foreign vendor, I’ve put my early information in, I’ve gotten in touch with my case officer, I know what risks you’re looking at, but now I have no idea what happened to my application, right? It’s gone into the bureaucratic black box. The new website offers a little more clarity there as well. Tell us how you’re helping people kind of know where they are in the process.

Chris Pilkerton So obviously you have the touch points with the case officer. There’s a variety of different stages in the CFIUS process, but from a statutory perspective, at its longest, there’s a 90-day statutory framework. And what we’ve also done for the first time is create something called Operation Shot Clock. So as you know, CFIUS is made up of nine different agencies. So you’ve got a lot of folks that have different inputs, different ideas, different concerns around national security. And part of my job is to coordinate all of that to ensure that we present a sort of timely and predictable process for the folks that are applying. So Operation Shot Clock basically says we have to pick particular days within that 90-day calendar, so to speak, that if we don’t have the information that we need from agencies, it immediately escalates. So it goes from the staff level to the director level to my level and ultimately up to the secretary as well. And the reason that’s important, and all of the secretaries who make up the committee have committed to this, the reason it’s important is to try to give that level of certainty and predictability. Because we certainly appreciate that a lot of people submit forms to the federal government and just get on their knees and hope and pray they’re going to hear back. We don’t want to be part of that process.

Terry Gerton A lot of companies only interact with CFIUS periodically, maybe even only once. As you’re putting more of this information out there on the web and folks are having a chance to consider it in advance, what makes a successful CFIUS application? What should companies be thinking about if they’re going down this road?

Chris Pilkerton So it’s a great point that you make. Because we do see what I’ll call, you know, one-off companies coming through, but we also do see companies that are coming back time and time again. And as part of that, we’re creating something called the Known Investor Program. When you think about a CFIUS transaction, you’ve got the parties that are making the transaction and then you’ve gotten the actual details of the transaction itself. And in that 90-day period, we have to focus on both of those. What this program will allow us to do is sort of do essentially a super-due diligence on companies that may be coming through the process more than once, so that we can focus our concerns around the risk, around the transaction itself. But as far as the applications go, as I mentioned in the pre-filing consultation, you can put as much or as little information as you want. We have a standard that we don’t start an application until we have all the information. So I think the advice that I would give is to be as comprehensive as you can — once again, CFIUS has confidentiality associated with this, that’s in statute — but also give sort of what your larger framework is going to be. Why are you doing this? Because it’s helpful to understand that. So for example, you may have someone that’s interested in coming in and making an investment in some kind of artificial intelligence company, but then they also may be interested down the road in getting involved in some sort of energy platform. So it’s important for us to kind of understand comprehensive approach that this company may want, and to the point that we were just talking about, if they’re going to come through again and again, it helps us better understand who that company is, what they’re about and who’s sort of across all the different stakeholders.
Terry Gerton And as we said earlier, the website is fairly new, but are you seeing the impact in the way you expected as you watched the early filings come in?

Chris Pilkerton We absolutely are. I think CFIUS is probably one of the least-known acronyms in all of D.C. nomenclature. And we’re doing our best to try to get it out there more — that’s part of this conversation. But I have talked to a number of folks that engage in our process, the legal bar around CFIUS is relatively small, and I’ve had conversations with a number the lawyers, but also the companies, saying this is just incredibly helpful. Being able to understand what you need is something that will allow us, when we’re putting our package together and sharing information with you, we just didn’t know exactly what you needed before. Now we’re hoping to make sure that people better understand it.

However, average investors should be more interested in what big hedge fund managers are buying now. Here are two superb AI stocks billionaires are buying as they sell Nvidia. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) vaulted to the forefront of the AI space when it added $10 billion to its investment in generative AI leader OpenAI in early 2023. Despite its position as one of the most valuable companies in the world before the AI boom, artificial intelligence is proving to be a substantial growth area for the technology company. Several billionaire fund managers saw an opportunity to buy more shares of Microsoft in the first quarter, including: Ole Andreas Halvorsen: bought 1,596,887 shares, reestablishing a position in the stock for his Viking Global Investors fund. Steven Cohen: bought 566,749 shares, more than doubling Point72's stake in the stock. He also disposed of options positions, including 1,844 put options. Chris Rokos: bought 274,232 shares, increasing his hedge fund's stake by 172% from the fourth quarter. Microsoft's core AI product is Azure AI, which provides cloud solutions for AI developers looking to use existing foundation models to deploy new AI-powered software solutions. The company grew its Azure AI customers by 60% year over year last quarter, and the average expenditure per customer is growing, too. Microsoft is investing heavily in building out its data center capacity. But management said it will take some time for all of it to come online. As a result, it expects an acceleration in Azure revenue in the second half of fiscal 2025. That's quite a feat, considering it's already the fastest-growing hyperscale cloud provider today. Microsoft also offers its own AI assistants across its enterprise software portfolio, which is called Copilot. Adoption is growing quickly, with customers increasing 60% quarter over quarter. With over 400 million Office 365 commercial seats, there's a long runway for growth for the product. The stock currently trades around 30 times forward earnings estimates. While that's a significant premium to the S&P 500 , the stock seems well worth the price. It's leadership in enterprise software solutions and AI development should provide years of outsized growth. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) has long been at the forefront of AI development. Machine learning algorithms form the backbone of the content feeds on Facebook and Instagram, along with the up-and-coming Threads, which recently passed 200 million monthly active users. Recently, it's turned its attention to generative AI, developing and open-sourcing the Llama family of foundation models, which are behind its Meta AI feature in Instagram and Facebook as well as many other behind-the-scenes features. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has the ambition to turn Meta into "the leading AI company in the world." Billionaires are buying into Zuckerberg's vision and putting their money into the stock. Some high-profile purchases in the first quarter include: Chris Rokos: bought 377,551 shares, reestablishing a position for his hedge fund for the first time since 2022. Stanley Druckenmiller: bought 63,930 shares, reestablishing a position. While Meta already uses AI across its family of apps for content recommendations, it's starting to integrate it into its advertising services. Zuckerberg said he sees a day when "advertisers will basically just be able to tell us a business's objective and a budget, and we're going to do the rest for them," during Meta's second-quarter earnings call. He also sees Meta facilitating the creation of AI service agents for business, which opens the door for more business messaging monetization opportunities. Put it all together, and AI will have a considerable impact on Meta's continued revenue growth. Increased engagement combined with lower hurdles to creating and targeting advertisements and improving the algorithms needed to target those advertisements as accurately as possible should all result in strong revenue and profit growth for the social media company. Meanwhile, its hardware business, including its Oculus VR headsets and Ray-Ban sunglasses, is showing strong growth bolstered by its AI features. Meta shares currently trade around 23 times forward earnings estimates, which is considerably lower than most AI stocks. That's despite the fact that Meta's bottom line continues to grow at a steady rate in the mid to high double digits, giving it a very attractive PEG ratio. Its continued investments in AI should ultimately produce strong returns for the company and its shareholders. extraction.body: Billionaire investors did not make their fortunes on luck. Most of them have been investing for decades and have experience across many cycles, allowing them to recognize the makings of a successful investment before the rest of the market does. That's why many investors are always anxious to see what billionaires are buying and selling each quarter. Retail investors should never just follow billionaires. Most billionaire investors run hedge funds, which invest on much shorter time horizons. You won't find out about their trades until after they make them, often at least a few months later. However, following billionaires and their investments can be a good way to get new ideas and test your investment thesis. In the second quarter of the year, billionaires sold six artificial intelligence stocks . Should you? All year, investors have been back and forth on the AI trade. Hyperscalers have committed to spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI-related infrastructure due to what they claim is off-the-charts demand. While one cohort of the market certainly buys the hype, another is worried that the returns on this capital investment will not be strong enough to justify it. Furthermore, they grow worried that companies once known as cash-generating machines are now generating negative free cash flow. Investors are also cautious in general right now, believing a correction or market reset is needed after several strong years of returns. In Q2 of the year, billionaires or their funds sold six key stocks in the "Magnificent Seven," which have carried the market for several years now: Investors should understand that no one, not even billionaire investors, knows how the AI trade will play out. Billionaires also aren't selling these solely because they don't believe in AI. It also has to do with the individual companies themselves. For instance, in Q2, Appaloosa sold Microsoft but initiated a new position in Apple while increasing its stakes in Meta, Amazon, and Alphabet. Ultimately, I would advise investors to take a similar approach. Don't simply sell all stocks with AI exposure. Evaluate them on a company-by-company basis. Of the six mentioned above, I would certainly stay away from Tesla, which has launched an autonomous ride-hailing fleet and intends to build humanoid robots. The technology does not appear to be perfected, but Tesla's valuation of nearly 215 times forward earnings already assumes significant success in these business lines, which isn't guaranteed. Of the others, while I think there is an investment case for each, Amazon and Apple are my top picks right now. While Amazon is planning for $220 billion of capital expenditures this year, the company's Amazon Web Services cloud division just posted 37% annual revenue growth, its best performance in 18 quarters. I like Apple simply because it has not invested hundreds of billions in data centers, yet it can still benefit from AI by integrating the technology into its many popular consumer products. While one cohort of the market certainly buys the hype, another is worried that the returns on this capital investment will not be strong enough to justify it. I like Apple simply because it has not invested hundreds of billions in data centers, yet it can still benefit from AI by integrating the technology into its many popular consumer products.
