An investment of $10,000 in Nvidia stock made five years ago is now worth an impressive $102,000. Meanwhile, Micron has turned a similar investment into nearly $135,000 over the same period. The strong earnings growth rate of these semiconductor stocks , along with their attractive valuations, is likely to lead to more gains by 2030. However, there's another emerging AI hardware play that could make investors significantly richer by the end of the decade. Jabil ( JBL -2.30% ) is a contract electronics manufacturer that designs, engineers, and manufactures electronic components and hardware for multiple industries. AI has supercharged its growth, and I won't be surprised to see the stock doubling by 2030. Let's see why that may be the case. Jabil's fiscal 2026 ended on a strong note. The company reported $36 billion in revenue for the fiscal year ending Aug. 31, up 21% from the prior year. The company's core operating margin increased by 40 basis points last fiscal year, resulting in a 34% increase in non-GAAP earnings per share to $13.09. The growth rate improved in fiscal 2025, when Jabil posted a 3% increase in revenue and a 15% increase in earnings. AI played a central role in boosting Jabil's growth. The company manufactures AI server racks, cooling systems, and power management solutions for major hyperscalers, such as Meta Platforms , Amazon , and Alphabet 's Google, as noted by investment bank UBS . These partnerships helped Jabil deliver $14.4 billion in AI revenue in fiscal 2026, up significantly from $5.4 billion in the previous year. Importantly, Jabil expects its AI revenue to jump to $22.1 billion in fiscal 2027, implying a 54% increase over last year. However, don't be surprised to see Jabil's AI revenue growing at a stronger pace. That's because Jabil's hyperscale customers are ramping up their AI infrastructure deployments. For instance, Jabil management noted on the latest earnings call that its "second hyperscale customer started with a single capability and has grown into a storage program above $1 billion in annual revenue." The company added a third hyperscale customer in the third quarter of fiscal 2026. Given that Jabil is offering more than just server racks, its customers end up buying cooling and power management solutions as well. This land-and-expand strategy helps Jabil to get more business from existing customers, enabling it to clock stronger growth in both revenue and earnings. Also, there is a solid chance that Jabil's AI-focused customer base will expand further owing to continued investments in AI infrastructure. For instance, Gartner expects the AI infrastructure market to reach $1.48 trillion in revenue in 2026 from $982 billion last year. The firm expects the size of this market to expand to $1.98 trillion next year. AI pioneer Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang estimates that AI infrastructure spending could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. As server racks, cooling systems, and power management solutions play a critical role in AI data centers, the demand for Jabil's offerings should continue improving. So, it is easy to see why the company expects a stronger increase of 23.6% in revenue in the current fiscal year to $44.5 billion. Additionally, it sees a 34% jump in non-GAAP earnings per share to $17.55. However, Jabil could exceed expectations amid strong AI infrastructure spending , which is precisely why analysts have significantly raised their growth expectations for the company. Jabil's earnings per share are poised to grow at healthy double-digit rates over the next three years, according to consensus estimates. JBL EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts The chart above indicates that the company could report $25.93 in earnings per share in fiscal 2029 (ending in August 2029). Assuming its bottom line grows by even 15% in fiscal 2030, its earnings per share could reach $29.82 after four years. If this AI stock trades at even 22 times earnings at that time, in line with the tech-laden Nasdaq-100 index's forward earnings multiple, its stock price could reach $660. That's 128% higher than Jabil's stock price, indicating that a $10,000 investment in this stock could be worth over $22,750 by the end of the decade. However, if Jabil outpaces analysts' expectations, it could command a premium valuation and deliver bigger gains. So, if you've $10,000 in investible cash right now, buying Jabil with that money could be a smart move given its healthy upside potential. passages: Nvidia and Micron Technology have made investors significantly richer over the past five years, and there is a solid chance that both artificial intelligence (AI) hardware specialists will surge higher by the end of the decade amid strong demand for AI data center infrastructure.

An investment of $10,000 in Nvidia stock made five years ago is now worth an impressive $102,000. Meanwhile, Micron has turned a similar investment into nearly $135,000 over the same period. The strong earnings growth rate of these semiconductor stocks , along with their attractive valuations, is likely to lead to more gains by 2030. However, there's another emerging AI hardware play that could make investors significantly richer by the end of the decade.

Jabil ( JBL -2.30% ) is a contract electronics manufacturer that designs, engineers, and manufactures electronic components and hardware for multiple industries. AI has supercharged its growth, and I won't be surprised to see the stock doubling by 2030. Let's see why that may be the case.

Jabil's fiscal 2026 ended on a strong note. The company reported $36 billion in revenue for the fiscal year ending Aug. 31, up 21% from the prior year. The company's core operating margin increased by 40 basis points last fiscal year, resulting in a 34% increase in non-GAAP earnings per share to $13.09.

The growth rate improved in fiscal 2025, when Jabil posted a 3% increase in revenue and a 15% increase in earnings. AI played a central role in boosting Jabil's growth. The company manufactures AI server racks, cooling systems, and power management solutions for major hyperscalers, such as Meta Platforms , Amazon , and Alphabet 's Google, as noted by investment bank UBS .

These partnerships helped Jabil deliver $14.4 billion in AI revenue in fiscal 2026, up significantly from $5.4 billion in the previous year. Importantly, Jabil expects its AI revenue to jump to $22.1 billion in fiscal 2027, implying a 54% increase over last year.

However, don't be surprised to see Jabil's AI revenue growing at a stronger pace. That's because Jabil's hyperscale customers are ramping up their AI infrastructure deployments. For instance, Jabil management noted on the latest earnings call that its "second hyperscale customer started with a single capability and has grown into a storage program above $1 billion in annual revenue."

The company added a third hyperscale customer in the third quarter of fiscal 2026. Given that Jabil is offering more than just server racks, its customers end up buying cooling and power management solutions as well. This land-and-expand strategy helps Jabil to get more business from existing customers, enabling it to clock stronger growth in both revenue and earnings.

Also, there is a solid chance that Jabil's AI-focused customer base will expand further owing to continued investments in AI infrastructure. For instance, Gartner expects the AI infrastructure market to reach $1.48 trillion in revenue in 2026 from $982 billion last year. The firm expects the size of this market to expand to $1.98 trillion next year.

AI pioneer Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang estimates that AI infrastructure spending could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. As server racks, cooling systems, and power management solutions play a critical role in AI data centers, the demand for Jabil's offerings should continue improving.

So, it is easy to see why the company expects a stronger increase of 23.6% in revenue in the current fiscal year to $44.5 billion. Additionally, it sees a 34% jump in non-GAAP earnings per share to $17.55. However, Jabil could exceed expectations amid strong AI infrastructure spending , which is precisely why analysts have significantly raised their growth expectations for the company.
Jabil's earnings per share are poised to grow at healthy double-digit rates over the next three years, according to consensus estimates.

Assuming its bottom line grows by even 15% in fiscal 2030, its earnings per share could reach $29.82 after four years. If this AI stock trades at even 22 times earnings at that time, in line with the tech-laden Nasdaq-100 index's forward earnings multiple, its stock price could reach $660.

That's 128% higher than Jabil's stock price, indicating that a $10,000 investment in this stock could be worth over $22,750 by the end of the decade. However, if Jabil outpaces analysts' expectations, it could command a premium valuation and deliver bigger gains. So, if you've $10,000 in investible cash right now, buying Jabil with that money could be a smart move given its healthy upside potential.

extraction.body: MACAO, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- To counter the emerging network security challenges posed by quantum computing, CTM has actively embraced the national quantum strategy. It is designing a quantum-secured framework to build an integrated QKD-communication network security foundation, further enhancing the end-to-end transmission security of critical data. In addition, CTM plans to roll out quantum-secured private lines for enterprise and government sectors to unlock new growth opportunities while supporting Digital Macao and fortifying digital security across the Greater Bay Area. CTM and Huawei are pioneering the world's first integrated QKD-communication target IP network, driving the development of the quantum industry chain throughout the region. The rapid advancement of quantum computing is driving a disruptive shift in the global network security landscape. Encrypted data that would take traditional computers trillions of years to crack can now be breached in just minutes using quantum computing. This poses an unprecedented, seismic challenge to the security defenses of critical digital assets and sensitive data. To strengthen China's digital security defenses, the 15th Five-Year Plan Outline has designated quantum technology as a strategic future industry. CTM and Huawei have jointly launched the world's first integrated QKD-communication target network. Innovative QKD-communication integration combines the quantum, negotiation, and communication channels into one, while seamlessly integrating communication and quantum networks into a single network to create a next-generation communication network foundation with quantum security. The network will serve as a shield against quantum computing threats for core and sensitive services such as government office, financial transactions, and critical infrastructure, ensuring end-to-end secure transmission of critical services. Mr. Poon Fuk Hei, CEO of CTM, stated that as a core enabler of Macao's digital and intelligent transformation and a trusted guardian of its communication security, CTM has long been dedicated to building and strengthening local communication networks. It has been a key driver behind the evolution and real-world deployment of the network foundation powering Digital and Intelligent Macao. He added that, aligning with national strategic goals and Macao's regional digital security needs, CTM has proactively deployed a local quantum-secured network foundation, fully accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge quantum security technologies in Macao. Leon Wang, President of Huawei's Data Communication Product Line, stressed that security and resilience is one of the three defining characteristics of IP bearer networks. He noted that in the realm of quantum security—a crucial subset of security and resilience—Huawei has maintained continuous investment and innovation across hardware, software, algorithms, and more. For example, Huawei pioneered the industry's first router with built-in QKD. This innovation helps operators to reduce TCO by over 60%. This empowers CTM to build a quantum-secured network foundation featuring QKD-communication integration, providing robust security assurance for the digital transformation and core data transmission of government and enterprise customers. Looking ahead, CTM and Huawei will continue to deepen their strategic partnership in industrial development and technological innovation, designing products specifically for quantum-secured private lines while accelerating their deployment on live networks. Meanwhile, leveraging Macao's unique geographical advantages and technical expertise, the two companies aim to drive collaborative development, technological innovation, and practical applications of the quantum security industry within the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, ultimately safeguarding the high-quality development of the region's digital economy.

passages: 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At Network X 2026, CTM delivered a keynote speech about its secure target network, highlighting its accelerated efforts to evolve networks from traditional connectivity pipes into intelligent, deterministic, and secure infrastructure, thereby speeding up the digital and intelligent transformation of enterprises in Macao.

Beyond charting the course for enhancing Macao's network competitiveness, these technology evolution roadmaps provide global carriers with a new blueprint for transitioning to intelligent, secure networks in the AI era.
CTM believes that future network security planning must extend beyond simply setting up a firewall at the network edge; security should instead be a built-in capability of the network itself.
Guided by this vision, the industry can explore network modernization across three key areas:

By introducing AGW and AI broadband network gateway (BNG) capabilities, CTM equips the network with intelligent service awareness and dynamic scheduling, intelligently steering traffic to optimal paths to elevate user experience and reduce international bandwidth costs.
Moving into AGW 2.0, CTM will integrate telemetry with AI-powered analytics to drive a major leap from manual optimization to AI-driven auto-optimization.
This will deliver a deterministic, differentiated experience for high-value scenarios, fueling revenue growth for government and enterprise businesses.

extraction.body: MACAO, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- To counter the emerging network security challenges posed by quantum computing, CTM has actively embraced the national quantum strategy. It is designing a quantum-secured framework to build an integrated QKD-communication network security foundation, further enhancing the end-to-end transmission security of critical data. In addition, CTM plans to roll out quantum-secured private lines for enterprise and government sectors to unlock new growth opportunities while supporting Digital Macao and fortifying digital security across the Greater Bay Area. CTM and Huawei are pioneering the world's first integrated QKD-communication target IP network, driving the development of the quantum industry chain throughout the region. The rapid advancement of quantum computing is driving a disruptive shift in the global network security landscape. Encrypted data that would take traditional computers trillions of years to crack can now be breached in just minutes using quantum computing. This poses an unprecedented, seismic challenge to the security defenses of critical digital assets and sensitive data. To strengthen China's digital security defenses, the 15th Five-Year Plan Outline has designated quantum technology as a strategic future industry. CTM and Huawei have jointly launched the world's first integrated QKD-communication target network. Innovative QKD-communication integration combines the quantum, negotiation, and communication channels into one, while seamlessly integrating communication and quantum networks into a single network to create a next-generation communication network foundation with quantum security. The network will serve as a shield against quantum computing threats for core and sensitive services such as government office, financial transactions, and critical infrastructure, ensuring end-to-end secure transmission of critical services. Mr. Poon Fuk Hei, CEO of CTM, stated that as a core enabler of Macao's digital and intelligent transformation and a trusted guardian of its communication security, CTM has long been dedicated to building and strengthening local communication networks. It has been a key driver behind the evolution and real-world deployment of the network foundation powering Digital and Intelligent Macao. He added that, aligning with national strategic goals and Macao's regional digital security needs, CTM has proactively deployed a local quantum-secured network foundation, fully accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge quantum security technologies in Macao. Leon Wang, President of Huawei's Data Communication Product Line, stressed that security and resilience is one of the three defining characteristics of IP bearer networks. He noted that in the realm of quantum security—a crucial subset of security and resilience—Huawei has maintained continuous investment and innovation across hardware, software, algorithms, and more. For example, Huawei pioneered the industry's first router with built-in QKD. This innovation helps operators to reduce TCO by over 60%. This empowers CTM to build a quantum-secured network foundation featuring QKD-communication integration, providing robust security assurance for the digital transformation and core data transmission of government and enterprise customers. Looking ahead, CTM and Huawei will continue to deepen their strategic partnership in industrial development and technological innovation, designing products specifically for quantum-secured private lines while accelerating their deployment on live networks. Meanwhile, leveraging Macao's unique geographical advantages and technical expertise, the two companies aim to drive collaborative development, technological innovation, and practical applications of the quantum security industry within the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, ultimately safeguarding the high-quality development of the region's digital economy.

extraction.body: Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic. “That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage. Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December. But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music). Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news. “Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said. As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy. “There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful. “You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said. Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users. For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device. Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. passages: Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic.
“That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage.
Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December.

But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music).

Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news.

“Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said.

As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy.

“There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful.
“You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said.

Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users.

For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device.

Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant.

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

extraction.body: For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule. It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies. Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference. “The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.” Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.” Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.” He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said. Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added. Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.

Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.

“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”

Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”

Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”
He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.

Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.
Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

The Roadster features an angular design, which is not as aggressively futuristic as the Cybertruck. The reveal car features an aerospace-inspired 'Ano White' finish, gold-tinted glass and a white interior with a touchscreen infotainment system in the center.

The Roadster, according to Tesla's official website, is available in three trim levels: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. The Performance trim is the base trim with the multi-mode suction system and active aero. It does not feature cold-gas thrusters.
Tesla's U.S. reservation page requires a $50,000 reservation payment for the Performance version, consisting of $5,000 upfront and another $45,000 within 10 days.

On the other hand, Tesla says that the Thrust trim, which will be a limited release , will feature seating for two and its multi-mode suction system paired with cold-gas thrusters that result in an under-1-second 0-60 mph time.

The Rocket trim is currently not approved for public-road use and will feature seating for one and have cold-gas thrusters in the periphery of the vehicle to support "forward" and "upward acceleration" as well as "lateral rotational movement." Tesla says that the trim will also feature the multi-mode suction system and is invite-only.

The multi-mode suction system, according to the automaker, is a "downforce generator" that pulls air out from beneath the vehicle, providing enough "suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary."

CEO Musk, during the launch event, said that the Roadster will enter production in 2028. Tesla also said that the car will feature a range of more than 300 miles and a redesigned steer-by-wire system with a steering yoke.
Tesla also said that the thrusters work with electric actuators and complete "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second" to help stabilize the vehicle in flight.

passages: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”
Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years.
Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car.
Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.
Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair.
The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026.
Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again.
It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”
Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price.
The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.
The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

coreStoryFacts.text: This article Elon Musk Unveils Tesla Roadster That Can Fly, Drive Upside Down and Barrel Roll With SpaceX Thrusters originally appeared on Benzinga.com
The clip showcased the Roadster's thrusters making the car do a 'barrel roll' mid-air like an aircraft.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ: TSLA ) has officially unveiled the awaited Roadster high-performance vehicle , showing off the car's hovering capabilities powered by thrusters from Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ).
CEO Musk, during the launch event, said that the Roadster will enter production in 2028.

In a post on the social media platform X following the Roadster debut event , Musk shared a clip of the vehicle launching itself over a row of Tesla's Cybercab, Cybertruck, the Semi, the Model 3 and the Model Y.

The multi-mode suction system, according to the automaker, is a "downforce generator" that pulls air out from beneath the vehicle, providing enough "suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary."
Investors Press Elon Musk on Robotaxis, HW3 FSD and More Ahead of TSLA's Q3 Earnings
OMG the Tesla Roadster just flew in the air! pic.twitter.com/vdIabzyyPx
Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”
Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years.
Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car.
Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.
Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair.
The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026.
Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again.

CEO Musk, during the launch event, said that the Roadster will enter production in 2028. Tesla also said that the car will feature a range of more than 300 miles and a redesigned steer-by-wire system with a steering yoke.

extraction.body: Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.” Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion. “This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.” Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car. All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour. Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.” Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels. Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket. Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster. “If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said. “This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’” Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event. In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet. “Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions. Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024. As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again. “Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay. These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman. “They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. passages: Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.
All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.
Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.”

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event.
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.
“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.
These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

Although the name ‘flying car’ seems to be a little misleading here, this is what the demo showed us as short flights, but nothing more. Tesla’s next generation of Roadster concept was first presented to the public in November 2017, with the deliveries scheduled for 2020. It is important to note that this is still a planned production date rather than a date of deliveries to customers. The final purchase price of the redesigned Roadster has not been firmly confirmed. Reported reservation amounts provide an indication of its premium positioning. These figures represent reported reservation payments, not necessarily the complete vehicle prices. Tesla’s reservation terms explain that final purchase prices may change as configurations are confirmed. The Indian consumer might have to wait past the projected production start date to access the Roadster in India. Up till now, there is no official launch date set by Tesla for India or the showroom price. Additional costs from import taxes, logistics, duties, and homologation processes will further drive up the Indian price. Until Tesla officially announces their availability in India, any price estimate floating on the internet cannot be confirmed as the final price. As part of the launch event, Tesla presented acceleration performance that was estimated to get the car from 0 to 60 mph in just 0.81 second as equal to 96.6 km/h. Whether these systems will appear unchanged in customer vehicles remains uncertain. Tesla has not given its final specification on the interior of the new Roadster. It is fair to expect the cockpit of the vehicle to be designed for performance and have digital control of the vehicle and a minimalist approach; however, one should take into consideration that these are just assumptions about the equipment of the car and not something confirmed. However, there is no definitive list of the colours for the redesigned Tesla Roadster since this is still not officially disclosed. The white-coloured version exhibited during the reveal event does not provide a clue on how many colour choices would be offered to customers. The Roadster’s most unusual feature is its cold-gas thruster system, developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Unlike conventional cars, which rely on their tyres to maintain contact with the road, the system uses compressed gas to help the vehicle perform brief aerial manoeuvres. During the Texas demonstration, the Roadster lifted off, performed a rotation and returned to the ground. The company also showcased the vehicle jumping over a row of Tesla models. These demonstrations suggest that the technology can support controlled movements beyond ordinary driving. Tesla has made ambitious performance claims for the new Roadster, including acceleration from zero to 60 mph (around 97 km/h) in less than one second in its most advanced configuration. The company has also listed a top speed of more than 230 mph (about 370 km/h). If the production model delivers these figures, the Roadster would compete in the extreme-performance electric sports-car segment. However, these figures remain manufacturer claims, and the final production model will need to demonstrate its performance under real-world conditions. Tesla has not yet begun mass production of the redesigned car. The unique motion of the Roadster uses special equipment and not wings as expected. One must look into the refund policy, the final specs, the warranty period and the delivery details before actually spending the money to book a car. It is also crucial to verify whether the car chosen is legal to drive on public roads. sources.title: Tesla reveals pre-production flying Roadster with air thrusters - Autocar India
passages: Tesla has revealed a pre-production electric sports car, called the Roadster, which will enter production in 2028.
It will be available in a standard Performance trim, and Thrust and Rocket packages (or 'augments' in Tesla-speak).
It gets an underbody suction fan for additional grip, and optional air thrusters that help the Roadster perform airborne manoeuvres.
Tesla claims a 0-100kph time of under a second for the new Roadster, although final production powertrain specifications, including battery capacity, motor output and range, are yet to be revealed.
The Rocket version drops the passenger seat to make room for the additional hardware required for its flight system, setting it apart from the two-seat Performance and Thrust versions.
The redesigned pre-production model adopts a more angular, wedge-shaped silhouette like the Tesla Cybertruck, with aircraft-inspired styling from the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-35 fighter jet.
Interestingly, the 2026 Roadster concept has seen a thorough exterior and interior redesign from the 2017 concept, now sporting two seats but missing out on a removable roof.
The thrusters use pressurised cold air expelled through nozzles to generate thrust, allowing the Roadster to briefly lift off the ground and control its movement in the air.
The system is distinct from a conventional rocket engine, as it relies on stored pressurised air rather than burning propellant.
The front gets concealed headlights, while the rear features a full-width LED tail-light and a prominent active rear wing.
Flush-mounted surfaces and slim-spoke wheels contribute to the cleaner design, with the wing adjusting to balance downforce and aerodynamic drag.
Tesla has also introduced an ‘Ano White’ paint finish, alongside gold-tinted glass and titanium accents.
The yoke is designed to work with a steer-by-wire system, while braking and throttle inputs are also electronically controlled.
The interior is finished in white, with grey microsuede detailing and more heavily bolstered seats.

extraction.body: Tesla has revealed a pre-production electric sports car, called the Roadster, which will enter production in 2028. It will be available in a standard Performance trim, and Thrust and Rocket packages (or 'augments' in Tesla-speak). Bookings for the Performance trim and Thrust package are underway in India at Rs 5 lakh, while the Rocket augment is an invite-only programme. It gets an underbody suction fan for additional grip, and optional air thrusters that help the Roadster perform airborne manoeuvres. Interestingly, the 2026 Roadster concept has seen a thorough exterior and interior redesign from the 2017 concept, now sporting two seats but missing out on a removable roof. The upcoming electric sports car will mark the second run for the Roadster nameplate after it was discontinued in 2012. The thrusters use pressurised cold air expelled through nozzles to generate thrust, allowing the Roadster to briefly lift off the ground and control its movement in the air. The system is distinct from a conventional rocket engine, as it relies on stored pressurised air rather than burning propellant. The Performance trim features an underbody suction fan that can generate 2G of grip. As mentioned earlier, it serves as the base for the other two configurations. The Thrust package adds four rear-mounted thrusters, and the Rocket package adds 10 more thrusters, which enable airborne manoeuvres. Tesla claims a 0-100kph time of under a second for the new Roadster, although final production powertrain specifications, including battery capacity, motor output and range, are yet to be revealed. The new design marks a significant departure from the original concept from 2017, which featured a rounded nose, flowing bodywork and a removable glass roof. The redesigned pre-production model adopts a more angular, wedge-shaped silhouette like the Tesla Cybertruck, with aircraft-inspired styling from the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-35 fighter jet. The front gets concealed headlights, while the rear features a full-width LED tail-light and a prominent active rear wing. Flush-mounted surfaces and slim-spoke wheels contribute to the cleaner design, with the wing adjusting to balance downforce and aerodynamic drag. Tesla has also introduced an ‘Ano White’ paint finish, alongside gold-tinted glass and titanium accents. The 2017 Roadster concept featured a curved central touchscreen, a conventional two-plus-two seating layout and a removable glass roof. The redesigned model adopts a more focused, two-seat cabin, with a yoke-style steering unit with physical controls and a central touchscreen. The yoke is designed to work with a steer-by-wire system, while braking and throttle inputs are also electronically controlled. Tesla has opted for a fixed seating position, with the cabin using lightweight materials such as carbon fibre, magnesium and titanium to help keep weight in check. The interior is finished in white, with grey microsuede detailing and more heavily bolstered seats. The Rocket version drops the passenger seat to make room for the additional hardware required for its flight system, setting it apart from the two-seat Performance and Thrust versions. Tesla says the Rocket is “not approved for public road use”, but the road legality of the standard Performance with the suction fan and the Thrust augment, which features additional air thrusters in the rear, is uncertain in India.

extraction.body: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children. A notification from Snapchat, one of the ten platforms affected, had lit up her screen, warning she'd be booted off when the law kicked in this week – if she couldn't prove she was over 16. Though she had let Isobel use TikTok and Snapchat with tight supervision – preferring that to the teenager using it covertly – she had been hoping the ban, as promised, would help parents like her protect their children from the dangers of the online world. That hope has now wavered, as a series of experts – and kids themselves – sound the alarm on the viability and safety of the landmark policy, which is being closely watched around the globe and eyed with trepidation by some of its most influential companies. There's concern about the reliability of the technology enforcing the ban, along with fears it could isolate vulnerable children and push others into darker, less-regulated corners of the web. The question nervously being asked in the halls of Canberra, in households across the nation, and in tech boardrooms around the world: is this actually going to work? You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms. Their protestations to the contrary fall on unsympathetic ears. "We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC. The pair were among the parents and public figures who lent their voices to a headline-grabbing national campaign calling for a new minimum age for social media. Some experts, including Australia's online safety tsar, warned banning children from social media was not the solution, but their concerns were swept away by a tide of parental passion and political pressure. In November 2024, the prime minister announced the legislation, promising parents and children wouldn't be penalised. It'd be up to the platforms to take "reasonable steps" to ensure account-holders were at least 16 years old, or face fines of up to $49.5m (US$33m, £25m) for the most serious breaches. "This one is for the mums and dads... They, like me, are worried sick about the safety of our kids online," Anthony Albanese said. The policy – limited versions of which have been attempted with little success by other jurisdictions around the world – would help free children from addictive algorithms exposing them to harmful content like violence, pornography and misinformation, proponents said. It would also reduce cyber-bullying and online child exploitation. It would force kids outside, help them sleep better, improve their physical and mental health, it was suggested. Noticeably absent from Albanese's announcement was a plan on exactly how the government was going to do this – it gave itself a year to work that out. A government-funded, industry-run trial looked at the main methods of age assurance and earlier this year reported all were technically possible – but none were foolproof and all carried risks. Verification using IDs was the most accurate approach, but that requires users to hand over sensitive and important documents when polling shows most Australians don't trust social media firms. Age inference, which draws conclusions based on users' online activity, and facial assessment technology both lacked the precision to be reliably applied to teenagers. Its findings weren't without controversy. Two former advisory board members levelled accusations of bias and "privacy-washing". And though the trial considered ways teenagers might bypass barriers, it was not tasked with testing them. Tips have flooded social media: everything from signing up with a parent's email and moving to platforms not explicitly named on the government's hit list, to using VPNs, which can disguise a user's location. There was a temporary surge in VPN use in the UK after it introduced tougher age checks for pornography earlier this year, and experts are expecting the same here. Polling conducted for the government in May indicated a third of parents intended to help their kids circumvent the ban, and an experiment by the University of Melbourne showed that a $22 Halloween mask was enough to defeat facial assessment technology in some cases. "If I do end up getting banned, I'll just find another app to use." That's up for discussion, Mel clarifies. But she and a host of others fear the platforms and the regulator are set for a relentless game of "whack-a-mole" – identifying and shutting down loophole after loophole, and listing emerging platforms only for kids to flock to another. The social media firms also have a motive to subtly undermine the policy, lest other countries follow suit, analysts say, and the vague "reasonable steps" outlined by the government leave the door ajar. "They're going to try to drive a truck through [it]," says Stephen Scheeler, who led Facebook in Australia and New Zealand between 2013 and 2017. The key question is not can children get around it, Mr Allen says; that answer is yes. But will enough of them be bothered to? "To be a successful policy, it doesn't have to get to a point where 100% of children aren't on social media," he says. "It only really has to get about 80% of them and the rest will follow." Some exasperated parents just want to be able to say it is illegal. They don't want their kids to feel entitled – or pressured – to access social media. "We've always said, whether the law was enforceable or not, our main aim in all of this was to establish a new social norm," Mr Elachi says. "You're not stopping behaviour, you're just moving that behaviour to other platforms," says Tim Levy, head of online safety company Qoria and one of the trial advisers who quit. "Telling the concerned Australian parents that it's all good now is a very dangerous message." The science on social media and health is complex and still evolving too. Alongside the studies linking it to poor outcomes is also evidence it can be a lifeline for some children, particularly for those from LGBTQ+, neurodivergent or rural communities. "We've heard very little officially about what is being done to address the unmet needs of these more vulnerable children who for positive reasons have sought help or a sense of belonging and connection online," former children's commissioner Anne Hollonds tells the BBC. Before her agency was officially charged with implementing this policy, eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman-Grant made similar arguments. "We do not fence the ocean or keep children entirely out of the water, but we do create protected swimming environments that provide safeguards and teach important lessons from a young age," she said in June last year. To that, Minister Wells counters: "We can police the sharks" – a biting reference to social media firms. Many of the critics are right about the challenges ahead, she told the BBC. But this is just a starting point – a digital duty of care, a legal obligation that firms prevent foreseeable harm to their users, is next on her list. The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.

extraction.body: Age gates can be staggeringly counterproductive, pushing kids to darker corners of the web. Closing loopholes will only make things worse. Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked. Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences. Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place. For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want. Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands. Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business. Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are. Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization's work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census . Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.
