passages: Azerbaijan has joined a growing list of countries imposing social media restrictions on minors, passing a law that bars under-16s from platforms at a time when governments worldwide are questioning whether the digital industry can regulate itself.Australia became the first country to implement a nationwide social media ban for children under 16.France has tightened its laws on the age of digital consent, the UK passed the Online Safety Bill, and the EU has been increasing pressure on technology companies.Now Baku has decided to move in the same direction.Social media addiction, self-esteem problems and cyberbullying are producing documented psychological consequences among teenagers.

They organise social experience, and they shape habits before beliefs, and attention before judgment."Nazarova described recent legislation as an attempt by states to rebuild protective barriers around childhood that digital feeds had dismantled."From this perspective, the proposed age limit in Azerbaijan reflects a transformation in the way states understand their role," she said.The practical test of Azerbaijan's law, experts agree, will come after its adoption: whether the restrictions can be enforced in practice, and whether they are accompanied by the education and support structures needed to change behaviour rather than simply push it underground.

"Schools should focus on replacing screen time with meaningful digital activities, such as programming, robotics, and media literacy clubs," Dadashova explained."While a social media ban can offer positive effects, the real solution lies in cultivating healthy digital behaviour and real-world communication skills."What do digital platforms actually do?Laman Nazarova, a geopolitical analyst at the Caspian Analytical Centre, argued that the legislative push reflected a broader reassessment of what digital platforms actually do."Platforms have become one of the main environments where children acquire language, values, and social norms," Nazarova told Euronews.These functions previously belonged to families and schools, she added.

Unlike bullying, online harassment follows children into their homes and is harder to escape.Narmina Ismayilzada, a child and adolescent psychologist with 16 years of experience, told Euronews teenagers exposed to digital bullying frequently develop "a very strong sense of shame, decreased self-confidence, and anxiety," leading to social isolation and school avoidance.She supports state-level age restrictions but warns that a ban alone will not solve the underlying problems."Prohibiting something at this age can create reverse psychology," Ismayilzada said."Children show more interest in what is prohibited and may try to use these things in hidden ways," she pointed out."If parents forbid something without explaining the reasoning behind it, children simply hide their actions.

A healthy approach requires supervision paired with mutual trust and open dialogue."She said algorithmic feeds exploit adolescents' heightened sensitivity to physical appearance and social acceptance, damaging attention spans and academic motivation."Concentration problems and divided attention are among our most serious issues today.

It makes them more aggressive and impulsive," Ismayilzada said."When children compare themselves to idealised images on social networks, it naturally leads to self-confidence problems, body-image dissatisfaction, and, in worst cases, depressive symptoms."The solution, she said, begins at home.

"Governments have begun to recognise that digital platforms do not merely transmit information.

They organise social experience, and they shape habits before beliefs, and attention before judgment."Nazarova described recent legislation as an attempt by states to rebuild protective barriers around childhood that digital feeds had dismantled."From this perspective, the proposed age limit in Azerbaijan reflects a transformation in the way states understand their role," she said.The practical test of Azerbaijan's law, experts agree, will come after its adoption: whether the restrictions can be enforced in practice, and whether they are accompanied by the education and support structures needed to change behaviour rather than simply push it underground.

coreStoryFacts.text: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children.
You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms.
Their protestations to the contrary fall on unsympathetic ears.
"To be a successful policy, it doesn't have to get to a point where 100% of children aren't on social media," he says.

The social media firms also have a motive to subtly undermine the policy, lest other countries follow suit, analysts say, and the vague "reasonable steps" outlined by the government leave the door ajar.
"They're going to try to drive a truck through [it]," says Stephen Scheeler, who led Facebook in Australia and New Zealand between 2013 and 2017.
They don't want their kids to feel entitled – or pressured – to access social media.
The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.
"We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC.
Many of the critics are right about the challenges ahead, she told the BBC.
Indonesia is set to become the second country to outright ban children under 16 from using major social media platforms.
Australia imposed similar restrictions last year, and laws banning social media for kids are advancing across Europe.

In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.
When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services.
The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations.

In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents.

When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence.
It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities .

extraction.body: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children. A notification from Snapchat, one of the ten platforms affected, had lit up her screen, warning she'd be booted off when the law kicked in this week – if she couldn't prove she was over 16. Though she had let Isobel use TikTok and Snapchat with tight supervision – preferring that to the teenager using it covertly – she had been hoping the ban, as promised, would help parents like her protect their children from the dangers of the online world. That hope has now wavered, as a series of experts – and kids themselves – sound the alarm on the viability and safety of the landmark policy, which is being closely watched around the globe and eyed with trepidation by some of its most influential companies. There's concern about the reliability of the technology enforcing the ban, along with fears it could isolate vulnerable children and push others into darker, less-regulated corners of the web. The question nervously being asked in the halls of Canberra, in households across the nation, and in tech boardrooms around the world: is this actually going to work? You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms. Their protestations to the contrary fall on unsympathetic ears. "We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC. The pair were among the parents and public figures who lent their voices to a headline-grabbing national campaign calling for a new minimum age for social media. Some experts, including Australia's online safety tsar, warned banning children from social media was not the solution, but their concerns were swept away by a tide of parental passion and political pressure. In November 2024, the prime minister announced the legislation, promising parents and children wouldn't be penalised. It'd be up to the platforms to take "reasonable steps" to ensure account-holders were at least 16 years old, or face fines of up to $49.5m (US$33m, £25m) for the most serious breaches. "This one is for the mums and dads... They, like me, are worried sick about the safety of our kids online," Anthony Albanese said. The policy – limited versions of which have been attempted with little success by other jurisdictions around the world – would help free children from addictive algorithms exposing them to harmful content like violence, pornography and misinformation, proponents said. It would also reduce cyber-bullying and online child exploitation. It would force kids outside, help them sleep better, improve their physical and mental health, it was suggested. Noticeably absent from Albanese's announcement was a plan on exactly how the government was going to do this – it gave itself a year to work that out. A government-funded, industry-run trial looked at the main methods of age assurance and earlier this year reported all were technically possible – but none were foolproof and all carried risks. Verification using IDs was the most accurate approach, but that requires users to hand over sensitive and important documents when polling shows most Australians don't trust social media firms. sources.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.

extraction.body: Age gates can be staggeringly counterproductive, pushing kids to darker corners of the web. Closing loopholes will only make things worse. Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked. Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences. Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place. For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want. Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands. Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business. Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are. Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization's work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census . Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

story.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.

facts.text: It took 13-year-old Isobel less than five minutes to outsmart Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children.
You'd struggle to find anyone in Australia who feels social media companies are doing enough to shield users – particularly children – from harm on their platforms.
Their protestations to the contrary fall on unsympathetic ears.
"To be a successful policy, it doesn't have to get to a point where 100% of children aren't on social media," he says.

The social media firms also have a motive to subtly undermine the policy, lest other countries follow suit, analysts say, and the vague "reasonable steps" outlined by the government leave the door ajar.
"They're going to try to drive a truck through [it]," says Stephen Scheeler, who led Facebook in Australia and New Zealand between 2013 and 2017.
They don't want their kids to feel entitled – or pressured – to access social media.
The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.
"We have zero faith the tech companies will do anything other than protect their profits," Dany Elachi, a father of five and anti-smartphone campaigner, tells the BBC.
Many of the critics are right about the challenges ahead, she told the BBC.
Indonesia is set to become the second country to outright ban children under 16 from using major social media platforms.
Australia imposed similar restrictions last year, and laws banning social media for kids are advancing across Europe.

In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.
When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services.
The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations.

In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents.

When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence.
It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities .

passages: CME Group announced on September 22 that it will list Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures on October 19, pending regulatory review.
Bitcoin Cash jumped from roughly $267 to the $300s within hours, a move Forbes pegged as high as 36% to $366, while CoinMarketCap and 24/7 Wall St. put the surge closer to 24% to 30%.

The exact number depends on which exchange and which hour you check, but the direction is not in dispute: this was one of the sharpest reactions to a derivatives listing announcement crypto markets have seen all year.
The price action is the part retail traders will remember, and it's worth being honest about what it means and what it doesn't.
The launch itself is still three weeks out and explicitly contingent on regulatory review, the same review every CME crypto product has to clear before it goes live.

Short squeezes and anticipatory buying, which Invezz reported played a role alongside renewed talk of a potential Grayscale Bitcoin Cash Trust conversion to an ETF, can evaporate just as fast once the news is priced in.
Two new tickers are coming to CME's crypto futures lineup.
The standard Bitcoin Cash contract will cover 250 BCH, with Uniswap's set at 10,000 UNI, plus Micro versions of each.
CME says Cardano, Chainlink, Stellar, Avalanche and Sui futures already topped $1 billion in combined volume this year.

CME Group ( NASDAQ: CME | CME Price Prediction ), the Chicago-based derivatives exchange, is preparing to list futures contracts for Bitcoin Cash ( CRYPTO: BCH ) and Uniswap ( CRYPTO: UNI ) on October 19, 2026, pending regulatory approval. Bitcoin Cash, a payment-focused spin-off of Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), is a separate network, while UNI serves as the governance token for Uniswap, a decentralized exchange that lets users trade tokens directly without intermediaries.

As both cryptocurrencies approach their futures listing, they face challenges. Uniswap is priced around $7 after a 10.4% decline over the week, while Bitcoin Cash is trading at about $264, down 10.7% in the same timeframe.
Typically, traders view the announcement of new futures as a potential buy signal. But do futures contracts tend to push a coin’s price up, down, or remain neutral?

Futures contracts are agreements to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price on a future date. On the CME, these contracts trade on a regulated exchange with a clearing house that ensures both parties fulfill their agreements, minimizing the risk of default.

For Bitcoin Cash, each standard futures contract covers 250 BCH, while a micro contract covers 25 BCH. Similarly, the standard Uniswap contract represents 10,000 UNI, with a smaller micro version covering 1,000 UNI. This structure allows larger institutions to trade significant amounts while smaller traders can participate without committing to a full contract.

The new listings join an existing suite of cryptocurrency futures that includes Bitcoin, Ether ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ), Cardano ( CRYPTO: ADA ), Chainlink ( CRYPTO: LINK ), Stellar ( CRYPTO: XLM ), Avalanche ( CRYPTO: AVAX ), and Sui ( CRYPTO: SUI ). According to CME, expanding into Cardano , Chainlink, Stellar, Avalanche, and Sui futures has added over $1 billion in total contract value this year.

In the first half of 2026, CME’s crypto futures and options averaged 279,800 contracts traded daily, worth about $8.3 billion in total value. The average open interest—the total number of contracts still active—was 264,600 contracts, valued at $15.4 billion.

However, historical data shows that launch days are often modest. For example, when Ether futures debuted on CME in February 2021, the first-day volume was only 388 contracts, representing roughly 19,400 ETH worth about $33 million, at an average of $1,700 per Ether. Compared with today’s daily trading volume, the initial figures for new contracts are quite small.

Hedging is the practice of taking an opposite position to mitigate risk, such as a Bitcoin Cash holder going short on CME to protect against price drops rather than selling coins, which can take pressure off the spot market where coins are traded immediately.

Conversely, short selling profits from a price decline. With futures, traders can take short positions without first borrowing the asset, giving sellers a new, regulated tool they didn’t previously have.

The disparity between the futures price and the spot price, known as the basis, can impact trading decisions. If the futures price is higher than the spot price, a fund might buy the asset and sell the futures contract, profiting from the difference when both prices converge at expiry. This process simultaneously buys the asset and sells the futures contract, allowing traders to benefit regardless of the price direction.

Moreover, certain institutional investors, such as pension funds , may not be allowed to hold cryptocurrencies directly but can participate in trading listed futures. This broader access may bring in more buyers, while short selling could increase selling pressure, creating a complex dynamic around price movement.

CME promotes the futures contracts as tools for risk management. Giovanni Vicioso, CME Group’s global head of cryptocurrency products, said, “As crypto markets continue to mature, participants require broader, regulated tools to navigate evolving digital asset-related price risk.”

Both Uniswap and Bitcoin Cash are entering this futures market after experiencing a rough week. Investors hoping for the new listing to reverse the downward trend should remember that while it could attract new buyers, it also welcomes short sellers who might increase selling pressure.

The overall impact will depend on which type of trader dominates the market. If hedgers and newly eligible institutional investors lead, futures may reduce selling pressure. Conversely, if short sellers dominate trading, it could add to downward pressure.
Early trading volume will also play a crucial role; if the contracts see limited activity, as with Ether’s launch, they could have minimal impact compared to regular spot trading of these coins.
In summary, while CME futures may add volatility, predicting a definitive price move for Uniswap and Bitcoin Cash remains uncertain, as the listing brings both buying and selling pressure into play.

The first check is whether both contracts go live on October 19 or slip due to regulatory review. After that, CME’s daily open interest reports are the figure to follow. If open interest rises week after week through November while both coins rally, hedgers and new institutions are outweighing short sellers. If open interest grows while both prices fall, the short side is winning.

Bitcoin Cash futures will represent 250 BCH per contract, while Micro Bitcoin Cash futures will represent 25 BCH.
Uniswap futures will cover 10,000 UNI, with Micro contracts representing 1,000 UNI.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

"As crypto markets continue to mature, participants require broader, regulated tools to navigate evolving digital asset related price risk," Giovanni Vicioso, CME Group's global head of cryptocurrency products, said in a statement.
The launch comes as institutional investors seek more ways to hedge exposure to cryptocurrencies beyond Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO: $ETH), according to CME.

The new contracts will add to CME's existing futures offerings covering assets including Bitcoin, Ether, XRP (CRYPTO: $XRP), Solana (CRYPTO: $SOL), Cardano (CRYPTO: $ADA), Chainlink (CRYPTO: $LINK), Stellar (CRYPTO: $XLM), Avalanche (CRYPTO: $AVAX) and Sui (CRYPTO: $SUI).
CME Group announced on September 22 that it will list Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures on October 19, pending regulatory review.
Bitcoin Cash jumped from roughly $267 to the $300s within hours, a move Forbes pegged as high as 36% to $366, while CoinMarketCap and 24/7 Wall St. put the surge closer to 24% to 30%.

The exact number depends on which exchange and which hour you check, but the direction is not in dispute: this was one of the sharpest reactions to a derivatives listing announcement crypto markets have seen all year.
The price action is the part retail traders will remember, and it's worth being honest about what it means and what it doesn't.
The launch itself is still three weeks out and explicitly contingent on regulatory review, the same review every CME crypto product has to clear before it goes live.

Short squeezes and anticipatory buying, which Invezz reported played a role alongside renewed talk of a potential Grayscale Bitcoin Cash Trust conversion to an ETF, can evaporate just as fast once the news is priced in.
Two new tickers are coming to CME's crypto futures lineup.
The standard Bitcoin Cash contract will cover 250 BCH, with Uniswap's set at 10,000 UNI, plus Micro versions of each.
CME says Cardano, Chainlink, Stellar, Avalanche and Sui futures already topped $1 billion in combined volume this year.
The Micro sizing matters more than it sounds.
That's CME building out what now looks like a full institutional menu of the crypto assets with the deepest liquidity and clearest regulatory standing.
But demand from clients is also, bluntly, demand CME can see in its own order flow and in the flow of the regulated derivatives desks it serves.
This isn't a popularity contest decided by social media sentiment.
It's an exchange following where hedging demand already exists.

CME Group ( NASDAQ: CME | CME Price Prediction ), the Chicago-based derivatives exchange, is preparing to list futures contracts for Bitcoin Cash ( CRYPTO: BCH ) and Uniswap ( CRYPTO: UNI ) on October 19, 2026, pending regulatory approval. Bitcoin Cash, a payment-focused spin-off of Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), is a separate network, while UNI serves as the governance token for Uniswap, a decentralized exchange that lets users trade tokens directly without intermediaries. As both cryptocurrencies approach their futures listing, they face challenges. Uniswap is priced around $7 after a 10.4% decline over the week, while Bitcoin Cash is trading at about $264, down 10.7% in the same timeframe. Typically, traders view the announcement of new futures as a potential buy signal. But do futures contracts tend to push a coin’s price up, down, or remain neutral? Futures contracts are agreements to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price on a future date. On the CME, these contracts trade on a regulated exchange with a clearing house that ensures both parties fulfill their agreements, minimizing the risk of default. For Bitcoin Cash, each standard futures contract covers 250 BCH, while a micro contract covers 25 BCH. CME Group ( NASDAQ: CME | CME Price Prediction ), the Chicago-based derivatives exchange, is preparing to list futures contracts for Bitcoin Cash ( CRYPTO: BCH ) and Uniswap ( CRYPTO: UNI ) on October 19, 2026, pending regulatory approval. Bitcoin Cash, a payment-focused spin-off of Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), is a separate network, while UNI serves as the governance token for Uniswap, a decentralized exchange that lets users trade tokens directly without intermediaries.

As both cryptocurrencies approach their futures listing, they face challenges. Uniswap is priced around $7 after a 10.4% decline over the week, while Bitcoin Cash is trading at about $264, down 10.7% in the same timeframe.
Typically, traders view the announcement of new futures as a potential buy signal. But do futures contracts tend to push a coin’s price up, down, or remain neutral?

Futures contracts are agreements to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price on a future date. On the CME, these contracts trade on a regulated exchange with a clearing house that ensures both parties fulfill their agreements, minimizing the risk of default.

For Bitcoin Cash, each standard futures contract covers 250 BCH, while a micro contract covers 25 BCH. Similarly, the standard Uniswap contract represents 10,000 UNI, with a smaller micro version covering 1,000 UNI. This structure allows larger institutions to trade significant amounts while smaller traders can participate without committing to a full contract.

The new listings join an existing suite of cryptocurrency futures that includes Bitcoin, Ether ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ), Cardano ( CRYPTO: ADA ), Chainlink ( CRYPTO: LINK ), Stellar ( CRYPTO: XLM ), Avalanche ( CRYPTO: AVAX ), and Sui ( CRYPTO: SUI ). According to CME, expanding into Cardano , Chainlink, Stellar, Avalanche, and Sui futures has added over $1 billion in total contract value this year.

In the first half of 2026, CME’s crypto futures and options averaged 279,800 contracts traded daily, worth about $8.3 billion in total value. The average open interest—the total number of contracts still active—was 264,600 contracts, valued at $15.4 billion.

However, historical data shows that launch days are often modest. For example, when Ether futures debuted on CME in February 2021, the first-day volume was only 388 contracts, representing roughly 19,400 ETH worth about $33 million, at an average of $1,700 per Ether. Compared with today’s daily trading volume, the initial figures for new contracts are quite small.

Hedging is the practice of taking an opposite position to mitigate risk, such as a Bitcoin Cash holder going short on CME to protect against price drops rather than selling coins, which can take pressure off the spot market where coins are traded immediately.

Conversely, short selling profits from a price decline. With futures, traders can take short positions without first borrowing the asset, giving sellers a new, regulated tool they didn’t previously have.

If the futures price is higher than the spot price, a fund might buy the asset and sell the futures contract, profiting from the difference when both prices converge at expiry. This process simultaneously buys the asset and sells the futures contract, allowing traders to benefit regardless of the price direction.

Moreover, certain institutional investors, such as pension funds , may not be allowed to hold cryptocurrencies directly but can participate in trading listed futures. This broader access may bring in more buyers, while short selling could increase selling pressure, creating a complex dynamic around price movement.

CME promotes the futures contracts as tools for risk management. Giovanni Vicioso, CME Group’s global head of cryptocurrency products, said, “As crypto markets continue to mature, participants require broader, regulated tools to navigate evolving digital asset-related price risk.”

Both Uniswap and Bitcoin Cash are entering this futures market after experiencing a rough week. Investors hoping for the new listing to reverse the downward trend should remember that while it could attract new buyers, it also welcomes short sellers who might increase selling pressure.

The overall impact will depend on which type of trader dominates the market. If hedgers and newly eligible institutional investors lead, futures may reduce selling pressure. Conversely, if short sellers dominate trading, it could add to downward pressure.
Early trading volume will also play a crucial role; if the contracts see limited activity, as with Ether’s launch, they could have minimal impact compared to regular spot trading of these coins.
In summary, while CME futures may add volatility, predicting a definitive price move for Uniswap and Bitcoin Cash remains uncertain, as the listing brings both buying and selling pressure into play.

The first check is whether both contracts go live on October 19 or slip due to regulatory review. After that, CME’s daily open interest reports are the figure to follow. If open interest rises week after week through November while both coins rally, hedgers and new institutions are outweighing short sellers. If open interest grows while both prices fall, the short side is winning.

"As crypto markets continue to mature, participants require broader, regulated tools to navigate evolving digital asset related price risk," Giovanni Vicioso, CME Group's global head of cryptocurrency products, said in a statement.
The launch comes as institutional investors seek more ways to hedge exposure to cryptocurrencies beyond Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO: $ETH), according to CME.

The new contracts will add to CME's existing futures offerings covering assets including Bitcoin, Ether, XRP (CRYPTO: $XRP), Solana (CRYPTO: $SOL), Cardano (CRYPTO: $ADA), Chainlink (CRYPTO: $LINK), Stellar (CRYPTO: $XLM), Avalanche (CRYPTO: $AVAX) and Sui (CRYPTO: $SUI).
CME Group announced on September 22 that it will list Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures on October 19, pending regulatory review.
Bitcoin Cash jumped from roughly $267 to the $300s within hours, a move Forbes pegged as high as 36% to $366, while CoinMarketCap and 24/7 Wall St. put the surge closer to 24% to 30%.

The exact number depends on which exchange and which hour you check, but the direction is not in dispute: this was one of the sharpest reactions to a derivatives listing announcement crypto markets have seen all year.
The price action is the part retail traders will remember, and it's worth being honest about what it means and what it doesn't.
The launch itself is still three weeks out and explicitly contingent on regulatory review, the same review every CME crypto product has to clear before it goes live.

Short squeezes and anticipatory buying, which Invezz reported played a role alongside renewed talk of a potential Grayscale Bitcoin Cash Trust conversion to an ETF, can evaporate just as fast once the news is priced in.

After the announcement, Cardano and Stellar fell slightly, while Chainlink's price remained stable, showing little reaction compared with Bitcoin Cash's surge.
Grayscale's Bitcoin Cash Trust holds Bitcoin Cash, meaning an approved ETF would purchase the coin, unlike CME's futures contracts, which settle in cash and do not involve the actual coin.
Additionally, Bitcoin hit its highest price since January on September 22, contributing to the overall rally, as Bitcoin SV, another offshoot, rose about 20% alongside BCH.

A drop back below $267, which would represent roughly 24% from current levels, would signal fading momentum before the October 19 futures launch.

passages: Driving the current gadget and AI push is Amazon's hardware and services chief, Panos Panay, who's the latest guest on The Tech Download.
Amazon's foray into devices has seen it jump into speakers, doorbells and now wearables with its acquisition of Bee, a startup developing a wristband device.
Alexa is at the heart of tying all of those together in a world where "we might be moving away from a world of apps and screens," Panay said.
The smartphone has been at the center of our digital life for so long.
Now with more advanced AI, what if a screen isn't needed and instead you could do more with voice?
This is what Amazon, along with other device companies are thinking about.
What the best future gadgets look like is still up for debate.
But Amazon is certainly cooking a few things up.
My final big takeaway from the conversation was about semiconductors.
For those of you who know me, you know chips are one of my favorite topics.
For the first time publicly, Panay discussed Amazon's semiconductor efforts for its consumer electronics.
I remember using one and thinking there was definitely a future here for these kinds of devices.
Trump bought Apple, Nvidia and other tech giants before tariff reversal fueled rebound, according to a CNBC analysis.
This means that Amazon is designing the chips that go into its devices.
By having more control over the hardware and software integration, Amazon will be able to deliver more differentiated experiences around Alexa.
More than a decade ago, before we were talking about "AI agents," Amazon launched its digital voice assistant Alexa and the smart speaker branded Echo.
"I have a lab full of devices," Panay said, adding that there is a "whole roadmap of on-the-go devices."
"On some of the more critical devices right now, our focus is end-to-end silicon," Panay said.

sources.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
passages: Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to.
To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done.
Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls.
That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

sources.title: End of Apps? Amazon's Panos Panay says future AI gadgets will do everything for you
passages: This is the app-less future Amazon is betting on.Speaking at the TechCrunch Disrupt event on Thursday, Panos Panay, Amazon’s Senior Vice President of Devices, Alexa & Leo, said the tech industry is moving toward a world of "ambient computing".

According to Panay, this ambient technology will allow people to put down their screens, stay more present with their friends and family, and stop worrying about missing important details.Meet Amazon's New "Bee" WearablesTo kickstart this new era, Amazon has launched a fresh lineup of AI gadgets under the "Bee" brand.

Panay, who spent 19 years at Microsoft's Surface computer division before joining Amazon, wants our gadgets to fade into the background.By using advanced sensors and AI, future devices will simply listen and figure out your tasks automatically.

Panay believes the next generation of users won't hunt for specific apps; they will simply expect their technology to understand their surroundings and get the job done.- EndsAlso Read | Amazon cuts nearly 1,000 jobs, retail employees in India impactedAlso Read | Amazon launches AI wearables that can listen in on your conversations and remember everythingAlso Read | Google says AI can help Indian farmers deal with climate change better

For instance, if you make dinner plans while talking to a friend, the AI can automatically draft a calendar invite.While users get 14 days of memory and basic summaries for free, an $11.99 monthly "Bee Pro" subscription unlocks unlimited memory and connects the AI directly to apps like Gmail, Outlook, and Amazon shopping.The Privacy QuestionA device that constantly listens to your day naturally raises major privacy concerns.
Amazon has tackled this by ensuring Bee devices do not store any raw audio recordings.

Furthermore, the text transcripts are locked using encryption keys that only your specific device controls, meaning not even Amazon employees can read your data.Even with these safety features in place, privacy experts still have concerns.
Panay described our current habit as "point, shoot, return", you have to remember exactly what you need and which app can do it.
Panay clarified that smartphones will remain important, noting that one piece of hardware rarely replaces another completely.Instead, a new "intelligence layer" will connect all our devices together.

coreStoryFacts.text: Driving the current gadget and AI push is Amazon's hardware and services chief, Panos Panay, who's the latest guest on The Tech Download.
Amazon's foray into devices has seen it jump into speakers, doorbells and now wearables with its acquisition of Bee, a startup developing a wristband device.
Alexa is at the heart of tying all of those together in a world where "we might be moving away from a world of apps and screens," Panay said.
The smartphone has been at the center of our digital life for so long.
Now with more advanced AI, what if a screen isn't needed and instead you could do more with voice?
This is what Amazon, along with other device companies are thinking about.
What the best future gadgets look like is still up for debate.
But Amazon is certainly cooking a few things up.
My final big takeaway from the conversation was about semiconductors.
For those of you who know me, you know chips are one of my favorite topics.
For the first time publicly, Panay discussed Amazon's semiconductor efforts for its consumer electronics.
I remember using one and thinking there was definitely a future here for these kinds of devices.
Trump bought Apple, Nvidia and other tech giants before tariff reversal fueled rebound, according to a CNBC analysis.
This means that Amazon is designing the chips that go into its devices.
By having more control over the hardware and software integration, Amazon will be able to deliver more differentiated experiences around Alexa.
More than a decade ago, before we were talking about "AI agents," Amazon launched its digital voice assistant Alexa and the smart speaker branded Echo.
"I have a lab full of devices," Panay said, adding that there is a "whole roadmap of on-the-go devices."
"On some of the more critical devices right now, our focus is end-to-end silicon," Panay said.

Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to.
To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done.
Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls.
That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.

sources.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
passages: Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to.
To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done.
Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls.
That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said. Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone. These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them. Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work. “You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you. “I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. sources.title: End of Apps? Amazon's Panos Panay says future AI gadgets will do everything for you
passages: This is the app-less future Amazon is betting on.Speaking at the TechCrunch Disrupt event on Thursday, Panos Panay, Amazon’s Senior Vice President of Devices, Alexa & Leo, said the tech industry is moving toward a world of "ambient computing".

According to Panay, this ambient technology will allow people to put down their screens, stay more present with their friends and family, and stop worrying about missing important details.Meet Amazon's New "Bee" WearablesTo kickstart this new era, Amazon has launched a fresh lineup of AI gadgets under the "Bee" brand.

Panay, who spent 19 years at Microsoft's Surface computer division before joining Amazon, wants our gadgets to fade into the background.By using advanced sensors and AI, future devices will simply listen and figure out your tasks automatically.

Panay believes the next generation of users won't hunt for specific apps; they will simply expect their technology to understand their surroundings and get the job done.- EndsAlso Read | Amazon cuts nearly 1,000 jobs, retail employees in India impactedAlso Read | Amazon launches AI wearables that can listen in on your conversations and remember everythingAlso Read | Google says AI can help Indian farmers deal with climate change better

For instance, if you make dinner plans while talking to a friend, the AI can automatically draft a calendar invite.While users get 14 days of memory and basic summaries for free, an $11.99 monthly "Bee Pro" subscription unlocks unlimited memory and connects the AI directly to apps like Gmail, Outlook, and Amazon shopping.The Privacy QuestionA device that constantly listens to your day naturally raises major privacy concerns.
Amazon has tackled this by ensuring Bee devices do not store any raw audio recordings.

Furthermore, the text transcripts are locked using encryption keys that only your specific device controls, meaning not even Amazon employees can read your data.Even with these safety features in place, privacy experts still have concerns.
Panay described our current habit as "point, shoot, return", you have to remember exactly what you need and which app can do it.
Panay clarified that smartphones will remain important, noting that one piece of hardware rarely replaces another completely.Instead, a new "intelligence layer" will connect all our devices together.

Panos Panay, Amazon’s senior vice president of Devices, Alexa & Leo, said AI-enabled products could handle more tasks without apps, though he expects smartphones to remain important to personal computing. Speaking Thursday, Panay described ambient devices that use sensors and AI in the background to help identify what needs to be done. Instead of remembering which tool to ask or opening an app for each task, users could get help from devices that recognize a need and surface useful information. He said the approach could let people stay present and spend less time directing their tools. Panay sees a future in which people may ask technology to understand what they need instead of requesting a particular app. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful,” he said. He described that layer as a way to connect different devices, rather than a shift to one product type. Amazon’s two Bee devices offer examples of this approach. One is a band that can be worn on the wrist or detached and used as a pendant. The other is a credit-card-size accessory that attaches magnetically to a smartphone. The devices capture conversations to create notes and surface possible to-dos, reminders and insights for later use. Bee does not store raw audio. It processes audio in real time and deletes it when processing is finished. Conversation transcripts are encrypted with keys created and controlled by the user’s device. Others, including Amazon employees, cannot access the files unless the user chooses to share them. Panay said he does not expect one device form to replace another. Smartphones will remain part of personal computing, he said, as sensors and AI connect devices and bring assistance into more settings. His comments describe a possible direction for personal technology, rather than an immediate end to apps or phones. Simon Yoon reports on blockchain technology for TokenPost. story.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps

facts.text: Driving the current gadget and AI push is Amazon's hardware and services chief, Panos Panay, who's the latest guest on The Tech Download.
Amazon's foray into devices has seen it jump into speakers, doorbells and now wearables with its acquisition of Bee, a startup developing a wristband device.
Alexa is at the heart of tying all of those together in a world where "we might be moving away from a world of apps and screens," Panay said.
The smartphone has been at the center of our digital life for so long.
Now with more advanced AI, what if a screen isn't needed and instead you could do more with voice?
This is what Amazon, along with other device companies are thinking about.
What the best future gadgets look like is still up for debate.
But Amazon is certainly cooking a few things up.
My final big takeaway from the conversation was about semiconductors.
For those of you who know me, you know chips are one of my favorite topics.
For the first time publicly, Panay discussed Amazon's semiconductor efforts for its consumer electronics.
I remember using one and thinking there was definitely a future here for these kinds of devices.
Trump bought Apple, Nvidia and other tech giants before tariff reversal fueled rebound, according to a CNBC analysis.
This means that Amazon is designing the chips that go into its devices.
By having more control over the hardware and software integration, Amazon will be able to deliver more differentiated experiences around Alexa.
More than a decade ago, before we were talking about "AI agents," Amazon launched its digital voice assistant Alexa and the smart speaker branded Echo.
"I have a lab full of devices," Panay said, adding that there is a "whole roadmap of on-the-go devices."
"On some of the more critical devices right now, our focus is end-to-end silicon," Panay said.

Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to.
To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done.
Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls.
That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

extraction.body: Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers. Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X. Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them. Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years. Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level. “Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model. Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies. Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said. The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude. Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

sources.title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
passages: Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States.
Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.

Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”

Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs. The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday. Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget . The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip. Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.” The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage. Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow. Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms. passages: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight artificial intelligence model that can run locally on Apple’s latest M5 Ultra Mac Studio computers, marking an unusual collaboration between the two technology companies.
The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture, activating only 42 billion parameters for each token rather than all 816 billion at once.
Meta says the model has been built for coding and agentic work, including long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering and multi-step reasoning.
Open-weight models make their trained parameters available to developers, allowing them to download, run and adapt the models rather than accessing them only through a cloud-based service.

extraction.body: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight artificial intelligence model that can run locally on Apple’s latest M5 Ultra Mac Studio computers, marking an unusual collaboration between the two technology companies. The model has been optimised to run across two Apple Mac Studios using Apple’s MLX machine learning framework. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the collaboration on X, writing that “Muse Spark Open – weights releasing today – runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple.” Apple CEO John Ternus responded to Zuckerberg, saying it was “amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk.” Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active at a time. It also has a 1-million-token context window and is natively multimodal, meaning it can process text, images, video and audio. Meta says the model has been built for coding and agentic work, including long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering and multi-step reasoning. How Muse Spark Open runs on Apple Mac Studio The Apple connection is significant because a model of this size would normally require data-centre infrastructure. Meta says Muse Spark Open can run on a desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, with each machine configured with up to 512GB of unified memory. Apple’s MLX framework allows the model to be distributed across the two Macs, with the machines connected using high-speed communication. Apple has also published technical details on running Muse Spark Open across multiple Mac Studios. Meta describes Muse Spark Open as its “most capable US open-weight model to date”. Open-weight models make their trained parameters available to developers, allowing them to download, run and adapt the models rather than accessing them only through a cloud-based service. The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture, activating only 42 billion parameters for each token rather than all 816 billion at once. This helps make the model more practical to run despite its overall size. Meta says Muse Spark Open has been tested with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, on software engineering tasks, including making bug fixes, adding features and completing a full build of an open-source Mastodon client. The company also tested it with DaVinci Resolve, where the model was able to review footage and identify and crop sections of video. Apple’s testing found that a cluster of four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open could generate more than 36 tokens per second. The setup demonstrates how Apple’s unified memory architecture and MLX framework can be used to run large AI models locally. Meta is making Muse Spark Open available through API platforms including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. The model weights are also available through platforms including Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models.

extraction.body: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) model designed for coding, complex reasoning and tasks that require multiple steps. The company says the model can run on a desktop setup using two Apple Mac Studios powered by M5 Ultra chips, making it possible to use an advanced AI model locally rather than relying only on cloud services. As stated by the company in its official announcement, Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters, with 42 billion active parameters, and supports a context window of 1 million tokens. Developers can access the model through several AI platforms or download its weights to customize it for their needs.Meta Muse Spark Open: Features and capabilitiesMeta said Muse Spark Open is designed for long-running tasks, complex software development and agentic AI workflows, in which a model can carry out multiple steps towards a goal.The model is natively multimodal, meaning it can work with different types of information. It has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active, and a context window of 1 million tokens. A large context window allows a model to process a substantial amount of information in a single interaction.Meta said it tested the model on tasks involving software development and video editing. In one test, the model was used to make bug fixes and add features to Ice Cubes, an open-source Mastodon client, before building the application. In another, it worked with DaVinci Resolve to review video footage frame by frame, identify suitable moments and crop clips into a vertical format.The company also said the model includes optimised GPU kernels that deliver kernel-level speed improvements of 1.03 to 3.95 times on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. Meta reported a 3% overall speed improvement on AMD MI350.How to access Muse Spark Open AI modelMeta says Muse Spark Open is available through AI inference platforms including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Developers can download its model weights through Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models. The model supports inference engines such as SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Developers can also customise it using PyTorch.For local use, Meta has optimised Muse Spark Open for Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio through the MLX framework. According to the company, two Mac Studios can work together to provide enough unified memory to hold the model.Meta said it has added safety training to the open-weight version and evaluated it under its Superintelligence Scaling Framework. The company said the model met the safety thresholds required for release.The model is being released under the Muse Model License, which allows many developers to use it for free but includes limited commercial terms. Its weights are available through the Muse Spark Open collection on Hugging Face.You use AI every day.

extraction.body: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight artificial intelligence model that can run locally on Apple’s latest M5 Ultra Mac Studio computers, marking an unusual collaboration between the two technology companies. The model has been optimised to run across two Apple Mac Studios using Apple’s MLX machine learning framework. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the collaboration on X, writing that “Muse Spark Open – weights releasing today – runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple.” Apple CEO John Ternus responded to Zuckerberg, saying it was “amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk.” Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active at a time. It also has a 1-million-token context window and is natively multimodal, meaning it can process text, images, video and audio. Meta says the model has been built for coding and agentic work, including long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering and multi-step reasoning. How Muse Spark Open runs on Apple Mac Studio The Apple connection is significant because a model of this size would normally require data-centre infrastructure. Meta says Muse Spark Open can run on a desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, with each machine configured with up to 512GB of unified memory. Apple’s MLX framework allows the model to be distributed across the two Macs, with the machines connected using high-speed communication. Apple has also published technical details on running Muse Spark Open across multiple Mac Studios. Meta describes Muse Spark Open as its “most capable US open-weight model to date”. Open-weight models make their trained parameters available to developers, allowing them to download, run and adapt the models rather than accessing them only through a cloud-based service. The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture, activating only 42 billion parameters for each token rather than all 816 billion at once. This helps make the model more practical to run despite its overall size. Meta says Muse Spark Open has been tested with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, on software engineering tasks, including making bug fixes, adding features and completing a full build of an open-source Mastodon client. The company also tested it with DaVinci Resolve, where the model was able to review footage and identify and crop sections of video. Apple’s testing found that a cluster of four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open could generate more than 36 tokens per second. The setup demonstrates how Apple’s unified memory architecture and MLX framework can be used to run large AI models locally. Meta is making Muse Spark Open available through API platforms including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. The model weights are also available through platforms including Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models.

extraction.body: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) model designed for coding, complex reasoning and tasks that require multiple steps. The company says the model can run on a desktop setup using two Apple Mac Studios powered by M5 Ultra chips, making it possible to use an advanced AI model locally rather than relying only on cloud services. As stated by the company in its official announcement, Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters, with 42 billion active parameters, and supports a context window of 1 million tokens. Developers can access the model through several AI platforms or download its weights to customize it for their needs.Meta Muse Spark Open: Features and capabilitiesMeta said Muse Spark Open is designed for long-running tasks, complex software development and agentic AI workflows, in which a model can carry out multiple steps towards a goal.The model is natively multimodal, meaning it can work with different types of information. It has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active, and a context window of 1 million tokens. A large context window allows a model to process a substantial amount of information in a single interaction.Meta said it tested the model on tasks involving software development and video editing. In one test, the model was used to make bug fixes and add features to Ice Cubes, an open-source Mastodon client, before building the application. In another, it worked with DaVinci Resolve to review video footage frame by frame, identify suitable moments and crop clips into a vertical format.The company also said the model includes optimised GPU kernels that deliver kernel-level speed improvements of 1.03 to 3.95 times on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. Meta reported a 3% overall speed improvement on AMD MI350.How to access Muse Spark Open AI modelMeta says Muse Spark Open is available through AI inference platforms including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Developers can download its model weights through Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models. The model supports inference engines such as SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Developers can also customise it using PyTorch.For local use, Meta has optimised Muse Spark Open for Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio through the MLX framework. According to the company, two Mac Studios can work together to provide enough unified memory to hold the model.Meta said it has added safety training to the open-weight version and evaluated it under its Superintelligence Scaling Framework. The company said the model met the safety thresholds required for release.The model is being released under the Muse Model License, which allows many developers to use it for free but includes limited commercial terms. Its weights are available through the Muse Spark Open collection on Hugging Face.You use AI every day.
